By: Paulanne Simmons

January 28, 2025: There’s nothing particularly new about a play based on correspondence between two friends (one can’t help thinking of A. R. Gurney’s Love Letters}. But Michael Griffo’s warm, evocative language and the excellent acting in this two-hander make Pen Pals, currently playing at Theatre at St. Clement’s, truly special.

The two correspondents are Bernadette and Margaret, who are brought together during their high school years curtesy of an innovative social studies assignment.  Bernadette, who already calls herself Bernie, soon christens Margaret “Mags.” But this is only the beginning of an epistolary friendship that supports, entertains and occasionally challenges the two girls as they become young ladies and mature women.

The two women are not only worlds apart geographically (Bernie lives in New Jersey, and Mags lives in Sheffield,  England). They are also quite different emotionally and intellectually. Mags Is shy and quiet. She loves to read.  Bernie is noisy and outspoken. She can only get through Jane Eyreby picturing Jane as her worst enemy at school.

But together they navigate all life’s major milestones, from their first kiss, through marriages and childbearing, along with all the joy and sorrow that comes with them. They don’t always understand or agree with each other’s decisions. Bernie is sometimes judgmental but doesn’t like being judged. Nevertheless, in the end their desire for friendship always prevents them from breaking the bond that is so essential in their lives.

The play features a rotating cast of formidable actors, and director Suzanne Barabas wisely does not interfere or distract from their talent. Jessica Parks has set the stage minimally. Mags has a writing desk; Bernie has a kitchen table. Music and sound effects are only used when necessary and appropriate.

The afternoon I saw the show, Ellen McLaughlin played Bernadette and Mary Beth Perl played Margaret. Both were so completely absorbed into their characters and attuned to each other their stories leap out of their letters and take on a life of their own. 

At a time when written communication has been reduced to an impersonal email or a brief text message, it is good to see the power of the written word so splendidly portrayed.

Pen Pals ***
Theater St. Clements
423 W 46th St.
Photography Russ Rowland

Runs through Feb. 9

By: David Sheward

January 24, 2025: In recent decades, the theatergoing public has had a love/hate relationship with Jerome Kern and Oscar Hammerstein II’s Show Boat. When Florenz Ziegfeld first produced it on Broadway in 1927, it was regarded as an epic breakthrough in musicals. Unlike the frivolous European-influenced operettas which preceded it, the score and the plot were fully integrated. Hammerstein’s book addressed issues of social consciousness, ushering in a new era of character-driven shows, with Hammerstein’s later collaboration with Richard Rodgers, Oklahoma!, leading the way. Based on Edna Ferber’s novel of show-folk traveling down the Mississippi, Show Boat addressed the controversial topic of racism and miscegenation, but only tangentially. The main story focuses on the syrupy romance between gambler Gaylord Ravenal and innocent Magnolia Hawkes, daughter of the riverboat captain. The show’s antiquated depiction of its African-American characters led to protests during Harold Prince’s 1994 Broadway revival. Audiences were still in love with the beautiful score, but had trouble swallowing the stereotypical characterizations.

David Herskovits has tackled this dichotomy head on in his re-imagined adaptation for Target Margin Theater (where he is artistic director), Show/Boat: A River, now in a short run at NYU Skirball as part of the Under the Radar Festival. The ten-member ensemble play multiple roles, sometimes switching races and genders. Kaye Voyce’s stark set features two entry ways cut into a scrim with the words “White” and “Black” crudely drawn in reverse letters. The production opens with the house lights on and the company broadly demonstrating Hammerstein’s racially charged dialogue, complete with the exaggerated gestures they would use in the “meller-dramers” the fictional company plays on the show boat stage. When they are assuming Caucasian roles, they don sashes with the work “WHITE” on them. This forces us to confront the brutal discrimination of the period (late 19th century into the 20th) and transforms the nostalgic valentine to a romantic past into an unflinching portrait of a merciless era. This approach is most effective when the secretly mixed-race but passing-for-white singer Julie (a moving Stephanie Weeks) is forced to reveal her true ethnic identity. She removes her sash and with her white husband Steve (beautifully bass-voiced Edwin Joseph) leaves the showboat by the “BLACK” exit.

Another interesting and arresting re-interpretation occurs in the second act, also involving Julie. Now reduced to an alcoholic wreck after Steve has left her, Julie is headlining a Chicago nightclub. After a stunning rendition by Weeks of Kern’s “Bill,” she discovers Magnolia (a sweet-voiced and tender Rebekkah Vega-Romero) is also destitute after Gaylord has flown the coop and desperately needs a job. In the original, Julie nobly sacrifices her own position by going on a binge, leaving her spot in the show open for Magnolia. In Herskovits’ staging, Julie hears Magnolia’s audition of “Can’t Help Lovin’ Dat Man o’ Mine,” a song identified with the black community, rips off her “W” for white button (they switch from sashes to buttons in the second act) and exits the theater in disgust. This bold staging suggests Julie recognizes the white appropriation of African-American music and quits the biz in protest. The irony is doubled near the end of the show when Weeks returns as Kim, Magnolia and Ravenal’s daughter and a star on white-dominated Broadway, and sings “Why Do I Love You,” her parents’ love song, like a 1950s rock-and-roll ballad, echoing the theme of cultural appropriation. Dan Schlosberg did the amazing orchestrations and Dionne McCalin-Freeney the intricate vocal arrangments. Both are also listed as music director. 

There are other startling moments such as the appearance of two Confederate gun-toting rubes, played for comedy in 1927 and in the 1936 movie version, but seen as racist menaces here, and a stirring arrangement of “In Dahomey,” originally a novelty number set in a racist exhibit at the Chicago World’s Fair, but in Herskovits’ version, an anthem to racial pride.

Unfortunately, these insightful sequences are combined with conventional renditions of the material and we get a mixed bag of traditional and progressive. It’s entertaining but confusing. Herskovits should have gone further in his radical re-interpretation of an established classic.

The cast does its best to balance the contrasting styles of performance. In addition to marvelous musical moments from Weeks, Vega-Romero, Joseph, and Philip Themio Stoddard as a virile, charismatic Ravenal, Alvin Crawford delivers a deeply-felt “Old Man River,” and Caitlin Nasema Cassidy amuses with a tart “Life Upon the Wicked Stage.” Temidayo Amay lends depth to several roles including the comedy-relief Frank. Steven Rattazzi is a lovable Captain Andy, Suzanne Darrell a strong Queenie, and J Moliere a sharp-tongued Parthy.

This Show/Boat offers much food for thought and many pleasing musical sequences, but fails to come together under a unifying vision.

Jan. 15—26. Running time: two hours and 30 mins. including intermission. nyuskirball.org.

Show/Boat: A River ***
Target Margin Theater at NYU Skirbal
566 LaGuardia Place, New York
Photography Greg Kessler

By: Isa Goldberg

November 5, 2024: In 1996, as we know, the landmark musical Rent at New York Theatre Workshop rocked the world of musical theater. Through its diverse cast of actors and its portrayal of impoverished artists in the East Village during the AIDS crisis, Jonathan Larson’s work forever changed the way people think about musicals.

Currently at NYTW, the musical We Live in Cairo follows the lives of six bohemian youths from February 2010 through the events leading to the Arab Spring in April 2011. As the story unfolds into the aftermath of the uprising, the audience witnesses its impact on their lives both collectively and individually.

Despite the hardships they face, their need to be seen, heard, and understood drives a fundamental message about empathy. In a program note, the cast expresses their intent, stating, “And when we are loved may we allow each other the dignity that is all of our birthright.”

As a production, Cairo is highly impactful. Placing the musicians on stage, as in Rent, while portraying endangered youths seeking love in an unforgiving land brings immediacy to our own politically polarized time.

Opening the show, Nadina Hassan as Layla delivers “Midnight in Cairo,” a reflective song about her fears as an artist and as a young woman. Lost late at night, she searches for the music studio where a new boy she met is singing. On the street, she encounters Fadwa (Rotana Tarabzouni), a young revolutionary whose life and soul lie at the heart of this story.

At the studio, Layla watches Fadwa’s friends perform a political satire about President Mubarak. Beckoning his disenfranchised citizens to “have fun,” he invites them to enjoy a popular Egyptian pastime—a few days at the beach resort, Sharm El Sheikh. Wearing a massive mask (designed by Raphael Mishler) that broadens his presence, Mubarak appears as a comic puppet head, gleaming with ambition. Portrayed by John El-Jor (who also plays Karim), Mubarak is a violently gyrating, corpulent figure whose greed and indulgence are apparent. Ann Yee’s vivid choreography, ending with a Presidential striptease, establishes the show’s energy and grit.

The production incorporates archival footage of Mubarak on television pleading with students for mercy, grounding the actors’ performances in the revolutionary spirit of the time. With this ensemble leading us into Tahrir Square, we sit on the edge of an election that means more to this nation than any other event.

David Bengali’s projections bring throngs of people into the square, where the actors sing, dance, and chant, “EL SHAAB YUREED ISQAT EL NIZAM!” (“the people want to bring down the regime”). Impressionistic in style, it’s a highly emotional scene that ultimately leads the audience to Mubarak’s fall from power.

In Act II, the revolutionary youths celebrate the end of his reign in an inspiring ballad sung in harmony, “I WAS ONE PERSON / WHO HAD AN IDEA / WHO MADE IT WORDS / AND SOMEONE HEARD / SOMEONE HEARD.” It’s truly rousing; however, Act II also highlights the litany of political crises that followed Mubarak’s fall.

Ultimately, this musical is not solely about politics, although it explores these thoughtfully; it’s about the people—the protestors—and how that political atmosphere affected their lives. It speaks to the loss of humanity as well as the need for unity.

Rotana Tarabzouni, outstanding in her revolutionary spirit, shines as Fadwa, a woman who surrenders her life but never her ideals. Her performance is both genuine and powerful. Ali Louis Bourzgui, as Amir—the Catholic man who falls in love with Layla, a Muslim—serves as the troupe’s beloved troubadour, while Michael Khalid Karadsheh as his brother Hany goes beyond empathy. This ensemble, bound by love and framed by political and social taboos, underscores the power of the people.

Set in a free-flowing space by Tilly Grimes, the production includes a live orchestra with strings and a keyboard on one side and, on the other, a bohemian hangout that transforms into exterior environments as the troupe leads us along. It’s their integrity and unity that director Taibi Magar clearly respects.

With a book, music, and lyrics by the young duo, The Lazours, the production shows us what promise truly means.

We Live In Cairo *****
NY Theater Workshop
79 E 4th St, New York, NY 10003
Photography Joan Marcus

By: Samuel L. Leiter

November 5, 2024: There was a time, not that long ago, when productions of Romeo and Juliet,Shakespeare’s tale of two passionate, star-crossed, young lovers, was conventionally staged to reflect some romantic historical period, often with lavish costumes and sets. Such productions culminated in the hotblooded, veristic Old Vic revival of 1960, direction and sets by Italian master Franco Zeffirelli, starring 26-year-old Judi Dench as Juliet and 24-year-old John Stride as Romeo. Seeing it when it came to New York’s City Center in 1962, with 24-year-old Joanna Dunham replacing Dench, I was totally blown away by the exquisitely poetic realism of the acting, directing, scenery, and costumes (by Peter J. Hall). 

The sense that one was in the hot and dusty streets of 14th-century Verona, and that the sword-bearing men in tights and the women in corseted gowns (or gamurra) were real, not actors, was made even more palpable in Zeffirelli’s enormously popular 1968 movie version, starring the 17-year-old Leonard Whiting and the 15-year-old Olivia Hussey. This proximity to the actual ages of the play’s romantic teens, combined with its authentic Italian settings (many scenes being shot in actual period-correct locales) and costumes, and a still memorable theme song, helped bring the tragedy to life so vividly that the film has remained an unmatchable depiction, despite multiple later screen versions (including the 1996 Leonardo DiCaprio-Clare Danes version titled Romeo + Juliet, like the revival reviewed below). 

So effectively did Zeffirelli recreate a world of Renaissance beauty, it would seem, that many subsequent  stagings, both here and abroad, chose to abandon the “costume drama” approach and modernize the characters, their behavior, their appearance, and even their language. In a way, such productions of Romeo and Juliet were reversing history, making the play into West Side Story, again and again, with the battling Capulet and Montague families reconsidered as contemporary street gangs.

Over the past decade or so, since 2013, there have been four New York productions of Romeo and Juliet, two of them—including the one directed by Sam Gold now at the Circle in the Square—on Broadway. All have been designed in some version of modern dress, each with its consequent creative innovations (read: gimmicks), and each vulnerable to critical slings and arrows. 

That, however, hasn’t kept Gold’s version from being a palpable hit, filling every seat with excited young audiences, presumably drawn by the presence of 20-year-old British TV star Kit Connor of TV’s “Heartstopper” and 23-year-old Rachel Zegler, who played Maria, the Juliet equivalent, in the recent movie remake of West Side Story. The theater’s downstairs lobby has been turned into a stuffed animal fairyland for teens still into such things, and there’s even a voting information station. So many girls were present when I went that the line to the ladies’ room, tripling in on itself like a string of sausages, looked like a record breaker, even before the play began!  A few of the bolder young ladies, some splaying their fingers over presumably shocked eyes, bashfully invaded the men’s room to save time. 

Gold’s staging is packed with hopefully original directorial choices, many having been seen before, even in the three other local revivals. The script has been severely cut, removing such scenes as Romeo’s confrontation with Paris (Gían Pérez) at the Capulet tomb, so it matches “the two hours traffic of our stage” (plus a lengthy intermission, probably to accommodate all those juvenile pishers). Paris also was removed from this scene in the 2013 Off-Broadway staging. The most important characters who don’t appear at all are Romeo’s parents. With a company limited to 10 actors, many roles are doubled and tripled, not to the play’s advantage. (The 2015 Off-Broadway revival struggled even more, with only five actors.) The least successful, or, should I say, most illusion-busting, example is the casting of trans actress Tommy Dorfman as both Tybalt and the Nurse, each distractingly eroticized.

Envar Chakartash’s costuming, much of which suggests a world of egregious teen excess, often makes no sense. Although there are costume changes, it’s still not always possible to differentiate one character from another played by the same actor. Some costumes are simply bizarre, Dorfman’s female Tybalt, for example, being dressed in a sexy white bustier. With her shaggy, bleached blond hair unchanged, Dorfman wears a spangled bra-like top as the trampy-looking Nurse. Both her roles look like Madonna wannabes. And, while they suit Gold’s conceptual goals, neither comes close to being a convincing stage character in the play’s world. It’s impossible, for example, to imagine that Juliet’s conservative parents would allow her governess-like nurse to gad about like a floozy. 

Similarly, Paris, described by Lady Capulet, Juliet’s mother, as “the gallant, young, and noble gentleman,” is turned into a clown so ridiculous looking, it makes you wonder if Lady Capulet is myopic. This noble suitor is tastelessly garbed in the baggiest of below-the-knee shorts, and an oversized, brightly colored, too-large shirt worn over a t-shirt on which are the words “Gift of God.” If you’re familiar with the play, such anything-for-a laugh or just-to-be different folderol will drive you batty. The uninitiated will have to fend for themselves until such time, if they’re lucky, they see something truer to Shakespeare’s intentions.

With minimalist scenery designed by the collective called dots, the play is presented in the full round, a relative rarity at the Circle in the Square where a U-shaped arrangement is more common. The show does everything it can to goose up the performance for a younger audience. It’s hard to escape the feeling that the audience, regardless of age, is being patronized. For the rooms in Juliet’s bedroom, we get a mattress that, much of the time, hangs suspended in midair (not unlike the 2013 Broadway revival), serving also as the balcony for the famous love scene. At one point, a large, disc-shaped section of the floor opens like a flip phone to create a floral-covered area, one half raised on a slant; looking more suited to A Midsummer Night’s Dream, itspurpose/locale remains uncertain.  

Jack Antonoff has composed the youth-oriented music, from heavy-on-the-beat, rave-like dance music to a couple of pop-style tunes. Sonya Tayeh is responsible for the movement and choreography the music inspires. A sample of the original lyrics in a song performed by Paris includes, “I TELL THE BEST IT WAS FINE/CAN’T FUCK UP THE FEELING.” Such musical support activates the energetic younger characters, Juliet herself piping in, mic in hand, with the ballad “Man of the House,” its lyrics including: “HOW SWEET/YOU’RE THE MAN OF THE HOUSE TO ME/I WATCH YOU FROM THE WINDOW/WHERE I SEE/THE GOOD IN YOU/THE GOOD IN ME.” It takes chutzpah to insert such lyrics into a play by Shakespeare, but there they are. I refuse, however, to comment on the present-day profanities dropped into the actual dialogue, as if to assure the audience that the bard is really dope. 

Shakespeare rarely stints on the violence, of course, and Romeo + Juliet offers plenty, much of it dependent on hand-to-hand fighting (crafted by Drew Leary). Tybalt, Mercutio’s killer, meets his maker at Romeo’s hands by strangulation. There’s enough blood to go around, though, requiring that Tybalt’s own hands, having become incarnadined, remain so, incongruously, when Dorfman switches roles to play the Nurse.

The actors, for the most part, are supple and personable, and they generally speak Shakespeare’s lines with understanding if not poetic grace or distinctive characterization. Connor makes an intensely dramatic Romeo, his energy and focus consistently on the right track, despite a tendency to shout too much. Zegler’s slight physical presence, set off by her short shorts, allows her to look almost like Juliet’s age of 13, but her line readings typically skim rather than delve. Her speech before taking the sleeping potion, for instance, sounds more like rhetorical fancies than a child’s frightened thoughts about what could go wrong. 

Surprisingly, the standout performance is not from any of the leads, be they Tybalt, the Nurse, Mercutio (Gabby Beans, who also plays the Chorus, Friar Lawrence, and the Prince), or Benvolio (Taheen Modak, who doubles as the Apothecary). Instead, it comes from Capulet, portrayed by Sola Fadiran (Camelot), who also plays Lady Capulet, although it’s not always easy to discern husband from wife.  His scene when he denounces his recalcitrant daughter, however, is so boomingly ferocious it inspires a deserved round of applause. The great Chris Cooper was similarly dominant in this secondary role in the 2013 Broadway version.

For those interested in comparing some of the elements in this revival of Romeo and Juliet with its most recent predecessors,here are my reviews of the three that preceded it: Condola Rashid and Orlando Bloom, Broadway, 2013; Elizabeth Olson and Julian Cihi, Off Broadway, 2013; and Elise Kibler and Taylor Mayer, Off-Broadway, 2015.

Romeo + Juliet **1/2
Circle in the Square
1633 Broadway, NYC
Through February 16, 2025
Photography:  Matthew Murphy + Evan Zimmerman

By: Samuel L. Leiter

November 3, 2024: Regardless of how familiar you’ve previously been with Nicole Scherzinger, the lead singer of the unusually successful, early 2000s’ girl band The Pussycat Dolls, you’ll never get her out of your head once you’ve seen her eye-popping beauty, heard her ear-popping voice, and observed her slender physical emotionality as Norma Desmond in the revival of Sunset Blvd. (as it’s now being spelled) at Broadway’s St. James Theatre.

Premiered in London in 1993 and New York a year later, the musical was revived on Broadway only seven years ago, in 2017, starring Glenn Close. The current version, running two hours and 20 minutes, comes from its hit London production, with Scherzinger directed by Jamie Lloyd to within an inch or her expressive life. She stops the show with its two best-known numbers, “Just One Look” and “As If We Never Said Goodbye,” belting these power ballads out of the St. James like Aaron Judge home runs leaving Yankee Stadium. They bring a roaring audience to its collective feet for several minutes of ecstatic applause acknowledging the arrival of Broadway’s newest diva.

Unfortunately, unless you prefer a hyper-jacked star performance, suppported by dramatic lighting and live videography, to narrative drive, thematic interest, character interaction, and emotional depth, you may discover that this Sunset Blvd.  (music: Andrew Lloyd Webber; book/lyrics: Don Black, Christopher Hampton) favors innovative staging over emotional involvement. (Which isn’t to deny that the 2017 version didn’t have similarly serious problems.) 

This means that Lloyd Webber’s lush, semi-operatic score—especially in Scherzinger’s roof-shaking renditions—is often used more to bludgeon you with its theatricality than to evoke under-your-skin empathy. Scherzinger’s Norma may be brilliantly executed, but it’s a feat more technical than heartrending. Still, you’ll surely be anxious to see her in whatever she does next. 

Norma, of course, is the former silent movie star largely forgotten by Hollywood made into an iconic figure in Billy Wilder’s 1950 film classic of the same title about Hollywood’s famously cruel treatment of its aging treasures. Verging on madness, she’s seeking a “return” (she despises the word “comeback”) to cinema glory under director Cecil B. DeMille with a script she’s written for herself to star in as a 16-year-old Salomé. As if to highlight just how loopy her idea is, Lloyd introduces an imaginary, identically dressed Norma doppelganger in the person of the much younger dancer (Hannah Yun Chamberlain), who often floats about to suggest the Norma that was to the one that is.

To polish her hopeless script, Norma inveigles down-on-his luck, flat-broke screenwriter Joe Gillis (Tom Francis), who wanders onto her decaying mansion’s grounds when fleeing a couple of tough guy bill collectors. The interplay of Norma’s illusions and the reality of Hollywood filmmaking result in Joe’s demise, which isn’t a spoiler, since his corpse at the opening instigates the story that we follow as he recounts it from beyond the grave.

Barefoot and wearing just a black, silk slip, Scherzinger never covers her glorious raven hair with a fancy turban an image associated with previous productions. She plays Norma with such dramatically deranged overstatement, singing while waving her graceful arms around in serpentine gestures, that the closest analogue I can think of is Vampira. Not that her predecessors didn’t put their thespian pedals to the metal; they, however, at least looked like glamorously fading idols, not still ravishingly gorgeous sleepwalkers freely wandering about the loony bin.

It’s an impression made even stronger by the humongous closeups of her face, whose prominent cheekbones loom like the Himalayas over her exotic features. (Could these closeups be Lloyd’s ironic comment on Norma’s famous line, “Mr. DeMille, I’m ready for my close-up”?) Scherzinger carries off her portrayal stunningly but her overly stagy exaggerations cut into much of Norma’s vulnerability. 

Although set in 1949 Hollywood, as a projection informs us, Lloyd’s method is to abandon any pretense of capturing a visual reflection of time and place in favor of Soutra Gilmour’s essentially period-neutral, black clothing, highlighted by touches of white,worn on Gilmour’s usually bare, black, mostly propless stage, fitted with a giant movie screen. You won’t be seeing this Norma making a grand entry on a towering staircase. 

Jack Knowles’s lighting is striking, his beams often piercing more stage fog than you’ll see on any London day. A moment of color, when the background suddenly turns a blazing red, is unforgettable. Such effects, along with Nathan Amzi and Joe Hansom’s black and white video design and cinematography, conjure a noirish impression of Wilder’s film world. Especially impressive are the several ensemble scenes shown in silhouette.

If anything, Lloyd’s stripped-down approach surely has saved bundles compared to the costs of the more elaborate versions that preceded it, reportedly preventing them from making money. His approach has an expressionistic, dispassionate feel. The 16-member ensemble’s precisely executed movements—especially under Fabian Aloise’s often frenetic choreography—often feel robotic, with the four lead actors, even in two-character scenes, tending to face the audience rather than each other. The images on the screen usually focus on faces, sometimes in such tight closeups that you see little more than an eye. 

Technically, the most impressive moment occurs when Act Two opens purely via video, with Joe Gillis (or is it his actor Tom Francis ?) singing “Sunset Boulevard” upon appearing from a dressing room at the apex of a remarkably labyrinthine backstage world. The camera captures him from in front  as he walks down staircase after staircase, stopping on his way to peer into his costars’ dressing rooms (supplied with Sunset Boulevard in-joke props), nodding to a cardboard cutout of Lloyd Webber, and making his way outside to W. 44th Street. He passes along the theater’s front, with all its show signage, halting in front of a poster of himself (Joe or Tom?), before proceeding back inside, down an aisle, to join the company on stage. Eye-catching as it is, what this meta potpourri of self-referential directorial cleverness – reminiscent of a scene in the Michael Keaton movie, Birdman – has to do with Sunset Blvd. or the lyrics Tom/Joe is singing, beats me; the audience eats it up, of course, but it seems little more than a gratuitously pretentious intrusion. 

The 25-year-old Francis, who bears a strong resemblance to Jeremy Allen White of “The Bear, won an Olivier Award for his performance in London, as did Scherzinger, whose nomination for a Tony would seem to be a lock. He’s solid, attractive, and talented, but he’d be more convincing as the cynical Joe if his life-weary treads looked a bit more worn. Scherzinger, at 46, looks much younger, but she’s only four years off Gloria Swanson’s age when that former silent movie star created Norma in the movie. Without a deeper motivation provided for her abandonment, you’re forced to imagine one of your own.  

In this connection, two years ago, then 92-year-old former movie star Nancy Olson [Livingston], who played script editor Betty Schaeffer, Joe’s secondary romantic interest, in the film, was interviewed by the New Yorker about her just published memoir, A Front Row Seat: An Intimate Look at Broadway, Hollywood, and the Age of Glamour. “‘Gloria Swanson was the one person on that set who understood what a great film this was, because she understood the truth of it,’ Livingston said. ‘She was beautiful, but she was over the hill for them.’ Not everyone wanted the truth. Wilder screened the movie for Louis B. Mayer, the producer who co-founded M-G-M. Livingston said, ‘When it was finished, Billy was walking up the aisle and Louis B. Mayer says, ‘How could you do this to us?’ And Billy said, ‘Go fuck yourself.’” 

The musical’s two other featured cast members are Grace Hodgett Young as Betty, and David Thaxton as Max Von Mayerling, Norma’s manservant and one-time Svengali of a director. Both are fine singer-actors but neither leaves much of a footprint. Erich von Stroheim made Max one of the most haunting elements film history, but Thaxton never comes close to capturing his aura of mystery, danger, and secrets. Then again, could anybody?

Of course, Nicole Scherzinger isn’t Gloria Swanson. She’s Nicole Scherzinger, and that should be enough for anyone, closeup or longshot.

Sunset Blvd. ***
St. James Theatre
246 W. 44th Street, NYC
Open run

By: David Sheward

November 3, 2024: Delia Ephron’s memoir Left on Tenth: A Second Chance at Life is a moving, heartbreaking account of the author’s reclaiming love and life after losing a beloved husband, finding a second amour, being diagnosed with leukemia and cancer, and dealing with endless phone prompts with Verizon. It’s funny, moving, and joyful. However, the material does not translate well from the page to the stage in Ephron’s theater adaptation now at the James Earl Jones. Perhaps it would have worked better on film since many of the scenes are so brief, some lasting only a few seconds. Though the subject matter is shattering, given that it really happened, the evening is strangely unmoving since Ephron’s script and Susan Stroman’s rapid-paced direction move so quickly we barely have time to register any reaction to the stage Ephron’s travails. The surface-oriented performances by top-billed Julianna Margulies and Peter Gallagher don’t help. They both look good, but fail to delve deeply into their roles. It’s like a Reader’s Digest version of the book.

The title refers to Ephron’s Greenwich Village residence on Tenth Street, beautifully realized by set designer Beowulf Borritt’s book-lined abode which transforms to a number of settings and Jeanette Oi-Suk’s painterly projections of an idealized NYC. The play begins with writer and recent widow Delia (Margulies) explaining to the audience her frustrating struggles with Verizon which cut off her Internet access when it disconnected her late spouse’s land line.  She writes a New York Times opinion piece on her conflict with the communications giant, which leads to her re-connecting with forgotten old beau Peter (Peter Gallagher), a Jungian psychologist. There’s lots of direct-address monologues, reading of emails, and many instances of the characters telling us what’s happening, but very little showing of Delia coming back to life and the couple falling in love. The tone shifts from romantic comedy to stark drama as Delia’s diagnosis—frighteningly similar to that received by her late sister Nora—is revealed. 

The only sequences that truly move the emotional needle occur when Delia is at her absolute lowest. Stroman finally slows the action down and Margulies is able to deliver a truly shattering sense of her character’s pain and desperation. From her hospital bed, Delia curses Peter and pleads with him to let her die. In a brilliant stroke of stagecraft, Stroman has a tear-inducing Barbara Cook ballad play as Peter struggles to up Delia’s oxygen levels, with her falling numbers projected on the back wall. Performances, direction, design, and music all come together to convey Delia’s life-and-death climb and Peter’s loving attention. Too bad this comes towards the end of the play’s one hour and forty minutes.

The admirable Peter Francis James and Kate MacCluggage are reduced to scene-shifters as multiple friends, servers, doctors, and nurses, wheeling on gurneys, placing and removing appetizers and desserts, providing exposition. The pair, listed in the Playbill as “Featured Actor and Actress” do manage to create flashes of credible individuals with the aide of Jeff Mahsie’s versatile costumes and Michael Buonincontro’s character-defining wig and hair design. James is moving as a gay neighbor who survived AIDS and MacCluggage has several moments of connection as several of Delia’s supportive girlfriends. The dogs Nessa Rose and Charlie deserve mention for obeying commands and inspiring “awws” from the audience. The play similarly seeks to trigger Pavlovian responses of empathy, but fails to truly earn them with a quick, shallow summarizing of Ephron’s original.

While Left on Tenth is based on truth and aspires to be a life-affirming tear-jerker, Sam Gold’s sexy, rock-infused production of Romeo + Juliet is a great work of fiction and succeeds in tearing our hearts out. Left on Tenth is neat, sleek, and orderly, while this R+ J reflects the insanity of youthful passion. Like Gold’s previous Broadway Shakespearean outings—his hodgepodge King Lear with Glenda Jackson and his jumbled Macbeth with Daniel Craig and Ruth Negga— his R + J is messy, but there is a method to its scattered madness. 

The star-crossed lovers and their families are out of control, fiery, and the production mirrors that white-hot intensity and disorder. The rock-club set by the design team of dots is littered with stuffed animals of all sizes, like a high school on Valentine’s Day, reflecting the characters’ immaturity and their discovery of first love. The costumes by Enver Chakartash are hip and form-fitting while Isabella Byrd’s lighting creates romantic and ominous environments and moods. Halfway through the first act, the central floor flips open to reveal a carpet of flowers. Juliet’s bed descends from the flies for Romeo to chin himself up on. All of these elements contribute to the head-rush atmosphere of impulsive love, beyond the puppy stage and also impulsive violence which tears the lovers and their families apart.

Identities and genders are fused and confounded. The same actor, Sola Fadiran, plays both mother and father to Juliet. (This was the only role-doubling that didn’t work for me. Fadiran makes a credible blustering Lord Capulet, but minces swishily as the Lady. He didn’t always differentiate between the two, so it got confusing at times.) The transgender actress Tommy Dorfman plays the Nurse and Tybalt, bring out the masculine and feminine aspects of each character. The Prince of Verona, Mercutio and Friar Laurence are played by the estimable Gabby Beans, who acts as a narrator of the action, guiding us along passion’s paths. She also provides juicy japery as Mercurio and sage sturdiness as the Friar.

The leads are perfectly cast. Hunky Kit Connor makes an emotionally tortured and athletic Romeo, bounding from platform to platform and from infatuation to pure love. Rachel Zegler, who played the Juliet role in Steven Spielberg’s remake of West Side Story, is equally fierce, but also conveys the heroine’s precocious intuitive intelligence. She rocks Jack Antonoff’s original song “Man of he House” and provides the rock-solid center of this youthful and exciting Romeo + Juliet. 

An interesting side note: the audience at the Wednesday matinee attended for Left on Tenth was mostly female, white and older. By contrast, Thursday night’s Halloween performance of R+J was attended by a much younger, more diverse crowd. It was exciting to see a youthful audience getting enthused about Shakespeare.

Left on Tenth **1/2

By: Carol Rocamora

October 31, 2024
Teddy bears? 
Really?!!!

What are all those warm and fuzzy teddy bears doing in the lobby of the Circle in the Square theatre? Not a few, but dozens of them…
My guess is that they’re setting the stage for an unconventional (to say the least) production of Shakespeare’s Romeo & Juliet. 

Director Sam Gold has done it again – he’s chosen a bold, gutsy, unapologetic approach to a classic, one that clearly appeals to a young audience.  This interpretation is his most extreme – and surprising – thus far.  From the moment you descend the escalator into the theatre lobby, you’re immersed in the pounding sound of rock music and the sight of stacks of those teddy bears piled sky high.  Once in the theatre, you’re greeted with the sight of ten young performers on stage, gyrating, dancing, romping, sporting, cavorting their hearts out.  High above one end of the empty oval stage, an electric keyboard produces deafening rock music; on a platform above the other end, a giant teddy bear lies in wait of its star occupant: actor Kit Connor, who will play one of the most winning young Romeos you’ve ever seen.  

In short, it’s a spectacle you’d hardly expect in a production of a Shakespeare play – certainly not a tragedy like Romeo & Juliet.   And that’s just the disarming effect that director Gold wants.

Indeed, the exuberance of youth – embodied by this kinetic ensemble – is the defining energy that pulsates throughout Shakespeare’s “two-hour traffic” on this stage.   You might say that the ten-member company itself is the “star” of the show” – and the embodiment of the director’s equitable approach to casting.  With the exception of Romeo (Kit Connor) and Juliet (Rachel Zegler), the other company members each play multiple roles, irrespective of gender. For example, the talented Gabby Beans – who provides a metatheatrical introduction to the other performers at the top – plays The Friar, The Prince, and Mercutio.  Even more conspicuous and attention-grabbing is the double-casting of Tybalt and the Nurse, both played by Tommy Dorfman.  And the most unusual casting choice is Sola Fadiran, playing both Capulet and Lady Capulet.

Gold’s vision for the production has both challenged and inspired his collaborators.  Foremost is the creative movement direction and choreography by Sonya Tayeh.  The young company moves and grooves together like one large, living phalanx, resulting In the most dynamic, exciting ensemble movement on stage that I’ve seen in a long time.   This wonderful human spectacle takes place on a stage in-the-round designed by “dots” that constantly surprises – morphing from an empty floor to splitting in half and revealing a bed of flowers upon which the lovers lie.  Instead of a balcony for Juliet, a bed is lowered from the theatre ceiling where Juliet awaits her beloved (and athletic) Romeo – who manages to leap from the floor, swing from the elevated bed, and hoist himself high enough to give her that anticipated kiss.  The costumes by Enver Chakartash are equally imaginative – I especially loved the green gossamer shirt that Juliet wears on her clandestine wedding day. 

Speaking of Romeo (“oh Romeo”), Kit Connor gives a heart-throbbing interpretation that has the audience utterly enchanted (yes, he has the advantage of a native British accent, but it’s supported by superb, skilled, passionate acting).  As Juliet, Rachel Zegler has the advantage of having played Maria in Stephen Spielberg’s film adaptation of West Side Story, so the role is like her second skin.  

As you can see, there’s a lot going on in Gold’s interpretation that is both distracting and at the same time disarming, asking an audience to eschew traditional interpretations of Shakespeare’s most familiar masterpiece and look at it through fresh, younger eyes (hence, the teddy bears, I suppose.) 

Frankly, I could easily have done without those fuzzy bears – as well as the songs which Juliet sings (although they are tuneful and she delivers them beautifully).  There is enough background music throughout, composed by Jack Antonoff and played on the electronic keyboard by Sarah Goldstone, to provide the contemporary texture that director Gold is seeking.

Ultimately, the joyful energy of this gifted young ensemble is infectious, and the audience (ranging in age from nine to ninety on the matinee I attended) is swept up and away.  Apparently, Gold is trying to emphasize the temporal joy of adolescence, and its descent into the inevitable tragedy of fate.  Director Gold has put his whole heart into this youthful interpretation – and it shows.  In comparison to his recent darker interpretations (of The Glass Menagerie, for example) or his eclectic King Lear, it’s as if the energy of youth, inspired by Romeo & Juliet, has infected him as well, and freed him to conjure up this joyous version.

Romeo and Juliet ***1/2
 By William Shakespeare, Directed by Sam Gold, now playing at the Circle in the Square Theatre.

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 29, 2024: My name is Sam and I am not an alcoholic, recovering or otherwise. However, in Another Shot: A New Play by Spike Manton and Harry Teinowitz, at Off Broadway’s Linney Courtyard Theatre, many people are (when they’re not recovering drug addicts), both the six we see and the numerous unseen ones whose names and years of sobriety are projected on the walls during breaks in the action. 

Another Shot is the latest contribution to the well-meaning, inspirational, educational/cautionary genre widely classed as temperance dramas. It also belongs to the subject grouping focused on the rehabilitative process of group therapy, which ranges from substance abuse to a variety of psychological problems: The White Chip, Bill W. and Dr. Bob, Good for Otto, Slave Play, The Fears,and the just-opened Rawshock are among those that come to mind.

Although the therapy process shown is much the same, you won’t hear “AA” or “Alcoholics Anonymous” mentioned because the five rehab patients and their therapist (herself a recovering junky), are at a private facility. It’s designed by Beowulf Borrit as an institutional green, cinderblock-walled, basement space, furnished with a small desk, a couch, a couple of arm chairs, and metal folding chairs set up as needed. Mextly Couzin lights it efficiently, Alejo Vietti supplies the everyday costumes (which change often as time goes by), Stefania Bulbarella projects suitable images on the walls surrounding the three-sided setup, and Daniel Baker & Co. handle the sound, including voiceovers of the various unseen substance abusers whose names flash by.

Another Shot is mostly based on the actual experiences of former Chicago sports radio host (ESPN 1000) and stand-up comic Harry Teinowitz, whose last name is never spoken. A Windy City celebrity well-known for his convivial guzzling, he lost his broadcasting job after he was arrested for drunken driving in 2011. The play, written with Spike Manton, and first seen in Chicago as When Harry Met Rehab in 2021, focuses on the middle-aged Harry (Dan Butler), a feisty, zinger-slinging guy in a White Sox jacket (the real Harry is an avid Cubs fan). When we first meet him, he insists to the facility’s therapist, Barb (Portia), that despite his arrest, he has no need of rehab, and he’s only there to save his job. It’s an arrogant refrain he repeats until circumstances prove how being a high liver doesn’t guarantee a healthy liver.

Stepping into and out of the action to narrate its progress, Harry—whose jokey attitude toward his situation will eventually come back to bite him—takes us on a journey through his eight weeks of rehab in what the publicity calls “a comedy that’s intended to take sobriety seriously.” It’s an experience made possible only because of the warm support of his rehab buddies, whose mutual assistance and friendship is so crucial to each of them, the need for such assistance forming the play’s chief theme. 

We never learn, though, why this facility—which isn’t free—seems to have only five patients, all of them required to attend three hours of group therapy daily. It’s anything but a prison, though, as the patients are allowed to leave the building for necessities, which they occasionally do by going to a nearby Walgreen’s. This allows for some incidental suspense, as when one of the characters can’t be found.

What little overarching drama the play has is centered on how and if the characters—with our eyes chiefly on Harry—will achieve sobriety. (The play was originally conceived of as a solo piece before Manton convinced Teinowitz to add additional characters, all fictional.) The sole female patient, Andrea (Samantha Mathis), is a five-time married, five-time rehab recidivist. Vince (Chiké Johnson), another recidivist, is a sturdy African American family guy whose seeming stability belies the truth. Isaiah (Gregg Mozgala) has issues of veracity regarding his relationship with his girlfriend. And, the problems of the youngest, George (Quentin Nguyen-Duy), center on his estrangement from his mother. (Both Butler and Johnson were in the Chicago version, with Melissa Gilbert of “Little House on the Prairie” as Barb.) 

While I’m sure many recovering substance abusers, or those with close relationships to such persons, will be affected by Another Shot (a well-dressed elderly woman near me kept dabbing her eyes), those whose only experience of such situations is from countless movies and plays will likely find it more of the ho-hum same. The attempt to find humor in these barely interesting, moderately clichéd, people and their conflicts, while admirable, would be better appreciated if the comedy were funnier. Audience laughter when I went was mild and sporadic. 

Under the upbeat direction of Jackson Gay (who also staged the Chicago original), Dan Butler (Bob “Bulldog” Briscoe on TV’s “Frasier”) holds the swift-moving 90-minute piece together with a solid performance and good comic timing as the initially obnoxious radio personality, with a riposte for every occasion. The single-named Portia is both demanding and warm as the motherly therapist and amateur magician (she pulls off at least one trick) who has all the frightening facts and statistics about addiction at her fingertips. The remaining ensemble members are all passably convincing, if unmemorable, at portraying their schematic characters.

Perhaps I’m wrong, but Another Shot seems too unsurprising to make much of an impact on theatergoing New Yorkers who don’t have an immediate connection to its subject. A few highlight moments aside, its presence serves a purpose more social than artistic. I expect it to have a life in places where its message can do the most good.  

Another Shot ***
The Pershing Square Signature Center/Romulus Linney Courtyard Theatre
480 W. 42nd Street, NYC
Through January 4, 2025

By: Isa Goldberg

October 29, 2024: If you can’t imagine Nicole Scherzinger as Norma Desmond in Sunset Blvd., head over to the St. James Theatre. This uncanny production—a reimagining of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s classic musical—hails from London’s West End. The fact that one could even find a sober reason to perform it in this post—trying to be post—Hollywood apocalypse seems odd. 

Fortunately, this production is as odd as anything on Broadway. Poles apart from the show’s 1997 Broadway premiere, in which Glenn Close portrayed a Nora of vulnerability and complexity, Scherzinger’s performance is an over-the-top vamp. To be even more perturbing, her faded movie star image is distinctly diabolical, quite a bit like M. Night Shyamalan’s reborn doll in The Servant.

As a surrogate for some heightened form of humanity, her Norma is quite the dramatic artist—a severe one, and without a grain of frailty. Of course, she is the centerpiece of director Jamie Lloyd’s satire of this twisted, dystopian Hollywood society. Ironically or not, his staging is such an utter mimicry of contemporary Belgian director Ivo van Hove that it, too, begs the issue of originality.

Known for his avant-garde theatricality, including the use of cameras to magnify the actors and to bring live video footage into the stage story, van Hove came to the attention of New York audiences around the turn of this century. In a 2007 production of Molière’s Misanthrope at the New York Theater Workshop, for example, he had the actors go out into the street and collect garbage while the video camera portrayed them to a curious audience.

Here, Norma’s love object, Joe Gillis, in an understated, albeit triggering performance by Tom Francis, walks out of her Beverly Hills mansion onto the avenue, Broadway, thronged by his fans. It is as if he were walking on the Via Della Rosa; only in this case, he’s heading to Schubert Alley.

Still, the most stinging, sarcastic video footage here links this musical about a nest of Hollywood vipers to van Hove’s reimagining of Luciano Visconti’s The Damned, about the rise of the Third Reich. As staged in Paris by the Comédie-Française, the camera follows the lead actress running through the grand staircase, passing statues of the giants—Hugo, Racine, Molière, ad nauseam. She runs and runs, trying to hang on to her fortune.

Only backstage at the St. James, our lead, Joe, heads to the stage through stairwells with “no smoking” signs and union placards in narrow hallways. It’s not quite the Comédie-Française, and Joe Gillis is not escaping the theater of World War II, but it’s a peak experience anyway, and it’s accompanied by Andrew Lloyd Webber’s propulsive, repetitive rhythms.

Humorous and jarring as it is, the heavy-handed style can get relentless and repetitive. It’s not difficult to get the point, but beating it to death apparently replicates the kind of abuse for which Hollywood is best known. In addition to the camera, the central character in every Hollywood movie, Grace Hodgett Young, portrays Bette, an aspiring filmmaker and Joe’s love interest. Her beautiful voice carries the sheen of innocence. On the other hand, David Thaxton, as the aged Max, paints a picture of jaded that is more one-dimensional by nature.

In his Broadway debut, Olivier Award-winning choreographer Fabian Aloise achieves a style of choreography that is clearly concept-driven. In an opening ballet, Hannah Yun Chamberlain, as young Norma, portrays her as she must have appeared, and so beautifully, early in her career. However, the very next scene features a lineup with the chorus pitched vertically on the stage and perpendicular to the audience, immediately creating a sense of juxtaposition and opposition.

Later scenes bring the lives of these young actors and studio types into playful dancing and social engagement in a way that looks natural—like a departure from choreographed movement.

Jack Knowles’ lighting and Adam Fisher’s sound design are indispensable to the horror movie effects in which the production abounds. A screaming Psycho-like image certainly stands out.

But for the rigorous put-downs, Scherzinger’s self-mockery, and Lloyd’s well-placed stabs at all of his predecessors, there is no excuse. It’s as funny as anything you can imagine, with a perspective that brings a sense of relief.

Sunset Boulevard ****
The St. James Theatre
246 West 44th Street
Between 7th Avenue & 8th Avenue
Runs approximately 2 hours and 35 minutes, including one 15-minute intermission. The show begins promptly at curtain time.

By: Paulanne Simmons

October 27, 2024: At the very beginning of Thornton Wilder’s 1938 play, Our Town, the Stage Manager, who narrates, tells us, “The name of the town is Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire – just across the Massachusetts line: latitude 42 degrees 40 minutes; longitude 70 degrees 37 minutes. The First Act shows a day in our town. The day is May 7, 1901. The time is just before dawn.” This kind of specificity makes the current revival directed by Kenny Leon not only misguided but also somewhat troubling. One can’t help but wonder why he made certain choices and what they have to do with this play.

A while later, the Stage Manager adds, “Religiously, we’re eighty-five percent Protestants, twelve percent Catholics; rest indifferent.” But Leon’s version of the play begins with a mixture of Muslim, Jewish and Christian prayers. Who is singing these prayers and why? 

When the  Stage Manager describes the population of Grover’s Corners, the only minority groups he mentions are a  few Slavs and some people who come from somewhere in the Mediterranean. But Leon’s Grover’s Corners is as diverse racially as It is religiously. The Gibbs family is played by African American actors: Billy Eugene Jones is Dr. Gibbs, Michelle Wilson is Mrs. Gibbs and Safiya Kaijya Harris is their daughter, Rebecca. The Webb family is played by white actors: Richrd Thomas plays Mr. Webb, Katie Holmes plays Mrs. Holmes, Hagan Oliveras plays their son, Wally,  and  Zoey Deutch plays their daughter, Emily. 

Perhaps more peculiar, when Emily and George decide to marry, no one in either family bats an eye. It’s nice to know that early 20th century New Hampshire was so progressive. And just to make sure we know Leon has left no one out, the milkman, Howie Newsome (John McGinty), is deaf and communicates in sign language, which is apparently understood by all the others in town. Surely, that would have made Wilder happy.

Even Dede Ayite’s costuming is inconsistent. While the townspeople are dressed appropriately for the time, Emily wears a mid-thigh skirt that would probably have gotten her sent home from school. And on the day of Emily and George’s wedding, George comes to visit his bride-to-be wearing a gold chain around his neck and a wifebeater covering his manly chest.

Beowulf Boritt is an excellent scenic designer. But why was he brought in to supply the scenery for a show that specifically calls for no curtain and no scenery?

Compelling acting might have saved the production somewhat. But Jim Parsons’ Stage Manager seems more like a snarky television newscaster than a crusty New Englander. Sykes and Deutch never get George and Emily’s love to rise above a childhood crush. And even Jule Halston, who is generally wonderful, turns the gossipy Mrs. Soames into a joke. 

Our Town is not a comedy. It is not social commentary. It is not about diversity. It is, in Wilder’s words, ”an attempt to find a value above all price for the smallest events in our daily life.” To do this he has “set the village against the largest dimensions of time and place.”

Wilder was trying to reach the universal through a detailed description of the specific. When the audience has no idea where or when the action takes place Our Town is lost in space. 

As the director, Kenny Leon has every right to his unique interpretation of the work. But here Leon seems to be not so much working with Out Town as working against it. If Leon has problems with certain aspects of this play, perhaps he would do better to devote his talents and energy to another play more to his liking.

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 25, 2024: The minute I walked in the door at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre to see director Kenny Leon’s much-lauded revival of Thornton Wilder’s beloved 1938 classic, Our Town, I could sense that something was off. 

Beowulf Boritt’s lovely set, visible on the curtainless stage, shows a huge wall of wooden planks, with a door set into it up center. Overhead hangs an exquisite mobile of lantern-like amber instruments (atmospheric lighting by Allen Lee Hughes), like a galaxy of stars in the firmament. Striking, yes, but, as anyone familiar with the play knows, Wilder, influenced by traditional Chinese theater, insisted there be no scenery, only whatever spare furnishings are needed for seating and the like. Typically, the show is set against a brick wall, with sawhorses used to create tables. 

As becomes clear, the set and lights, however attractive, prove less effective than the simpler approach asked for by the playwright. For example, when Emily and George talk to each other from their windows, Wilder has them do it while standing high up on ladders; here, they open small windows high on the rear wall to converse, a far more literal approach. In the cemetery scene, traditional performances arrange rows of chairs on the stage floor for the buried townsfolk. In this production, they’re arranged across a multi-tiered platform placed upstage for just this scene. An added feature is the two small seating areas at either side for onstage audience members.

Then the cast enters (many from the aisles, as during the play proper), singing the Hebrew prayer, “Shema Israel,” which morphs into Muslim and Christian themes in an arrangement by Abraham Jam called “Braided Prayer.” Jewish and Muslim music? Our Town is a play whose narrator, the Stage Manager (Jim Parsons, Mother Play), clearly notes all the religious denominations present in Grover’s Corners, the fictional, idyllic New Hampshire town where the play is set at the turn of the 20th century; although ecumenical in spirit, he never once mentions any non-Protestant or Catholic place or form of worship. Grover’s Corner was not New York City.

Obviously, regardless of logic or historical accuracy, Leon seeks to emphasize a universal theme of man’s spiritual unity in Grover’s Corners, also demonstrated in his interracial casting, despite Wilder’s failure to mention any races other than white. It’s a choice that, anachronistic as it is, serves to remind us that things in America were not always thus, and, in fact, still aren’t (the Black population in New Hampshire now is about 10%). Just as in my own production of Our Town at Brooklyn College in 1996, the Gibbs family of Dr. Gibbs (Billy Eugene Jones), Mrs. Gibbs (Michelle Wilson), and Rebecca Gibbs (Safiya Kaijya Harris) is African American, while the Webb family of Mr. Webb (Richard Thomas), Mrs. Webb (Katie Holmes), Emily (Zoey Deutch), and Wally (Hagan Oliveras) is white. 

Such a choice, more acceptable today than in the 1930s—and perhaps even expected in this age of colorblind casting—doesn’t necessarily extend to things like the costumes, designed by Dede Ayite. These are represented by a puzzlingly eclectic mélange of clothes from throughout the 20th century. They’re presumably aimed at capturing the timelessness of Wilder’s subject matter, made so evident in those expository, Wikipedia-like speeches about the town delivered in Act One. But the play’s timelessness is made far more apparent by replicating the extremely explicit world of 1901-1913 Grover’s Corners crafted in Wilder’s immortal poetic prose. His words want us to recognize how things were at a specific time and place, based on which we can ponder the larger thoughts expressed in the Stage Manager’s monologues.

So, amid the several garments very loosely suggestive of early 20th-century garb, we get—to cite just a few—a tank-top undershirt for the muscularly pumped-up George Gibbs (Ephraim Sykes) when visiting the Webb house on the morning of his wedding; a flared miniskirt showing off the graceful gams of Emily (Zoey Deutch); and, among other questionable choices, a navy-blue ensemble of sleeveless, close-fitting shirt and skintight shorts for newsboy Howie Newsom (John McGinty). 

Most egregious of Leon’s directorial decisions is having the Stage Manager serve almost like a dedicated station master determined to keep the trains running on time. Parsons, speeding up his familiar sing-song Texas lilt, moves the action along as if he needed to get us out of the theater so we could make it home on time. At an hour and 40 minutes, this must be the fastest Our Town on record. When Acts One and Two end, the Stage Manager simply announces the fact (omitting Wilder’s mention of an intermission), and we chug immediately into the following scene. In a rare nod to Wilder’s wishes, all hand props are mimed, so I wouldn’t have been surprised to see Parsons sneaking peeks at an imaginary pocket watch. Since Wilder has a stage direction directing the Stage Manager, hearing a train’s whistle, do just that, maybe Parsons did it and I simply missed it.

This fleet pacing infects much of the acting, robbing many speeches and conversations of the kind of down-home, cracker barrel honesty required. Everyone seems more intent on performing than being, and the dialogue often sounds more rhetorical than natural. Despite a cast including highly regarded actors, not one managed to touch any of my emotional buttons. The well-loved talents of one my favorite comic actresses, Julie Halston, playing the minor role of Mrs. Soames to the max, are duly noted by Leon’s finding ways—watch that special on her in the cemetery—to highlight her stylishly coiffured, blonde presence. These, however, only draw attention to their obviousness. 

Of all the performances, Jim Parsons’s is the biggest letdown, lacking in relaxed gravitas, kindness, believable practical and philosophical wisdom, and folksy, humorous sincerity. Zoey Deutch’s rendering of Emily’s big speech about clocks ticking is no better than many of those I’ve heard over the years from student actresses. Richard Thomas and Katie Holmes, polished as they are, fail to capture the everyday reality of Mr. and Mrs. Gibbs. Similarly, the Gibbs family—Michelle Wilson, Billy Eugene Jones, Ephraim Sykes, and Safiya Kaijya Harris—is more actorish than convincing.

Kenny Leon’s directorial intrusions and innovations include making Howie Newsome deaf and having multiple characters communicate with him in ASL. He also has the local historian, Professor Willard (Shyla Lefner), described by Wilder as “a rural savant, pince-nez on a wide satin ribbon,” played with little conviction as a fashionably dressed, modern woman. And when the Congregational Church choir sings under the command of the demanding, alcoholic Simon Stimson (Donald Webber, Jr.), they do so with the harmonic perfection of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir.

Regardless, Wilder’s brilliant playwriting shines through, reaffirming my widely held conviction that this is America’s greatest play. The scene at the cemetery, even if not as well-acted as I would have hoped, is masterfully crafted and moving, even if not as deeply as is possible. And while the acting remains ordinary and the scenic design rubs against Wilder’s grain, you can’t deny the show’s inherent appeal, or Leon’s ability to fetch attention. 

This production may not be my vision of Our Town, but from what I’ve heard, it may very well be yours.

Ethel Barrymore Theatre
243 W. 47th Street, NYC
Through January 19, 2024

By: Carol Rocamora

October 24, 2024: If there’s one reason why you should go to see Sunset Boulevard, the radical revival now playing on Broadway it’s this: to see how far the contemporary theatre dares to go in reinterpreting a classic.

Jamie Lloyd’s brutally aggressive reinterpretation of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s
1993 musical is not a revival –quite simply, it’s a hijacking. Webber adapted it
from the 1950 film starring Gloria Swanson as the fading, self-deluded silent
film star and William Holden, the captive co-author of a film she’s written that
will hopefully gain her a comeback from Hollywood oblivion. The musical has
had numerous London and Broadway productions featuring multiple star
performers and eminent directors. Though plagued by mixed reviews and
legal issues, nonetheless it has garnered multiple awards in both capitals, and
made its way around the globe and back again.

The latest production – Lloyd’s – opened in London in 2023 and this month on
Broadway. If you’ve seen the original or any previous revivals, frankly, you’ll
find it almost unrecognizable.

From the moment you enter the St. James theatre, you know you’re in for an
extreme experience. Fog fills the darkened auditorium and the pre-show
house lighting is close to non-existent, creating an atmosphere of anxiety and
menace. That threatening atmosphere is intensified many times over once the
show begins, where the production values take over the musical itself. The
predominant palette is black, featured in the empty set (designed by Soutra
Gilmour) and a huge cast in contemporary costume. The dramatic lighting
(designed by Jack Knowles) piercing the darkness only intensifies it.

But the most dramatic feature of all is a huge upstage wall, almost 30 feet high,
upon which are projected the monstrous-sized faces of various cast members
in key dramatic scenes. (The overpowering video design and cinematography
is credited to Nathan Amzi and Joe Ransom.) These giant images overpower
the actors on the stage itself, and the effect, frankly, is terrifying. It’s as if
you’re watching a horror movie.

In the center of this nightmarish atmosphere is the protagonist, Norma
Desmond, the fading film star sequestered in her Los Angeles mansion, long
out of touch with reality. As played with a feral ferocity by Nicole Scherzinger,
a brilliant singer/dancer, she displays a stunning talent – but as a performer
in her 40s, dressed in a black slip throughout (no shoes), she seems too young
and vital to play a has-been. (Past Normas have included Patti LuPone, Betty
Buckley, and Glenn Close, all at an older age). It’s almost as if Jamie Lloyd has
made the show into a goth star vehicle for Nicole Scherzinger, who is far from
the fading star that Norma Desmond was in the original.

Scherzinger, who is also a member of the pop group “The Pussycats,” plays the
role at the feverish pitch of a performer in a rock concert. In fact, that’s the
over-all ethos of this over-the-top production, which tumbles into the
darkness of the grotesque.

In contrast, the supporting cast is more believable. As Joe Gillis, the young
man she seduces to help her with the script she dreams of presenting to Cecil
B. DeMille, actor Tom Francis is more credible, as is Grace Hodgett Young, a
young studio writer whom he meets and grows to love. As Max von
Mayerling, David Thaxton is appropriately creepy as Norma Desmond’s
constant protector/body guard.

One actor deserves special mention. As the voice of DeMille’s enormous head
which appears in shadow on the upstage screen, Shavey Brown is especially
effective in augmenting the nightmarish quality of the production. For me, it
was the most terrifying moment of the show. It almost appeared as if he were
ready to devour the life-sized Norma whole.

Jamie Lloyd’s daring as a director of revivals is well known to New York
audiences. His Cyrano at BAM in 2022 featured James McAvoy playing that
classical role without an exaggerated nose – again, on an empty set, which
seems to be Lloyd’s frequent directorial “signature.” His 2023 revival of A
Doll’s House on Broadway starred Jessica Chastain in a stylized production
wherein the actors sat on a revolving stage (empty, again, of scenery), that
kept turning. In both instances, without sets or costumes, Lloyd’s
productions permitted the words of the classics to be the “stars of the show.”

With his Sunset Boulevard, however, Lloyd has stunned us into numbness
with his grotesque, “noir” aesthetic. Thankfully, we can still hear the soaring
orchestrations of David Cullen & Andrew Lloyd Webber (even though the
volume is deafening).

Every theatre season features revivals of the classics. Last year there were
multiple Uncle Vanyas in London and New York; this season, we’ll have a
revival of Romeo & Juliet at Circle in the Square and an imported King Lear
from London starring Kenneth Branagh. What choices will these directors
make? Will they honor the original in any way? Or will they overpower it?

Sunset Boulevard **
St. James Theatre on Broadway.
Music by Andrew Lloyd Webber, Book and Lyrics by Don Black
and Christopher Hampton and Directed by Jamie Lloyd.

By: Paulanne Simmons

October 21, 2024: Nancy Harris’s The Beacon, now at the Irish Repertory Theatre, is certainly an ambitious play. In fact, the playwright juggles so many plots and subplots many in the audience may become confused about exactly what point she’s trying to make.

Beiv (the astonishing Kate Mulgrew) is a successful Irish artist who has apparently put her craft above her duties as a mother. Indeed throughout the play, she talks about art and what it means to her. Is this a play about art and the artist?

Not really. It soon becomes obvious that her son, Colm (Zach Appelman), a software engineer, who after a long time living in the United States, has come to visit with his American bride, Bonnie (Ayana Workman), is angry about a lot more than mild neglect.

It seems Colm’s father, Michael, had many years ago left the very same cottage where his mother now lives, taken a boat out in the middle of the night and never returned. Many, including Colm, believe Beiv was somehow involved in his death. So in some ways, The Beacon is a mystery, with a frustrated and angry son searching for the truth.

But wait, it turns out Colm, once had a long-running sexual relationship with his neighbor by the seashore, Donal (the amiable Sean Bell). Colm is still attracted to Donal, and Donal still loves Colm, even after repeated rejections. How does Bonnie fit into the picture? Is this the story of a closeted gay man and the pain he inflicts?

And what about Colm’s bride? She seems like an ordinary eager-to-please twenty-three-year-old, but is there something troubled and troubling beneath her naïve questions? What does she know about Colm? What does she want to know? How will the truth affect their relationship? Workman, who is unable to bring any depth to her character, leaves that a mystery.

Towards the end of The Beacon we are introduced to Ray (David Mattar Merten), a podcaster who wants to make hay out of the old scandal. Merten brings great energy to the part. But it’s not easy to figure out why he’s in the play at all.

Director Marc Atkinson Borrull, set and lighting designer Colm McNally and sound designer Liam Bellman-Sharpe have  worked together to keep us constantly reminded, through projections and the sound of the awesome sea, that this cottage, which Beiv is in the process of renovating, like all the people who live nearby, is at the mercy of the sea. Is this a play about man versus nature?

Whenever she’s onstage, Mulgrew  manages to keep this production engrossing. But by the end, when the playwright is trying to tie up all the loose ends, even God couldn’t keep it all together.

The Beacon ***1/2
The Irish Repertory Theatre, 132 West 22 Street.
Runs through November 24, 2024.  irishrep.org

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 19, 2024: The Mint Theatre has built a well-regarded reputation for finding long-forgotten plays and giving them polished Off-Broadway productions. Of course, not all prove worth the effort to bring them back to life. Most choices, usually from the American or British archives, are of plays that have only minor production histories in New York or London, but a few originally had respectable runs. One often wonders how much reading of so many abandoned scripts transpires before someone says, “Eureka! There’s gold in them thar plays!” 

I’m sorry to report, however, that the Mint’s current production, at Theatre Row, Sump’n Like Wings, by Oklahoma playwright Lorrie Lynn Riggs (1899-1954), is fool’s gold, perhaps made shinier by Riggs’s association with the great musical, Oklahoma!, adapted from his rarely revived Green Grow the Lilacs, given 64 performances in 1931 by the Theatre Guild. 

Lynn Riggs (Lorrie was rarely used) wrote close to 30 plays, including nine one-acts, but only a tiny handful of his full-length plays made it to New York stages, most being flops. Big Lake managed 11 performances Off Broadway in 1927; Roadside, seen on Broadway in 1930, also lasted 11 nights; Cherokee Night had two showings Off Broadway for an invitation-only audience in 1932; Russet Mantle, on the other hand, did rather well on Broadway in 1936, garnering 116 performances; The Cream in the Well, at the Booth, shut down after 24 showings in 1941; and 1950’s Borned in Texas, seen in 1930 as Roadside, lasted a week Off Broadway. 

Whatever promise Riggs may have possessed—Oklahoma! and, perhaps, Russet Mantle apart—it evaporated, although he does have his advocates. Based on this production of Sump’n Like Wings, at any rate, it’s hard to accept the views of those who claim this Great Plains writer’s poetic and dramatic gifts were the unsung equivalents of Tennessee Williams and Eugene O’Neill. The Mint, as per its mission, obviously thought there might be some treasure hidden in an oeuvre dominated by works either never seen at all or mostly produced outside New York. Sump’n Like Wings, written in 1925, for instance,had a single performance in Detroit and one in Brussels, of all places, in French! Reportedly, three New York producers took out options on it but never followed through.

Publicity for the play emphasizes that Riggs was a gay man of part Cherokee heritage. Although he addressed issues related to Native Americans in other plays, he doesn’t touch on them here, and whatever gay-related theme might be present is subliminal, if there at all. Like some others of his plays, this one is set in his home town of Claremore, Oklahoma, in the early 20th century, between 1913 and 1916, to be precise. Everyone speaks with a strong Sooner accent. It concerns people whose circumstances chain them from flying free (as suggested by the title). Within that context, sexual tension is present between lustful men and defensive women in a crude world where townsmen mingle with cowmen. In the play, impudent youths rebel against conservative adults, marital relations are strained, babies create crises, and protofeminist choices are made. Similar things can be found in other Riggs plays, like Russet Mantle. In fact, given that work’s warm reception nearly 90 years ago, it might have been a more suitable choice for revival.

Riggs sets his first five scenes (divided among three “episodes”) in the dining room, office, and upstairs hall of Claremore’s St. Francis Hotel for Ladies and Gents. The final scene takes place in a “light-house keeping room in Loomis’ Rooming House.” Perhaps for budgetary reasons, set designer Junghyun Georgia Lee’s spare design is little more than a pair of sidewalls with large entrance openings and a rear wall of horizontal wooden strips through which we view an occasional character against a nicely lit (by Isabella Gill-Gomez) cyclorama. Little differentiates one scene from another other than the rearrangement of the furniture, inspiring visual monotony and confusion.

Sump’n Like Wings focuses on three principal characters: Mrs. Baker (Julia Brothers), who runs the hotel dining room, a strict, socially conservative, middle-aged woman, who later becomes a religious zealot; her pretty, rebellious daughter, Willie (Mariah Lee), 16 when we first meet her, and 19 at the end; and the warmhearted, avuncular voice of reason, Uncle Jim Baker (Richard Lear), Mrs. Baker’s brother, who manages the hotel and buffers the conflict between Willie and her mother. 

Another rebel, a rambunctious young woman named Elvie Rapp (Lindsey Steinert), appears early on, promising to be a major character; once she’s served her purpose, though, she never returns. That purpose is to underline the theme of the need for freedom to pursue one’s personal path. This is symbolized by Elvie being jailed by Sheriff Beach (Andrew Gombas) to control her, only for her to snatch his keys and release all the inmates. 

What remains is the tale of Willie’s realization that the only way out of the psychological prison her overprotective mother has created is to run off with a married local swain, Boy Huntington (Lukey Klein), once he gets a divorce. Many viewers will immediately reckon the fate in store, not only for Willie, who returns home after two years with her baby, but for the child as well. When life with the overbearing Mrs. Baker proves untenable, Willie goes to live alone in a seedy rooming house populated by lubricious men. Ultimately, Willie’s forced to choose between living with her oppressive mother or facing life on her own.

Riggs’s clichéd writing might have been salvaged by quality direction, but director Raelle Myrick-Hodges’s contribution is uninspired, going little beyond an often slow-paced, paint-by-numbers approach to staging and characterization. With a few exceptions for honest, person-to-person dialogue, the actors, even the best of them, too frequently deliver their lines to the invisible fourth wall rather than to one another. This isn’t to deny that Mariah Lee is a good choice for Willie, who convincingly ages from a juvenile 16 to a matured, even hardened 19; or that Julia Brothers makes Mrs. Baker a sturdy maternal presence, with a couple of fierce moments; and that Richard Lear’s Uncle Jim, while sometimes too broad, has several fine scenes, as when he tries to convince his sister to let Willie move back in. 

The casting of a few others, though, is problematic. In the most egregious misstep, Lukey Klein, who plays the fellow with whom Willie elopes, lacks one iota of romantic chemistry, made more irritating by a piping high voice more appropriate to a prepubescent choir boy than a Lothario. Further, those actors who double as two characters—Mike Masters, Andrew Gombas, and Buzz Roddy—look and act pretty much the same in both, regardless of their costuming (by Emilee McVey-Lee), creating as much of a muddle as do the barely dissimilar settings. Those costumes, by the way, hint at the period much more than they mirror it.  

The other cast members are unremarkable, the interstitial action and chitchat—including a sleep-inducing song sweetly sung by a guest named Opalina (Leon Pintel)—uninvolving, and the comic bits unfunny. Hopefully, the Mint’s next offering will be sump’n better.

Sump’n Like Wings **1/2

Through November 2, 2024
