By: Isa Goldberg

October 18, 2024: In Thoreau and Emerson lie the roots of theater in America. So, it is blissfully discovered in Kenny Leon’s contemporary staging of Thornton Wilder’s Our Town.

By beginning with a concert of religious music – Jewish, Muslim, Christian, Gospel, etc. – the production builds a picture of a community in peaceful harmony.  Here in Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire, transcendentalism is an everyday practice. Its denizens value simple living, the land, nature, and the environment that sustains them. 

Early in the first act, the Stage Manager (Jim Parsons) opines, “Grover’s Corners…let me see…Grover’s Corners lies on the old Pleistocene granite of the Appalachian range. I may say it’s some of the oldest land in the world. We’re very proud of that.”

While in our own time, it might seem facetious to claim pride in the native lands that we have exploited and destroyed, Leon shrewdly introduces contemporary anachronisms that highlight the play’s nuances. 

In this blended cast, Dr. Gibbs is portrayed by Billy Eugene Jones, an African American actor well known for his work on Broadway. Even a quick Google search unearths the obvious: in 1900 only 1.3% of physicians in the U.S. were Black. Unfortunately, the casting demonstrates that not a lot has changed, as the 2023 data shows that African American doctors constitute only 5.7%  of the U.S. population. 

Most interesting in that respect is the casting of the romantic duo, George Gibbs and Emily Webb, on whom the story turns. Portrayed respectively by Ephraim Sykes (Ain’t Too Proud), and Zooey Deutch (“The Politician”) they are something of a humorous take on the couple in Grant Wood’s “American Gothic,” painted in 1930. The buff Mr. Sykes with his visible tattoos hardly passes for a sixteen-year-old farm boy, nor a twenty-something widow. Neither would Zooey Deutsch – a hot young screen idol – feel believable as the Farmer’s Wife. 

But the Photoshop effect of it all is transfixing visually and effectually. We accept them and their fate because they demonstrate what love can be in today’s world, even though intermarriage would not have been accepted in the early part of the 20th century.  More importantly, the way in which these lovers are framed, almost like puppets, cannot be overlooked, nor denied. 

Wilder, as his readers are happy to recall, explored the algorithms of life in Our Town as if these simple principles would tender a simple and clear purpose. There is respect for facts, and figures, and for scientific accuracy. As Professor Willard (Shyla Lefner) informs us, “The population, at the moment, is 2,642. The Postal District brings in 507 more, making a total of 3,149. Mortality and birth rates: constant. By MacPherson’s gauge: 6.032.”

Along with the statistician’s eye for truth, the palpable nature of these iconic town characters probes the audience to reflect on who we are, and what it means to be where we are. Such a divine moment occurs when Emily, returning from the grave to relive one day of her life, watches her father (Richard Thomas) bustle down the stairs saying, “Where’s my girl? Where’s my birthday girl?”

That deep connection between father and daughter is the moment we all truly wish for, yet seldom achieve. 

Creating this romance as it is happening – and so imaginatively – right in front of our eyes is the beauty of Our Town, and of this production in particular. The only props are chairs and all the actions are mimed. So, the act of creation is essentially in the hands of these auspicious actors. 

Delivering dairy products to people’s homes, John McGinty speaks in sign, voicing his good wishes to Mrs. Webb on the day of Emily’s wedding. Portrayed by Katie Holmes, Mrs. Webb is an unsentimental mother. She doesn’t encourage her daughter to dwell on how pretty she is, nor to seek admiration for it. But she is anything but dispassionate, blending into this ensemble with much aplomb.

As her husband and the editor of the town newspaper, Richard Thomas (John-Boy) brings an almost mythic quality to the sanctity of life in a small American town. Still, the actor is deftly understated.

In a cast of characters that speaks for itself, Julie Halston plays a surprisingly vocal Mrs. Soames. Along with the mellifluous Donald Webber Jr. as Simon Stimson, Willa Bost sings beautifully as the Townsperson.  

In addition, Michelle Wilson’s quiet portrayal of Mrs. Gibbs, the doctor’s wife, mother, and neighbor is perfectly iconic. The character – and the actor – appear almost selfless. 

Unto the stage directions, “there is no set,” – a command Beowulf Boritt resolves respectfully, and economically. Still, the painting of the town that the Stage Manager creates for us is so vivid and lifelike that it is just like going to the theater where you can see a scenic design of another world. 

Jim Parsons is wonderful to watch. His sense of timing, and his ability to  create each and every image so completely demands our joyful surrender. An actor with a breathtaking command of Wilder’s poetical writing, Parsons is completely alive in every moment, and in every word and gesture. 

The sheer ferocity of maintaining that energy with such exquisite grace throughout three acts without an intermission is a gift deserving of this great American play.

Our Town *****
Barrymore Theater, 243 W. 47th St., NYC. 
Running time: 100 mins. with no intermission. telecharge.com.
Oct. 10—Jan. 19, 2025.

By: Carol Rocamora

October 17, 2024: Kenny Leon’s extraordinary Our Town is more than just a revival – it’s a momentous event, one that unites us all in these contentious times.

Thornton Wilder’ s metatheatrical masterpiece (premiered in 1938) is familiar to us all – whether we performed it in high school (with or without the third act), or whether we marveled at Henry Fonda or Paul Newman or Spalding Gray or David Cromer who led their respective casts on and off Broadway over the years.  It’s part of “being an American,” whatever that means in these difficult moments.  But that’s just the point – director Kenny Leon reminds us what that means, and more: namely, at we’re all residents of the same town, that we’re all human, that we’re all participating in this extraordinary transcendent cycle of life and death and life again.

The first element that hits you in Leon’s inspired revival is the sheer magnitude of humanity on stage:  twenty-eight actors, led by a character called the Stage Manager (a commanding Jim Parsons) who narrates the story of our town in three cts.  They enter from offstage and from the back of the audience; on the set, they’re flanked by audience members on either side, seated in pews.  So when the musical soundtrack opens the show, featuring prayers from multiple religions, you know you’re part of a sacred, universal experience. 

In Act One entitled “The Daily Life”, set on the morning of May 7, 1901, the Stage Manager introduces us to all aspects of Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire, where the action takes place – population 3,149, with graveyard dating back to 1670. He invites us to meet the townsfolk – the Gibbs family and their son George (the father is a doctor); the Webb family and their daughter Emily (the father is a newspaper editor); the local policeman; the alcoholic church musical director and his choir members: and so on.  As we watch them eat their breakfast, go to and from school, do their work, fall in love, and so on, we realize that what we’re watching is not a play about specific characters, but rather about the  rituals  in life we all share and practice. 

It’s the job of the Stage Manager to guide us where Wilder is heading  – hence, the reference to death even as the play begins.  With every main character he introduces, he refers to their date of death – as if he’s living in their time and yet looking back on them from the future.  It’s an ominous dimension of the play, one that begins as a hint and crescendos as the play progresses.

Act Two: Love and Marriage, set three years later in 1904, centers around the ritual that everyone practices “before falling into the grave,” according to the Stage Manager (a reference to death again).   It’s the wedding of George and Emily after graduating from high school – which the entire town attends.

And then comes Act Three, Death and Eternity, set nine years later. It hits  you like a blow to the solar plexus.  Upstage on Beowulf Boritt’s striking set, a curtain rises suddenly to reveal a graveyard, where a number of those residents of Grover’s Corners (whom we met earlier) are seated before their tombstones.  After the Stage Manager explains who has died since Act Two and how, he prepares for us for the ultimate blow – a funeral for our favorite character, Emily, who has just died in childbirth.

Above the graveyard, Allen Lee Hughes’s shimmering lights hang like stars, paving the way from life to death and to life back again.  And that is where the miracle happens (only in the theatre).  Emily returns to earth to relive her 12th birthday – where she realizes what Wilder has been saying all along, through his characters: “You’ve got to love life to live life, and you’ve got to live life to love life.”  

According to Wilder’s specifications, there are no set elements or props.  The actors mime their prescribed tasks in exquisite detail.  It’s Wilder’s way of showing that ordinary life is truly extraordinary, indeed.

The inspired Kenny Leon directs a superb cast, including Zoey Deutsch as Emily, Ephraim Sykes as George, Katie Holmes as Mrs. Webb, Richard Thomas as Mr. Webb, Julie Halston as Mrs. Soames, Michelle Wilson as Mrs. Gibbs, and many others.  Together, they are one humanity, delivering the message that every moment in life should be treasured.  But when Emily asks the Stage Manager if people understand this message, he replies “No – the saints and poets maybe…” 

But thanks to Leon’s profound understanding of Wilder’s message, maybe now we will…

Our Town *****
By Thornton Wilder, directed by Kenny Leon, at the Barrymore Theatre, West 47th Street, through January 19.

By: David Sheward

October 16, 2024: Two new productions on and Off-Broadway feature a major male star best known for his work in media other than theater playing a world-renowned celebrity struggling with the forces of overwhelming fame, a rotting popular culture and his own colossal ego. Both leading men deliver credible performances and both plays attempt to address serious issues of media-mad society. One fails to live up to its noble intentions, while the other succeeds in presenting a complex, humorous and thought-provoking evening. The former is Ayad Akhtar’s McNeal starring Oscar winner Robert Downey Jr. at Lincoln Center’s cavernous Vivian Beaumont. The latter is Kenneth Lonergan’s Hold On to Me Darling with Oscar nominee Adam Driver at the more intimate Lucille Lortel.

McNeal certainly looks impressive in Barlett Sher’s dazzling, special-effects-laden production. Akhtar’s script deals with a narcissistic, Nobel Prize-winning novelist facing his own mortality and the encroaching dangers of artificial intelligence. Sher stuns us with a sleek, futuristic staging. The time is “the very near future” when three of the top volumes on the NY Times best-seller list are authored by AI. The cool, sterile sets by Michael Yeargan and Jake Barton, the eye-popping projections by Barton, and the impressive lighting by Donald Holder create a sci-fi, video-game universe fit for a Hollywood blockbuster. But the self-indulgent plot seems like an AI-generated melodrama extrapolated from the introspective works of Philip Roth.

After receiving a dire diagnosis from his stern doctor (solid Ruthie Ann Miles) to cut down the booze, winning that Nobel, and preparing for his latest work to be published, McNeal battles with his estranged son (overzealous Rafi Gavron), worried agent (brilliant Andrea Martin), and former lover (weepy Melora Hardin). Trouble is the explosive McNeal may have plagiarized the piece from his late wife (dead by suicide) and from the pervasive demons of AI.  

Akhtar does have some interesting and cogent arguments about AI and several other troubling trends in our screen-obsessed world. These are expressed in the sole gripping scene of the play—between McNeal and an antagonistic African-American woman journalist (a strong Brittany Bellizeare). Harvey Weinstein, Ronald Reagan, the Me Too movement, the dumbing-down of America and McNeal’s creed of truth above everything all figure in this stimulating exchange.  

Too bad it’s like an island of sane discourse is a sea of melodrama. Downey, Jr. exhibits his trademark bad-boy charm as the explosive author, but even he can’t make us care about the basically obnoxious author. Andrea Martin rescues her scenes with split-second timing and subtext-laden silent reactions. She turns a rapid telephone exchange with a stubborn publisher into a lesson in comedy. The remainder of the cast which also includes Saisha Talwar as the agent’s eager assistant, do their level best to bring life to this derivative and flashy play, but McNeal is a hollow retread of Roth’s washed-up, self-hating protagonist trope.

While McNeal attempts to analyze dangerous trends in our culture, Hold On to Me Darling actually does so through the lens of its hapless, filthy rich hero. Originally presented at the Atlantic Theater Company in 2016, Darling focuses on self-centered country-western superstar Strings McCrane, struggling to find happiness in the aftermath of his censorious mother’s death. Kenneth Lonergan’s nearly three-hour comedy-drama never drags in Neil Pepe’s solid-steel production (Pepe also directed the previous Atlantic staging). Adam Driver manages to make Strings sympathetic even though the character is constantly making impulsive decisions and leaving emotional wreckage in his glamorous wake. Speaking in country-western cliches, Strings is all id, driven by his immediate needs, regardless of the consequences.

Lonergan skillfully satirizes America’s glittering but empty celebrity culture as well as our national tendency to avoid moral responsibility as exemplified by Strings’ reckless behavior. Driver is simultaneously charismatic and pathetic, believably creating a star who could headline stadium concerts and Hollywood sci-fi epics. He’s not bad at singing or playing the guitar either. It’s understandable why people would be drawn to him, in spite of Strings’ erratic nature. 

Keith Nobbs’ needy assistant Jimmy, CJ Wilson’s down-to-earth brother Duke, and Adelaide Clemens’s innocent cousin Essie (all veterans of the 2016 production) and Heather Burns’ scheming girlfriend Nancy, all contribute layered and complex performances, each delivering their characters’ multiple motives. Though he only appears for a few minutes at the end of the play, Frank Wood has a devastating impact and unlocks Strings’ neuroses. Walt Spangler’s detailed, versatile set create a believable world of hotel rooms, feed stores and small-town dens in this penetrating and funny play from one of our most insightful dramatists.

Manhattan Theater Club offers another piercing drama on an Off-Broadway stage at City Center’s Stage I. Erika Sheffer’s Vladimir may evoke comparisons to last season’s Patriots, Peter Morgan’s harrowing drama of the rise of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin and the downfall of oligarch Boris Berezovsky. But, unlike Morgan’s piercing portrait of Russian power struggles, Sheffer keeps Putin off-stage and makes her title character a menacing, unseen monster. Like Patriots, Vladimir includes Boris Yelstin’s famous 1999 resignation as Russia’s president in favor of Putin who bathes his country in corruption and launches distracting wars. 

The focus of Sheffer’s script is on independent journalists Kostya (ribald and conflicted Norbert Leo Butz) and Raya (steely and striking Francesca Faridany), and on timid bookkeeper Yevgeny (sympathetic and moving David Rosenberg) who takes a surprisingly bold stand against Putin’s rotten regime. The action takes place mostly during 2004 right after the title character has been voted in for another term in a sham election. Kostya and Raya find their voices crushed and their lives threatened as the Russian state hurtles towards autocracy. Sheffer powerfully depicts the slow, incremental acceptance of Putin’s terroristic regime, directed with an adept hand by Daniel Sullivan. The parallels between Putin and Trump are subtle but unmistakable, as are the demonization of the Chechens with that of the Palestinians.

In addition to the sterling Butz, Faridany and Rosenberg, Erin Drake, Erik Jensen, Olivia Deren Nikkanen and Jonathan Walker offer sturdy support in multiple roles. Mark Wendland’s flexible set suggests a TV studio where Putin deceives his public with manufactured news, a striking metaphor for a dangerous administration and a warning for us Americans.

McNeal **

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 16, 2024: Kenneth Lonergan’s Hold on to Me Darling, seen at Off Broadway’s Atlantic Theatre in 2016, has returned, eight years later, to another Off-Broadway theatre, the Lucille Lortel. The star this time is the red-hot Adam Driver playing the red-hot country singer and movie star “Strings” Clarence McCrane, originally taken by Timothy Olyphant in a superior portrayal.

From among the 2016 artists Neil Pepe is once more the capable director; CJ Wilson again plays Strings’s half-brother Duke; Keith Nobbs returns as Jimmy, Strings’s obsequious assistant; Adelaide Clemens is back as Essie, who doesn’t deserve the way Strings treats her; and Walt Spangler recreates his turntable set, albeit in a smaller version. Tyler Micoleau is the new lighting designer and Suttirat Larlarb shares the costuming credit with Lizzie Donelan. Apart from Wilson and Nobbs, the actors are all new, and very good. Driver’s larger-than-life presence aside, the production seems much as I remember it from its earlier incarnation. 

I must declare up front, however, that I was unable to fully appreciate the show because, despite the cool weather outside, the air conditioning was on at full blast. We were seated in Row D, right side, directly beneath a blower sending ice cold air to the tops of our heads. When asked before the show if they could do something about it, the Lortel house management merely shrugged. The gentleman next to us in Row D simply left at intermission. One shouldn’t have to view, much less review, a show—especially a three-hour one—under arctic conditions. 

The premise of Lonergan’s (This Is Our Youth) comedy-drama, which, in this production,  I found less hilarious and moving than before, is simple. Strings is a vaguely Elvis-like, country-western idol and movie superstar (“the 3rd biggest crossover star in the history of country music”) involved in a big budget movie set in outer space while also booked to do a huge tour to promote his new album. The mama of this inveterate womanizer has just died and he’s so “tore up inside” he wants to move back home, give up his fame and riches, and become a good ole boy again, selling farming goods in his hometown feed store. 

Lonergan aims to satirize the excesses of our celebrity culture. However, more than I recall, his play’s three-hour length dissipates its vitality, especially as it’s more character- than plot-driven. Strings, the chief character, is a charming but unavoidably self-involved heel whose fame, talent, wealth, and skin-deep sincerity convince those around him to forgive his behavior. Will he or won’t he find redemption? By the end of the play, I’d lost interest in its outcome, unlike what I’d felt eight years ago.

As this inconsistent musician-actor—sometimes bright, sometimes dumb; sometimes earnestly kind, sometimes unintentionally cruel—Driver speaks with a downhome country twang not every word of which is clear. He’s unquestionably charismatic; his physical size—both clothed and unclothed—and unique presence seems almost too big for the Lortel’s stage. But even in Driver’s talented hands, Strings’s excessive emotionality, and the painful results on others of his eternally self-interested behavior, no matter how expertly portrayed, can grow disturbing over the play’s long stretch. Fortunately, this being a Lonergan play, it’s so abundant in cleverly crafted dialogue—zingers included—and character depiction, I can understand if others think it’s just as long as it has to be. 

Strings believes his success has cost him his humanity and that all that people see in him is the glitzy shell of who he really is. Women, he claims, want only to brag to their friends about having spent the night with him. As he tells his sycophantic PA, Jimmy, “How can they grab hold of a man who isn’t there? How can you touch somethin’ you can’t feel?,” words in which Jimmy immediately hears “a new song comin’ down the pike.” But Strings declares he’s finished with new songs; his mama’s passing has inspired him to abandon his career and to make it up to her for not having married, settled down, and raised a family like a normal person. Meanwhile, Jimmy, who surely has a yen for his boss, sets out silently to find String’s dad, who ran off when Strings was eight. 

Strings hates the publicity and prying into his private life; it’s part of a national celebrity-worshiping sickness for which he holds himself partly responsible. His moralizing, however, doesn’t stop him from serial seductions, which happen almost in spite of himself, as played out here in his relationships with two attractive women. 

First, there’s Nancy (a terrific Heather Burns), a self-deprecating (“I was raised with dogs and chickens”) yet smoothly manipulative masseuse he hooks up with after she gives him the Ambassador Grand Classic massage in his Kansas City hotel room. No sooner is Nancy in his clutches than Essie (Adelaide Clemens, ringing all the right notes) appears, his girl-next-door of a second cousin (twice removed) who, despite exercising her best judgment, isn’t able to resist him after they meet at his mama’s funeral. That’s also where Strings convinces Duke to go into the feed store business with him, a decision that incites a string of lawsuits that threaten to wipe out the star’s substantial assets.  

Spangler’s revolving set brings one small realistic set after another into view, from the hotel room, to Duke’s paneled den (which he calls “an ashtray with furniture in it”), to the funeral parlor where mama lies in rest, to Essie’s living room, to the quaint feed store. Micoleau’s versatile lighting provides just the right ambience for each, being particularly effective in the feed store scenes. And the new designers’ costumes work beautifully, from Strings’s casual black cowboy duds to Essie’s delicately feminine frocks to Buck’s farmer togs.

Lonergan’s comic dialogue garners many laughs, although my own laugh muscles—partially chilled by those arctic blasts—were more frozen than eight years ago. Strings lives his life on impulse, making almost everything popping out of his mouth a surprise. He and Duke demonstrate their Southern-fried creds with frequent expostulations of the “Jesus Christ in a downtown Memphis hair salon!” variety, and Duke recites a litany of feed store products that might almost sound poetic were it not so comically extensive. When Strings compliments Duke’s unseen wife, saying, “Now don’t fool yourself about that Ellie, old buddy. She is worth her weight in gold,” the grumpy Duke retorts, dryly, “Be quite a windfall if that was literally true.” And there’s a priceless bit about the “topless burka” Strings’s actress girlfriend wore in Afghanistan when feeding the hungry. 

The play has room for moments of feeling (most of them almost immediately blown up by an unexpected riposte). And you may not be prepared for a sentimental, anticlimactic scene in which veteran Frank Wood, as the long-lost dad (played by Jonathan Hogan in 2016), gives a subdued, heartfelt performance. Regardless of his cathartic reaction to his father’s visit, it doesn’t compensate for Strings’s earlier behavior, which, given his volatility, is just as likely to revert to familiar form later. 

For all that, there’s much to admire in Hold on to Me Darling. Just be sure to dress warmly and wear a hat and scarf if you’re sitting on the right in Row D.

Hold on to Me Darling ***1/2

By: Carol Rocamora

October 14, 2024: The Greek gods on Mt. Olympus must be trembling from the sound coming out of the Sheen Center. The ancient story of Medea is being retold with a power they hadn’t heard since it premiered in ancient Athens at the City Dionysia festival in 431 BC.

The Red Bull/Bedlam’s sensational new version of Euripides’s Medea is
shaking the foundations of today’s theatre with an astonishing artistic
choice. Called Medea Re-Versed, it’s performed (believe it or not) in
hip/hop style with rap lyrics! Don’t be shocked, because this brave, bold
choice is faithful to the original, which Euripides wrote in a similarly
rhythmic form, according to the dramaturgical conventions of his day –
namely, iambic trimeter (lines of 12 syllables). Moreover, this hot new
version by Luis Quintero, co-conceived and directed by Nathan
Winkelstein, is strictly faithful to the story, featuring the same larger-than-
life characters and horrific content.

As the story goes, Medea, granddaughter of the god of the sun, uses her
magical powers to help Jason obtain the Golden Fleece. To do so, she
betrays her father, King of Colchis, and murders her own brother.
After they flee to Corinth, Medea bears Jason two sons. But Jason soon
leaves Medea for the daughter of Creon, King of Corinth – to ensure the
safety of their sons, so he says. But his true motive is to satisfy own
ambitions – to rise in power and status and eventually rule the kingdom
himself. Creon banishes Medea, but – in response to her supplication –
agrees to give her twenty-four hours before she must leave. Medea uses
that time to secure a promise from King Aegeus, a compassionate
neighbor, to give her refuge in his kingdom. She then successfully
executes a plan to kill Creon and his daughter and commit the
unimaginable – the killing of her own children. Though she rationalizes
that she’s committing this horrific deed to protect them from punishment,
she has another motive – namely, to seek revenge on her unfaithful
husband.

What a story! And how faithfully these seven sensational performers tell
it! As you enter the black box Frank Shiner Theatre in the depths of the
Sheen Center, you’re greeted by the sight and sound of a pulsating trio-
band, featuring guitarists Siena D’Addario and Melissa Mahoney and beat-box percussion-vocalist Mark Martin. Rocking to their beat is Luis
Quintero – the author himself! – who greets you at the door, seats you,
and then becomes the show’s narrator and master of the Greek Chorus,
consisting of Stephen Michael Spencer, Jason Ming Trent, and himself.
After providing us with the backstory of Medea’s heroism for Jason’s
sake, and Jason’s ultimate betrayal, the scenes unfold, just as they do in
the original.

At the center of it all is the magnetic Sarin Monae West, playing Medea
with a charismatic, supernatural power befitting her role. Dressed in white
(costume by Nicole Wee), towering above her cheating husband Jason
(played by a slippery Stephen Michael Spenser, lithe and wily just like his
character), she’s the driving force of the production and you can’t take
your eyes off her. In the dual roles of cruel King Creon and
compassionate King Aegeas, Jason Ming Trent is alternately hateful and
hilarious. All this unfolds on Emmie Finckel’s sleek set, dramatically lit by
Cha See in flashes of gold and red. The stage is surrounded (three-
quarters) by a spell-bound audience, drawn into the action, cheering,
jeering, swaying to the beat – doing anything the narrator asks.

As for the rap lyrics, they are infectious, featuring clever rhymes like
“open-handed/pomegranate/plans for granted”; “Medusa/I usta’”; “good
gracious/ostentatious;” “abominable/abdominal;” to name only a few.
The audience loves them’.

What makes this faithful adaptation especially relevant today is the
compassion it elicits for Medea, a woman of exceptional powers who is
nonetheless manipulated, disenfranchised, and abused by powerful men.
The cumulative effect of this electrifying evening is one of catharsis – just
as the great Greek tragedies provided.

Until now, my favorite modern version of Medea was the version starring
Fiona Shaw, directed by Deborah Warner, originating in Dublin and
eventually opening on Broadway in 2002. But the powerful hip hop beat
and rap lyrics of this new version infuse it with a hypnotic energy and
urgency that is absolutely overpowering. Red Bull/Bedlam’s Medea Re-
versed is a brilliant new version of this classic ideally suited for our times.

Medea: Re-Versed *****

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 12, 2024: The Hills of California, now at the Broadhurst Theatre, is British playwright and screenwriter Jez Butterworth’s sixth play to transfer from London to New York, and the fourth to hit Broadway, where its three predecessors, Jerusalem, Rain,and The Ferryman, were critically acclaimed. Like the first and third of those plays, it’s got a large ensemble cast, a striking set, and a longish running time (two hours and 45 minutes with one intermission). With a title taken from a Johnny Mercer song, it mingles themes of grief, death, nostalgia, show business aspirations, memory, family dysfunction, and the value of harmony in a dramedy about four sisters gathering, after many years apart, at the family home to await the imminent death of their domineering mother. 

That family home, located in Blackpool, a fading English seaside resort city—something like Atlantic City—on the Irish Sea, is a large guesthouse that’s changed its name multiple times; by 1976, when half of the action (the other half is 1955) occurs, it’s simply the Seaview, although we’re reminded that you can’t actually see the sea from it. Its seedy Victorian parlour (exquisitely designed by Rob Howell—who also did the great costumes—and lit by Natasha Chivers), replete with tacky Tiki Bar and out-of-order jukebox, sits in the shadow of a series of long staircases ascending way above the stage to where they vanish. These lead to guestrooms called after American states, like Alabama, Colorado, Mississippi, and Alaska. Several times, a turntable brings into view the kitchen, which, with its upright piano, serves also as a space for song and dance numbers, even to the use of the large dining table as a stage.

The play begins in 1976, with the visit of a nurse, Penny (Ta’Rea Cambell), to look in on the cancer-afflicted, dying matriarch, Veronica Webb, offstage. Anybody familiar with hospice care will quickly understand Penny’s expository conversation with the repressed, glasses-wearing spinster, Jill (Helena Wilson), the only daughter to have remained with her termagant of a mother. Penny discretely suggests the availability of morphine to resolve Veronica’s suffering, and leaves a physician’s number to call, if need be. We’ll hear Veronica’s offstage shrieks, but won’t see her until the time shifts back to 1956, when she intimidated her four daughters, her guests, and whoever else had the temerity to cross her path. 

Jill awaits the arrival of the other Webb sisters, Gloria (Leanne Best), Ruby (Ophelia Lovibond), and Joan (Laura Donnelly, who also plays Veronica, in a spectacular tour-de-force of character differentiation). Joan’s lateness in arriving—and the possibility she may not even show up—heightens Gloria’s simmering resentment for Joan’s past actions. Waiting to learn about what these were establishes one of the somewhat rambling play’s few elements of suspense. 

Gloria and Ruby have trekked here separately in the midsummer heat, their henpecked spouses (Bryan Dick and Richard Short)—and Gloria’s squabbling teenagers (Liam Bixby and Nancy Allsop)—in tow. Sisterly tensions quickly bubble up, the persistently worked-up Gloria even sniping about Ruby’s Datsun having air conditioning. But the greatest bitterness is reserved for Joan, believed (because she’s been out of touch) to have become a well-off singer in the USA.

Well before adult Joan’s appearance, however, we meet her as a 15-year-old in 1956, when Veronica—a widowed fabulist who could teach Mama Rose a thing or two about stage mothering—is obsessed with the idea of having her girls launch a show business career as the Webb Sisters, an Andrews Sisters-style quartet, even to the point of making sure they know everything they can about the trio’s lives. The girls are well-played by Nancy Allsop as Gloria, Nicola Turner as Jill, Sophia Ally as Ruby, and Lara McDonnell as Joan. At the least sign of a crack in discipline, the offender is forced to sit in the corner. Smoking by anyone, be they guest or daughter, is strictly forbidden on the premises; thus, as grownups, the sisters, even the withdrawn Jill, smoke constantly. 

The musical premise, however, gives the girls several chances to launch into Andrews Sisters’ numbers like “The Boogie Woogie Bugle Boy” or “Straighten Up and Fly Right” (originally sung by Nat King Cole), which, dolled up in WW II military garb—garrison caps included—reimagined in glamorous pink silk, they carry off with pitch-perfect harmony. These 1940s standards, beautifully interpolated into the action, are among the most precious takeaways. Candida Caldicott did the excellent arrangements and Ellen Kane the fine period choreography.  

However, when an important American agent (David Wilson Barnes) comes to see the act, Veronica will learn a thing or two about contemporary musical tastes. For her part, young Joan, with her mother’s reluctant compliance, will be placed in a situation from which everything that follows in the sisters’ lives will proceed prior to their 1976 reunion. By then, we’ve watched the sisters go at one another with melodramatic hammer and tongs and operatic emotional results. When they finally resolve their differences, though, and join in on “Dream a Little Dream of Me,” an ironic reminder of dreams deferred, you’re almost ready to forgive the somewhat excessive histrionics.

Much as The Hills of California is consistently entertaining, its premise of siblings gathering to await the death of a loved one seems overly familiar. Here and there are moments that seem inauthentic, like Veronica’s belief that what the world needs now, only two years after the Andrews Sisters broke up, is a new version of them. Or that Joan’s fate would have been so totally unknown to her family. But Butterworth’s command of juicy dialogue (including the bad puns a street comic character [Richard Short] spouts like a joke fountain) is rich, and the guy knows how to craft compelling conflicts that actors can sink their chops into, especially under the guidance of Sam Mendes, one of England’s foremost directors.

Topping the list of vibrant performances (sometimes a bit too vibrant) in the cast of 17 (many from the London staging) is Laura Donnelly’s two-character turn. A Butterworth veteran ( his partner), she plays Veronica as a perfectly groomed martinet in tight, white blouse, trim gray skirt, and modest heels; her posture is ramrod straight, her stride purposeful, her gestures gracefully on point, and all without a crease apparent on her person or—until she’s challenged—her personality. The scene when she struggles to maintain her composure in response to the agent’s critique is itself worth a Tony nod.

Donnelly’s entrance as Joan, then, is all the more remarkable. Joan’s American sojourn has given her not only a Joplin-like coat with a long, fur-like collar, and a loose, hippie slouch, but a world-weary edginess refracted through a husky American accent. In fact, I thought it was too American; it’s hard to believe anyone, even if they’ve been living in the USA for 20 years, would so totally have abandoned any traces of the broad Lanky (from Lancashire) accent she had when she left. Her sisters speak it so thickly it’s sometimes difficult for American ears to comprehend, which may explain why so many people lined up at the intermission to ask for assisted listening devices. 

In The Hills of California family harmony is hard to come by in the normal course of events. But give these girls a song and harmony descends like a gift from the muses. As Shakespeare wrote, “If music be the food of love, play on.”

The Hills of California ****

235 West 44th Street, NYC

By: Paulanne Simmons

October 11, 2024At the beginning of Ayad Akhtar’s new play, McNeal, we see the protagonist, Jacob McNeal (Robert Downey Jr.) being scolded by his physician, Sahra Grewal (Ruthie Ann Miles) for his refusal to stop drinking, even though she’s told him alcohol does not  mix well with the new medicine she has prescribed. By the end of the play it’s hard to understand why anyone would want to prolong the life of such a miserable creature.

But McNeal is more than a sick and stubborn man. He is a world-famous novelist who will soon be awarded the Nobel Prize. His agent, Stephie Banic (Andrea Martin), knows she is dealing with gold. Her client is so priceless she can keep his longtime publisher waiting almost indefinitely.

Then it turns out McNeal has been mining the lives of his wife and son, Harlan (Rafi Gavron) to fill the pages of his novel. Even worse, his last novel is pretty much the work of his wife, who killed herself  a while ago, and his son has the original copy to prove it.

It gets messier. In fact, so messy director Bartlett Sher has his hands full tying the plot lines and characters together in any meaningful way.

Turns out McNeal drove his wife to suicide by constantly denigrating her work, mostly because of his own jealousy. And his wife, suffering from some undisclosed psychopathy, abused the son sexually. What’s more, McNeal had a mistress, former editor of The New York Times Book Review, Francine Blake (Melora Hardin), whom he got pregnant before abandoning after she had the abortion he advised. In case you still find McNeal sympathetic, Akhtar reveals him as something of a racist during an interview with an African American reporter, Nataxha Brathwaite (Brittanny Bellizeare).

Downey, who’s had his own problems with substance abuse, knows McNeal very well, but never lets him grow or change or even show genuine remorse. And Andrea Martin is marvelous, as always. But most of the other actors don’t make an impression, either because their characters are written so poorly or because the actors understand them no better than the audience.

For those who like to be stimulated intellectually, there’s plenty of talk about artistic integrity, particularly the dangers and possibilities of  A. I., which McNeal uses generously. Michale Yeargan & Jake Barton’s high-tech sets accommodate big screens to display text messages, created by both A.I. and humans, and projections of Barry Goldwater and Ronald Raegan (McNeal wrote a book about them), as well as psychedelic images, constantly reminding us of the cold and alienating world we live in.

McNeal could have been a tragedy about the downfall of a brilliant writer. It could have been a family drama exploring the painful relationships between wife and husband, parents and child. It could have been an exploration of an artist’s obligations to his family and his art. But Akhtar develops none of these themes in any satisfying way.

In the end, McNeal is a piece of sordid sensationalism masquerading as profundity.

By: Paulanne Simmons

October 12, 2024: Eugene O’Neill meets Gypsy, topped with a heavy Northwest Britain accent (sometimes unintelligible) in Jez Butterworth’s newest drama, The Hills of California, which has crossed the pond this season to land at The Broadhurst Theatre. Of course there’s much here that reminds us of other Butterworth plays, specifically The Ferryman. The production has a multistory set with a very sick mother at the top. There’s  music and dance and a family at odds.  And the play is about a half hour too long. But thanks to director Sam Mendes’s deft hand, there are only a few times when it achingly drags.

The Hills of California opens in the year 1976, when three Webb sisters, Jill (Helena Wilson) , Ruby (Ophelia Lovibond) and  Gloria (Leanne Best), gather in their childhood home, the Seaview Luxury Guesthouse in Blackpool, England. Upstairs, their mother, Veronica (Laura Donnelly) is dying of cancer, while downstairs the  women await the arrival of their sister Joan (also Donnelly) who has been living in California for the past twenty years. Ostensibly they need Joan to help them decide whether to put their mother out of her misery with a shot of morphine. But it soon becomes evident there’s a lot more misery they need to end.

Each one of the women has a distinct personality and relationship with their mother and each other. Jill, dutiful and virginal, has never left Veronica’s side. Gloria, the extra who never made the grade when the girls were performing at local gigs, is bitter and resentful, harboring not-so-secret grudges against Joan. Ruby is stuck in an unsatisfactory marriage. Joan is cynical, bored, vampish and vulnerable.

A series of flashbacks, facilitated by Rob Howell’s revolving set, bring us to the 1950s and the Webbs In their guesthouse kitchen, where Veronica plans the girls’ rise to stardom as a singing group fashioned after the Andrews Sisters. Their act shows just how delusional Veronica is. But Veronica and Joan’s ambition makes them easy prey for the  corrupt and predatory  American agent, Luther St. John (David Wilson Barnes).

What happens next is pivotal in the lives of both mother and daughters. It may explain why Joan escaped to the U.S., where she has a career that is only spectacular in the eyes of her sisters. But then, it could have been an unwanted pregnancy that  precipitated the move. 

The play has a large cast that is consistently quite wonderful. Even actors whose characters  could easily be eliminated (a good deal of the male roles) still make a mark. However, the real standout is Laura Donnelly as both the ambitious and mercurial mother, and Joan, the mother’s creation.

In many ways The Hills of California seems to just stop rather than end in any satisfying way. We don’t even hear Veronica’s death rattle. Do the sisters reconcile their differing views of family history? Can they understand that they have all suffered in their own way? Will they be closer and more forgiving in the future? Or are they just singing one more song for the road? 

Butterworth does not seem concerned with creating a work that has a definite structure or message. Rather, like a painter, he creates a panorama, a landscape where characters make their entrances and exits in a “strange eventful history.”

The Hills of California ****

235 W. 44th St., NYC.

By: David Sheward

October 10, 2024: Kenny Leon’s starry revival of Thornton Wilder’s classic 1938 portrait of everyday life, Our Town, features a diverse, multiethnic cast, but doesn’t hit you over the head with a message of inclusion or “wokeness.” Susan Miller took on that theme with her own adaptation of the play, called It’s Our Town, Too which incorporates gay couples into Wilder’s Grovers’ Corners. Leon adds a few 2024 touches such as opening the play with the company taking selfies, listening to a cacophony of music of different faiths (Justin Ellington did the masterful sound design and Abraham Jam wrote the song that incorporates the various prayers). There is a Jewish star and a Moslem moon among the gravestones in the final act which deals with death. But otherwise, the in-demand Tony winning director presents Wilder’s tribute to family and community largely in tact and without heavy-handed directorial frills. 

His staging is straightforward, stressing the touching love story between George Gibbs and Emily Webb which encapsulates Wilder’s eternal tale of birth, love and passing on. While this production does not achieve the devastating impact of David Cromer’s 2009 Off-Broadway production which made the final act into a hyper-realistic recreation of Emily’s childhood, Leon’s staging stands with previous memorable Broadway revivals in 1988 (with Spalding Gray) and 2003 (starring Paul Newman in his final stage role) in its beautiful simplicity.

Jim Parsons of The Big Bang Theory fame enacts the Stage Manager, the play’s narrator, with little inflection or characterization. He indulges himself with a sly twinkle in his eye and an ironic reading of a line or two which may be considered outdated, but his Stage Manager is mostly an observer of the small town. He allows the audience to draw its own conclusions on the universality of Wilder’s theme—that human beings are the same everywhere and at every time. The focus is on George and Emily, played with depth and feeling by Ephraim Sykes and Zoey Deutch. 

The couple make the journey from first love to last rites, detailing all the significant stops along the way. Skyes, who was the stand-out in Ain’t Too Proud: The Life and Times of the Temptations, proves he is equally strong with dramatic material as he is in musicals. He’s convincing and touching as a rowdy teenager whose main interest is baseball, a young man developing a sense of responsibility, and finally a shattered husband suffering the loss of his wife. Deutch is equally layered, especially as she re-experiences Emily’s twelfth birthday in the climactic final act. 

Billy Eugene Jones, Michelle Wilson, Richard Thomas and Katie Holmes bring warmth and humor to George and Emily’s parents. Donald Webber Jr. imparts reams of subtext as the troubled, drunken choirmaster Simon Stimson. Reliable Julie Halston makes the most of Mrs. Soames, who enjoys weddings to the point of near hysteria.

Beowulf Boritt’s rustic, rough-hewn set incorporates audience members seated in pews onstage, evoking churches and town halls. Dede Ayite’s contemporary costumes place us in the present though the residents all look as if they’re attending a picnic at a summer resort. Allen Lee Hughes’ atmospheric lighting creates the perfect homey glow for this heart-warming Our Town.    

James Ijames’ Good Bones at the Public Theater also takes on the importance of community and largely succeeds in exploring the conflict between gentrification and besieged minorty neighborhoods. His basic concept is sound, with several fiery clashes between his quartet of characters, representing different interests as the forces of change and social inequity threaten an African-American urban district. Ijames’ previous work at the Public, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Fat Ham which later transferred to Broadway, was an innovative metatheatrical flight of imagination, parodying Hamlet and skewering toxic masculinity and sexual stereotypes. Good Bones is strictly representational—Maruti Evans’ gorgeous set includes a literal kitchen sink. The playwright also introduces supernatural elements, but barely develops them. His plot also feels somewhat sketchy so that Good Bones seems like a rough draft rather than a completed project. 

Upwardly mobile African-American couple Aisha, a marketing exec, and Travis, a chef, have moved back to Aisha’s old neighborhood with dreams of renovation and renewal. Their contractor Earl also grew up in the same area which was rife with crime, but also full of connected, caring neighbors. The hood is currently undergoing a transition, a condition Earl fears and resents. When it’s revealed Aisha is on the team to bring a gigantic sports arena (nicknamed the Death Star) to the environs, Earl tries to make her see she is betraying her roots and destroying a vibrant network of families. Earl’s sister Carmen, an ambitious college student, enters late in the play, bringing her own concerns and conflicts.

The climactic confrontation between the quartet at a dinner party to celebrate the completion of Earl’s work is a scintillating, pitched battle with each side armed with valid arguments and passions. Aisha has strong points to make about her horrifying experiences in the projects, countered by Earl’s pleas for understanding and how African-Americans constantly get the short end of the stick. This final extended scene is intense and riveting but the hour leading up to it lacks drama and spark. The author interjects the idea of ghosts, but does not explain sufficiently who is haunting the house and what their objectives would be.

Saheem Ali delivers a proficient job of staging, building tension to the explosive dinner party. I enjoyed his gradual revealing of Evans’ magnificent kitchen design by having the characters take down a few tarps and plastic curtains at a time. 

Susan Kelchi Watson as Aisha, Mamoudou Athie as Travis, Khris Davis as Earl and Tea Guarino as Carmen each detail the internal struggles of their roles with subtlety and depth, but Good Bones feels like it needs further renovation.

Our Town ****

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 10, 2024: David Finnigan, a wiry, lightly bearded, slightly graying, 41-year-old man with a short mullet, is a playwright, actor, and game designer from Ngunnawal country, Australia. His bio says he “works with climate and earth scientists to create theatre and games about complex systems and planetary transformations.” Finnigan’s one-man play, Deep History, has been brought to the Public Theater by artistic director Oskar Eustis, who saw it at Sydney’s Belvoir St Theatre, the same source of another recently produced Public presentation, the epic Counting and Cracking. 

The show’s press materials contain a video of Finnigan’s TED talk about one of his earlier works. In fact, Deep History itself comes off more like a TED talk than a drama. This is not to deny its interest, significance, or even dramatic qualities. It must be noted, though, that, for all its personable features, it looks and sounds precisely like an illustrated lecture. The scientific and historic facts on which its based take on personal, metaphoric, and artistic values as Finnigan, playing himself, recounts his response to  the apocalyptic crisis of global warming.

Lecture or not, Deep History, crisply directed by Annette Mees,is well performed, the charismatic Finnigan speaking with an accent sounding—to my ears, at any rate—more man-in-the-street British than  what we usually identify as Australian. He wears a close-fitting ensemble of gray T-shirt and black slacks and, for undisclosed reasons, is barefoot. As with a lecture, no one is credited for any design elements.

The stage of the Public’s intimate Shiva Theater is bare, backed by only a projection screen. Two tables stand downstage, the one on our left with a small funnel device next to a webcam, that on our right with a laptop whose keyboard allows Finnigan to cue the projections and music, some of the latter recent pop tunes, the rest an original background score by Reuben Ingall. A bit further to our right is a vertical board over which hangs a sheet of brown wrapping paper on which Finnigan will write with a black magic marker. 

He begins the piece by informing us that his script was written in 72 hours at the end of 2019, when southeast Australia was suffering “the worst fire season in” its history. He says the script hasn’t been altered since, but, In fact, there are a few later, if minor, interpolations. Apart from the 2019 bushfires, no other climate-related events are mentioned.

The substance of Finnigan’s talk, presented with humor and humanity, although imperfect clarity, was inspired by the enormous configuration that burned huge swathes of Australia, creating a widespread, hazardous veil of smoke for months. The very act of breathing was difficult, even for those indoors. Speaking in direct, layman’s language, he discusses the implications of climate change, informing us that we’re now in an historical period he calls the “climate era,” suggesting there’s a roadmap for surviving in it. 

Much of Finnigan’s story involves fascinating material about his dad, J.J. Finnigan, once a leading rock climber. After a serious climbing fall, in 1969, precipitated by climate change conditions, his father moved the family to Australia from Great Britain and became a climate scientist. Three days before 2020, while recuperating in a hospital from a spinal infection traceable to the fall, he explained to his son that mankind is still in its adolescence; only when it learns to plan for the future will it move into adulthood. Having prepared an outline of six turning points in mankind’s development to serve as a guide for how to navigate the future, he sent it to his worried offspring in London. 

During his talk, Finnigan writes each point, as he comes to it, on the paper sheet, punctuating the moments by sharply slamming the marker to the ground. He tells us: “And from each of his six turning point moments, I’m going to find the moral or lesson for us here and now. We’re going to create a guide for how humanity can get through the climate era. It’s going to be optimistic and constructive and forward looking.” We learn many things, but his somewhat rambling talk never achieves this ambitious goal.

Rather than tell his story, as his dad would, through thermodynamic equations, Finnigan focuses on a single individual, a female, as reincarnated through time and across the continents. He begins this poetic conceit 75,000 years ago, narrating in colorfully casual prose and verse, with sprightly rhetorical flourishes, infused with personal reflections and reports from friends in Canberra caught up in the conflagration. Helpful projections (by Haley Eagan) of stills and videos help illustrate his ideas. Eventually, we move closer to today, as we view turning points taking us from 68,000 to 27,000 to 11,000 to 500 to 75 years ago. 

Finnigan’s expansive history introduces an unparalleled volcanic eruption in Indonesia that wiped out almost all humans and animals. The small number of human survivors (15,000) were our ancestors, the written turning point being, “SURVIVAL IS POSSIBLE.” 

To illustrate Earth’s growing population over the eons, Finnigan uses the stunningly simple device of dropping grains of white sand (standing in for the sugar of his narration) onto a table through a funnel, beginning with a tiny pinch, and eventually becoming a torrent that overflows onto the floor, representing billions of people.

As he now and then reads frightening texts from Canberra describing the wildfires, Finnigan casts a wide net teeming with historical topics. These include the extinction of species and the development of civilization, the wise ways in which indigenous people managed fire, pro and con attitudes toward climate change, man’s place among the hominids, his father’s fight against climate misinformation, his own decision to use theater as an informational tool, the forced migrations inspired by the reshaping of the earth’s topography, the rise of urbanization and the new power structures it produced, colonization, the atom bomb, pollution, and so on. 

Much of what we hear seems peripheral to fighting or surviving climate change; in fact, some of us may begin to wonder why, with so much historical smoke, there’s so little fire. I’m still not sure what his description, for example, of the first human artifact depicting sex has to do with giant fires. Finnigan himself appears to find himself unable to effectively handle the subject as he struggles to conclude on a positive note, or even, given his goal of providing six turning points, to hit that target. 

Perhaps the subject is simply too hot to handle, especially for a 65-minute play cum TED talk. While it lasts, David Finnigan’s Deep History offers some cool aperçus on one of the most pressing issues of our times. They’re just not cool enough to put out the fires.

Deep History ***1/2
Public Theater/Shiva Theater
425 Lafayette Street, NYC
Through November 10, 2024

By: David Sheward

October 9, 2024: Roundabout Theatre Company currently offers two diverse entertainments with varying ambitions, each succeeding on its own terms. In the company’s Broadway house, the Todd Haimes, Leigh Silverman skillfully directs David Henry Hwang’s Yellowface, a smart farce taking on political correctness, racial identity, media frenzy, and theatrical and journalistic conventions. At Roundabout’s Off-Broadway Laura Pels, director David Cromer brings out the tenderness and poignancy of a somewhat familiar premise in Meghan Kennedy’s intimate The Counter.

Hwang’s Yellowface has taken on richer depths and subtler ironies since it was presented Off-Broadway at the Public Theater in 2007. A clever mixing of fact and fiction, Yellowface skewers every participant in our raging cultural wars, including the author himself. The action starts when the semi-autobiographical figure DHH gets involved with the controversy over white actor Jonathan Pryce playing the Asian role of The Engineer in the Broadway transfer of the West End megahit Miss Saigon in 1991. (This was probably the most infamous and controversial example of the title practice of casting non-Asians in Asian parts.) 

DHH later writes About Face, a comedy satirizing the situation and inadvertently casts white Jewish actor Marcus in the lead Asian role, mistakenly believing the actor has the same ethnic background as the character. From there, DHH and his banker father HYH, a Chinese immigrant in love with the image of America, become embroiled in a scandal involving the Chinese and US governments, spies, money laundering, nuclear secrets and anti-Asian racism. Hwang has a lot to say about all these topics and says them with stingy wit. Silverman’s rapid-fire staging keeps the complex action clear, aided by Arnulfo Maldonado’s fluid set of mobile cubes and Lap Chi Chu’s multiple-location lighting.

Daniel Dae Kim combines comedic timing and dramatic pathos as the central figure DHH, hilariously attempting to justify the playwright’s shifting stances in a constantly changing cultural landscape. Francis Jue repeats his performance of HYH from the 2007 production, endearingly capturing the father’s grandiose dreams of emulating his beloved American movie stars like Jimmy Stewart. Ryan Eggold is charismatic, charming and conflicted as the devious and slippery Marcus. In an ironic stroke of casting genius a company of able, versatile actors—Marinda Anderson, Greg Keller, Shannon Tyo and Kevin Del Aguila—play all the remaining roles without regard to age, ethnicity or gender.

Meanwhile, in Roundabout’s Off-Broadway Laura Pels, in The Counter, playwright Meghan Kennedy, director David Cromer and a loving, small cast have breathed new life into a reliable trope. In an upstate New York diner (beautifully designed with realistic detail by Walt Spangler), two lonely souls reach out to each other. How many times have we heard that one before? But the author, Anthony Edwards as misanthropic regular customer Paul and Susannah Flood as empathic waitress Katie cook up a satisfying meal of comfort food. Amy Warren completes the cast as Peg, a prickly doctor and former love of Paul. She is able to express decades of attachment with a single touch on Paul’s winter coat. Cromer’s spare staging and the cast’s layered acting staging imparts the heartache and loneliness of these everyday people with final gestures and actions. When Peg brushes against Paul and when Paul crosses to the other side of the counter into Katie’s territory, the impact of these seemingly insignificant moments is devastating.

There are one or two caveats. The melodramatic twist that propels the plot is more than a smidgen hokey. Also, Katie appears to be the only employee of the diner (where’s the cook?) and Paul its sole patron, apart from a brief visit from Peg. But these are minor quibbles. The Counter is brief and powerful, like a well-crafted short story.

Nancy Harris’ The Beacon, making its North American debut at Irish Repertory Theater, is a little too well-crafted for its own good. The plot-heavy melodrama crowds in too many themes, ideas and relationships and collapses under its own weight. We’ve got the feminist, independent artist angle represented by Beiv, an iron-willed painter (Kate Mulgrew in a bravura performance) struggling with a deep, dark secret. Her estranged son Colm (Zach Appelman) brings his new bride, the flaky American Bonnie (Ayana Workman) for an extended stay to Mom’s studio-home on one of the islands off the Western Irish coast, but his motives are mixed and somewhat unclear. Hanging around the edges and renovating Beiv’s home is Donal (Sean Bell), Colm’s boyhood pal and erstwhile gay lover. (The attractive, cosy set is by Colm McNally.) Mysterious deaths, long-buried resentments and observations on art make for a confusing and heady brew. 

Director Marc Atkinson Borrull and the cast, which also includes David Mattar Merten as a sleazy podcaster who worms his way into Beiv’s home in search of a juicy scandal, do their level best to bring believability to this thriller, but it comes across as a steamy potboiler. Mulgrew almost brings it off with powerhouse lead limning. She’s given an award-bait climactic monologue calling for floods of emotion as Beiv reveals her big secret. But it’s also her quieter moments which make her characterization memorable. A sideways glance, a tilt of her head, a finger to her lips, all speak volumes. The Beacon could have done with more such subtext and less text.

Yellowface ****

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 9, 2024: At the center of the stage at the Laura Pels Theatre, where Meghan Kennedy’s The Counter is being performed, is a tiny coffee shop, occupying perhaps one third of the space. Walt Spangler’s intimate, almost claustrophobic set places us in a small New York town, somewhere “way upstate.” A counter runs downstage from the shop’s translucent upstage window, splitting the acting area in two. 

To the counter’s left (as we view it), where the coffee is brewed, is Katie (Susannah Flood, TV’s “For the People”), the fortyish woman who moved here two years ago and runs the place. To the right are several counter stools, on one of which sits a bearded, older man, Paul (Anthony Edwards, TV’s “ER”), who grew up locally; unable to sleep, he’s been the first customer nearly every morning, Monday through Saturday, presumably since Katie arrived. Apart from a scene with another woman of Paul’s age, a local doctor named Peg (Amy Warren, Adding Machine: A Musical), no one else appears. 

As in many such plays, Katie and Paul are lonely, ordinary people searching for connection. Each carries emotional baggage and reasons to be depressesd, although his case, at first, seems the more obvious one; each will have occasion to offer the other succor and advice over the course of the play’s hour and 15 minutes. Scene follows scene as Paul finishes his coffee, leaves, and returns the next day for more java and palaver. Katie and Paul’s friendly, often wry banter, despite what we might expect, is not prelude to a kiss but to an end to their individual dilemmas. These are partly attributable to matters of the heart, but also to the existential question of what, if anything, makes life worth living.

Paul has no romantic interest in deepening his friendship with Katie; instead, as they agree to share secrets with one another, he reveals that he wants her to poison him, the moment to be at her discretion. Naturally, she resists his attempts to persuade her. It’s Katie’s secret, however, that moves the action forward when she informs Paul that she moved here to get away from a love affair that failed (for reasons not all viewers will find convincing). The lover, however, has continued to pursue her, as evidenced by 27 voicemails woven into the plot.

As Paul seeks to help Katie resolve her romantic crisis, she, in turn, advises him on his, which involves the married doctor, Peg Bradley, with whom he had an affair five years ago. These discussions open a vein regarding the degree to which life itself is worth living: we learn of tragedies affecting both Paul’s family and Katie’s health, of the way in which our society thrives financially on suffering and death, and of the poor return life provides for the sacrifices we make on behalf of others. At the end, there’s a glint of hope for one of the main characters. For the other, who knows? 

The Counter is a low-key, slow-moving play of uneven plausibility and unsteady dramatic interest made palatable by the conviction of its performers. Under the intelligently insightful direction of David Cromer, Edwards, Flood, and Warren give stageworthy life to their not particularly interesting characters. Sarah Laux’s costumes look like what these untheatrical folk would wear, Stacey Derosier’s lighting contributes to the naturalistic look, and Christopher Darbassie’s sound design helps heighten the mood.

A lot of coffee is drunk in The Counter but the play itself too often feels decaffeinated. 

The Counter ***
Harold and Miriam Steinberg Center for Theatre/Laura Pels Theatre
111 W. 46th Street, NYC
Through November 17, 2024

By: David Sheward

October 6, 2024: The cast list for Mathilde Dratwa’s Dirty Laundry at the WP (Women’s Project) Theater, gave me pause. Three female characters are listed as Blue, Red, and Green. The remaining personae are Me, My Dad, and Another Woman. This generic designation on the single-sheet program (a full program is available digitally) struck me as potentially pretentious. But once the play started, the mysterious names made some sense and Dratwa’s moving, clever work unfolded, skillfully and compassionately depicting the messy, difficult business of family relations.

The play begins with a seemingly mundane phone conversation between Me (Lakisha May) and My Dad (Richard Masur) as the latter requests his estranged daughter to give him instructions on the simple task of washing his laundry. The action is narrated by the three characters named for different colors, though costume designer Lux Haac does not outfit them in corresponding hues (Her clothing choices are otherwise spot-on). Gradually, it’s revealed the mother has recently died, that she took care of all the household chores and that the father had been engaged in a long-term affair with Another Woman (Constance Shulman). The daughter is freshly furious about the infidelity as the three narrators, each representing a different aspect of her personality, explain. The metaphor of the dad’s confusion and the daughter’s impatience in this exchange over laundry is a perfect metaphor for their strained relation.

As with the strange names, having a trio of commentators raised my critical antennae. Normally, the playwright should show us her themes and intentions, rather than telling us through surrogates. One such narrator usually spells trouble, three sets off all sorts of alarm bells warning of weak dramaturgy. But Dratwa uses the device adroitly, employing the color-coded characters to highlight Me’s interior conflicts. Blue (Mary Bacon) is the writer, consulting a notebook and calmly ordering and offering insight into the events. She is the most motherly of the three. Red (Sasha Diamond) embodies the emotions, reacting with rage to her father’s actions. Green (Amy Jo Jackson) is the intellectual,  rational side of the daughter, offering medical and psychological motivations. She also enacts male figures such as the daughter’s empathic husband and a chilly professional doctor caring for the mom. (Ironically, the dad is also a doctor, clinically detailing his wife condition, further alienating the daughter.)

The action is relayed out of chronological order, but the back-and-forth timeline makes emotional and narrative sense as the fractured connection between father and child is examined and slowly heals. Rebecca Martinez’s direction keeps the disparate scenes flowing smoothly and clearly so that there is no confusion. She adeptly juggles the conflicting intentions of the characters, conveying the awkward, uncomfortable mash-up of love, hatred, and grief. 

The best example of these multiple-motive set pieces comes during the memorial service for the mother. While Me is delivering heartfelt tribute, expressing her parent’s sterling qualities as a teacher and mother, Red is simultaneously venting her anger at her dad, even going into the audience searching for Another Woman. The twin strands produce a volatile volcano of emotions, erupting with devastating force. May as Me and Diamond as Red deliver powerful performances here and thoroughout the play. Masur as My Dad is silent throughout this explosive scene, but you read volumes in his body language and expression. These eloquent actors, along with Bacon, Jackson, and Shulman beautifully convey the complex warring objectives of their characters in this surprisingly affecting family drama.

Dirty Laundry ***

Running time: One hour and 40 mins. with no intermission. wptheater.org.

But once the play started, the mysterious names made some sense and Dratwa’s moving, clever work unfolded, skillfully and compassionately depicting the messy, difficult business of family relations.

By: Samuel L. Leiter

October 4, 2024: It wasn’t until the 1930s that, apart from a few exceptions (including stars Ethel Barrymore and Walter Hampden), mainstream New York theater abandoned the practice of white actors playing Black characters in blackface. The practice of whites playing Asians in what is called yellowface—in the small number of cases where the roles were important (like The King and I or A Majority of One)—took longer to disappear, both on stage and on the screen. In the latter, for instance, only Anna May Wong ascended to female stardom, if mainly in B movies, while the most memorable Asian characters were played by such apogees of “Oriental” authenticity as Myrna Loy, Luise Rainer, Helen Hayes, and Katharine Hepburn!

The first important Broadway show with a fully Asian cast arrived in 1958 with Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Flower Drum Song; well, not completely, since Anna May Wong, slotted to play Madam Liang, had to bow out before the opening because of illness and was replaced by Juanita Hall, who was Black! Nevertheless, despite occasional protests, yellowface stuck around, in movies and Broadway theater, for many years, only being seriously challenged when Miss Saigon opened in 1991. That show caused a famous brouhaha because the role of the Engineer—half-white, half-Vietnamese—was to be played by Welsh star Jonathan Pryce, and the Asian American theater community screamed bloody murder.

I note these things because David Henry Hwang’s 2007 play, Yellow Face (he uses two words), now in a decent, if unexceptional, Roundabout revival at the Todd Haimes Theatre, is a semi-autobiographical account of Hwang’s involvement in the controversy and its aftermath. The subject of racially appropriate casting remains politically pungent and Hwang, focusing on plays with Asian characters, has a good time both satirizing the rabbit holes it can lead to as well as his own complicity, as the leading Asian American playwright (he won the Tony for M. Butterfly), in the debate.

In Yellow Face, Hwang, noted as DHH, played by Daniel Dae Kim (The King and I), stirs a hornet’s nest when he writes in the Times a scathing critique of the soon-to-open London transfer of Miss Saigon for casting a white actor as the Engineer. The actors’ union, Equity, is drawn into the ensuing conflict but, after first rejecting the casting, which—as per producer Cameron Mackintosh’s threat—would have led to the show’s cancellation, changes its mind, allowing the show to open. 

DHH uses the controversy as the subject of his next play, Face Value (a $2 million flop that closed before it opened), casting a white actor, Marcus Dahlman (Ryan Eggold, TV’s “The Blacklist”), as a leading Asian character, mistakenly thinking him Asian. When Marcus’s actual ethnicity as a Jewish white man can’t be denied, and the legal complexities of firing him on racial grounds are explained, DHH uses pretzel-twisting logic to claim that Marcus has family roots in Siberia, which is part of Asia. He even renames him Marcus Gee. Ironically, Marcus not only becomes a star based on his false identity but, to DHH’s annoyance, assumes the mantle of spokesman for the Asian American community. 

Much of this tongue-in-cheek, metatheatrical satire, which pokes fun at Hwang himself, is lightly amusing, although I laughed far less frequently than those around me. Partly this is because the play’s comic style is based on its fourth-wall breaking convention, with DHH narrating the events as background information is reported by a multi-ethnic cast—Shannon Tyo, Marinda Anderson, Kevin Del Aguila, and Francis Jue—playing multiple roles in brief jump-cut sequences. Often, they quote headline-like comments from various figures, including celebrities like Ed Koch, Dick Cavett, Mark Linn-Baker, B.D. Wong, and Jane Krakowski.

In an obvious nod toward the play’s concern with identity, these are assigned without regard to matching any actor’s ethnicity and gender to who it is they’re playing. A white actor, Del Aguila, for example, portrays B.D. Wong. The actors are enthusiastic, if not notably versatile, but much of their shtick doesn’t land. Even Del Aguila, so brilliant as Osgood in Some Like It Hot, works harder than he should, which is understandable given that he’s playing 23 roles.

Anyone who’s seen post-Miss Saigon shows with casts made up of reportedly Asian actors who either have non-Asian-sounding names or don’t particularly “look Asian” will recognize how loosely the standards of “authenticity” of ethnic casting are interpreted in practice. Hwang’s satirical thrusts at the dilemma are among the best things in Yellow Face.

But he also has other things in mind, which dominate the latter part of this intermissionless hour and 45-minute enterprise. (The lack of an intermission, I’ve learned, is a change from the original, and there are also a number of other changes, mostly minor.) These other things have to do with his proud, upbeat, immigrant father, HYH (a delightful Francis Jue, who played the same part in the 2007 production), founder of California’s Far East National Bank, whose cultural ignorance regarding his son’s profession is mildly spoofed. However, HYH, a Bill Clinton donor, gets into serious trouble, along with other notable Chinese Americans, when Senator Fred Thompson investigates them for illegally funneling money to China for nefarious political purposes.

DHH, who took a board position with the bank, is also dragged into the mess, as is Marcus; a contentious interview DHH holds with a pesky reporter, listed as “Name Withheld on Advice of Counsel” (nicely handled by Zack Shaffer, understudying for Greg Keller), gives the play an interesting dramatic kick while being emotionally out of sync with the comic spirit of what came earlier. DHH’s method of short-circuiting the reporter’s report is a negotiating masterstroke. Before the crisis can be dismissed, however, Marcus must decide if he’s ready to reveal his true identity. This is where Hwang plays a bit too fast and loose with his mix of fact and fantasy, but to describe it would be too much of a spoiler.

Arnulfo Maldonaldo has provided a minimalist design of two cubical structures that move about on a revolving stage and whose inner walls serve as screens for Yee Yun Nam’s projections, many of them showing newspaper articles with important words highlighted. DHH’s performance, though, is mostly downstage of them, efficiently lit by Lop Chi Chu. Anita Yavich has provided suitable everyday costumes, with effective variations to help differentiate the minor roles.

As DHH, Daniel Dae Kim projects an air of serious decency, his rich baritone giving him an almost stentorian air; he sometimes sounds more like the captain of the USS Enterprise or a broadcasting news reader than a harried, nervous playwright. His somber mien occasionally manages to evoke some comic charm, but his natural gravitas works better when he’s arguing with the reporter than when he’s dealing with his casting problems.

Yellow Face doesn’t fire on all cylinders but one can’t deny its relevance to contemporary concerns. As anyone who sees Broadway shows regularly will agree, there have been many developments regarding identity-related casting since 2007, much of it positive, but much still open to debate. Yellow Face is hopefully not the last word on the subject.

Yellow Face ***

Through November 24, 2024
