By: David Sheward

October 4, 2024: It took a while, but Safety Not Guaranteed, the new musical based on the 2012 indie cult film now playing at BAM’s Harvey Theater, gradually grew on me. By the end of its intermissionless hour and 45 minutes, I was rooting for its quirky characters to find resolution and/or romance. Nick Blaemire’s book, based on Derek Connolly’s screenplay, is initially too slick for its own good with one-liners and weird traits substituting for character development. As the seemingly silly plot progresses, the outlandish sci-fi elements and too-cool-for-school quips fall away to reveal a compassionate story of loneliness and alienation. The catchy score by Ryan Miller of the alt-rock band Guster is full of infectious tunes and intricate lyrics (I loved rhyming “the rainbow vanishes” with “twenty dollar sandwiches” to convey dashed dreams turning into adult money concerns.)

A capsule summation sounds like a goofy teen comedy. Rookie journalist Darius (powerful Nkeki Obi-Melekwe) finds a bizarre classified ad seeking a partner to go time-traveling. “This is not a joke,” the ad reads, “Bring your own weapons.” She smells a story and gets the OK to investigate from her cynical editor Jeff (sharply funny Pomme Koch). But, for ulterior reasons, he insists on accompanying her to the small town where the ad originated, along with laptop-obsessed office drone Arnau (Rohan Kymal, displaying hidden depths.)

The trio finds the placer of the ad, the off-center Kenneth (endearingly weird Taylor Trench) and we’re off on a strange ride through conspiracy theories, broken hearted backstories, teenage trauma, and adult angst. Ashley Perez Flanagan and John-Michael Lyles ably complete the cast in multiple supporting roles including love interests for the hard-bitten Jeff and the shy, gay Arnau. 

Lee Sunday Evans’s smart staging smoothly moves the story like a movie, transitioning through multiple locations, with the aide of Krit Robinson’s suggestive scenic design which features a plethora of witty set pieces including a fragment of a water tower to place us in Kenneth’s tiny town and a restaurant booth which could be found in Any Diner, USA. Reza Behjat’s versatile lighting also aides in the swift and fluid movement of the story.

The rock score helps propel and comment on the action. One of Miller’s songs, “One Man Wrecking Machine” was composed for his band Guster, but fits in with the plot nicely. Music director Cynthia Meng and the orchestra produce a spirited accompaniment with Drew Levy’s sound design finding the perfect balance between rock-concert volume (not too high) and lyric comprehension (not too low). 

Obi-Melekwe displays a mighty rock voice and skillfully peels back Darius’s tough exterior to expose the vulnerable, broken girl underneath. Likewise Trensch delivers a multi-layered performance as the whacky Kenneth. Sporting a Chaplin-esque mustache and cute winter hat with ear-flaps, Trensch garners guffaws with a delightfully physical interpretation of Kenneth’s kooky obsessions. He also breaks our heart as we discover the source of his nutty time travel fantasies—but are they all in his head? (No spoilers.)

Koch also digs deep into his role, giving Jeff a nasty side, but also a soft center once his illusions of an idealized adolescence are shattered. Kymal is fun to watch as Arnau comes out of his shell and becomes a “Wolf Robot” on the dance floor. Perez Flanagan and Lyles give full life to the many supporting roles. Safety Not Guaranteed is more than a science fiction adventure, it’s a rousing rock musical and a moving story rolled together. 

Safety Not Guaranteed ***

By Samuel L. Leiter

As “Good Bones,” TV’s popular home restoration TV program, indicates, an older house with such a skeleton has a solid foundation and sturdy structure, even if its exterior doesn’t look so hot. In James Ijames’s thematically promising but otherwise uninspired play, Good Bones, at the Public Theater, that description applies to an old townhouse being renovated in Dunbar Gardens, a rundown, but gentrifying, Black neighborhood of an unnamed city. The play itself, however, would benefit from better bones.

Good Bones, which premiered last year at the Studio Theatre in Washington, D.C. (which has been suggested as the play’s locale), is a domestic drama, sprinkled with a few laughs. It’s about a young, attractive, well-educated, well-dressed, comfortably middle-class African American couple, Aisha (Susan Kelechi Watson) and Travis (Mamoudou Athie). Their recently purchased townhouse, formerly owned by a revered community leader, Sister Bernice, first Black woman on the city council, is being restored by a handsome, youngish, local contractor, Earl (Khris Davis). 

Earl, who prides himself on his craftsmanship, even fabricates his own cabinet knobs, which he sells for $40 each. Aisha and Travis befriend Earl, and, later, his 19-year-old sister, Carmen (Tea Guarino), a finance major at the University of Pennsylvania, who insists that her romantic interest (unseen) be referred to by “they” and “their.”

Travis is a talented chef who’s opened an upscale soul food restaurant in town, while Aisha, who grew up nearby under strained circumstances, represents a company planning to raze much of the place to build a huge sports complex called the Jewel. Class distinctions between the college-educated characters and Earl are expressed in speech, Earl speaking in familiar Black vernacular and referring to Aisha and Carmen as “bougie,” suggesting self-conscious preoccupation with respectability. 

Earl is adding finishing touches to the house, which, when we see it on taking our seats, is largely hidden behind translucent plastic drop cloths. For some minutes after the play begins, the action is barely visible, forcing us to listen to the expository dialogue without seeing the set. Then Earl yanks down the front drop cloths, followed by those covering the upstage areas. Thus is Maruti Evans’s substantial, realistic set, effectively lit by Barbara Samuels, gradually exposed. A staircase is visible at our left and a wide kitchen/dining room at our right, all of it painted a boringly monochromatic gunmetal gray.

Good Bones runs an overlong hour and 45 intermissionless minutes; it only really crackles during its last 10 or 15 minutes when the subject of gentrification, the play’s raison d’être, is allowed to detonate after several earlier discussions. Until then it dithers along with various marital, decorative, familial, cooking, historical, and personal issues as you wait for higher stakes to kick in. 

They finally do, in the climactic, if vaguely resolved, conclusion during an increasingly tense dinner party. Aisha, aware from personal experience of Dunbar Gardens’s economic and social decline, and of its dangers from crime, believes that it will be vastly improved by the complex she represents. Aisha uses a small model of the proposed construction to point out specific neighborhood places where bad things happened, and which, we assume, can thereby be liquidated. 

Earl, with the anger of a community activist, insists that the complex will cruelly impact the neighborhood, evicting people from their homes, causing rents to rise, and forcing many to leave, thereby spoiling its character as a place where everyone appreciates one another as part of a true community. Of course, that’s a big “as if,” since we must accept his idealistic view purely on his own word. The arguments put forth on both sides, despite a few meritorious ones, can seem oversimplified, although no one doubts that gentrification brings with it all sorts of serious baggage.

Related to this dispute is a scene where Travis, unable to sleep because of a nearby block party still going strong at 1:00 a.m., whose music sends waves of house-shuddering bass through the theatre, uses an app to report it to law enforcement. When Earl finds out who made the call, he grows furious at Travis’s lack of respect for the neighborhood tradition. Why, Earl asks, didn’t he simply ask that the sound be lowered, instead of calling in the cops, with their prototypically violent behavior? Anyone who’s ever been in a similar situation could easily answer, if they managed to come back in one piece. But Ijames doesn’t go there.

Ijames came to prominence a couple of years ago with his creatively farcical satire on Hamlet called Fat Ham, which won the Pulitzer Prize, but Good Bones is much more in the straightforward manner of Ibsenian discussion drama. With the aid of the Public’s resident director, Saheem Ali (Fat Ham, Buena Vista Social Club), he gussies things up for theatrical effect with a few symbolic hints at a ghostly presence, using strange sounds (kudos to Fan Zhang for her noteworthy sound design), self-opening doors, spooky lighting, and the like to suggest supernatural forces. 

This is perhaps meant to tie in with Earl’s memories of sneaking into this house as a child, when it was abandoned, playing ghost hunters with Carmen. Presumably, the spirit of Sister Bernice remains as a benign presence, one that Aisha, in fact, seems to welcome. But, apart from an occasional reminder, it does little more than inject some mystery into an otherwise mundane play.

Aside from the set’s dull color, the only technical bone I must pick in Good Bones is with Oana Botez’s costuming. Everyone, even those in work clothes (like Carmen in her pristine, white, painting coveralls), looks too well dressed for a naturalistic play. But when Aisha, for her casual dinner party, appears garbed in a gold lame number that distracts from everyone and everything else, all bets are off. 

Respectably, if not memorably, acted, and lacking in sufficiently well-sustained dramatic interest, Good Bones tackles a serious problem but not without suffering a few setbacks in the process. This play may not pass inspection, but James Ijames is too unique a talent to easily dismiss. As the old song goes, “Dem bones gonna rise again.”

Good Bones ***
Public Theater/Martinson Hall 
425 Lafayette Street, NYC
Through October 27, 2024

By: Samuel L. Leiter

September 30, 2024: From February 28, 2022, to March 8, 2022, a 50-year-old Texas resident named Guy Wesley Reffitt was the defendant in a jury trial held before the United States District Court, District of Columbia. He was accused of five criminal counts for his participation in the January 6, 2020, insurrection at the U.S. Capitol, for which he pleaded not guilty. His accuser was his own 19-year-old son, Jackson, a community college student of political science, who reported his father to the FBI. Reffitt, the first person convicted for his activities on January 6, was found guilty on all counts, and was sentenced to seven years in prison.

The notion of a left-leaning son—who supported Bernie Sanders’s democratic socialist platform—turning on his own right-wing, firearm-packing father, whom he nevertheless professes to love, contains a built-in dramatic wallop, one that countless families riven by our divided nation can appreciate. It’s also a blow that Stephen Sachs has aimed at our political jaws by crafting a docudrama based strictly on the “court evidence, public statements, and the official transcript” of the trial in a production Sachs directed at Los Angeles’s intimate Fountain Theatre. That production, its creative and performing company intact, is currently at the City Center Stage II. 

The show makes no attempt to recreate a courtroom. Joel Daavid’s set consists of a carpeted area equipped with a couple of wooden tables and chairs fronting an abstract background of irregularly shaped units resembling green and rust-tarnished metallic sculptures. Alison Brummer lights it all dramatically. 

Four nameless characters appear, designated as U.S. Attorney (Anna Khaja), Defense Attorney (Larry Poindexter), Son (Patrick Keleher), and Father (Ron Bottitta). All are costumed by Danyele Thomas as you might imagine, the lawyers in business attire, the son in slacks, a sport jacket, and a white shirt, the father in black jeans and a black t-shirt before he shows up for the verdict in a baggy, brown suit.

Some scenes are staged in typical courtroom fashion, with the seated witness, the son, being questioned by one or the other attorney (the father never testified). Other scenes are in a neutral space where actions ostensibly described in the documents are fully reenacted. The dialogue—of which there is a good deal, drawn both from testimony and private conversations—presumably has been lifted verbatim from printed and recorded sources. 

Now and then, offstage recorded voices are heard as part of Stuart Blackwood’s complex sound design. Most obvious are the obnoxious outbursts of Donald J. Trump, in whom one might say the disgruntled father—who turned sour after losing his important job, located in Penang, Malaysia, when the oil industry floundered—found God. Addicted to watching Fox, he joined a radical group called the Three Percenters and read, reread, and quoted, as if it were gospel, Trump’s ghost-written book, The Art of the Deal.

The facts of Guy Reffitt’s case and trial can be read in various sources, as for example here, so they needn’t be repeated. The production, however, rather than providing a straightforward trial drama, chooses to mix the familiar cross examination process with verbatim recreations of scenes between the son and father, which one assumes were documented from memory in interviews. Some of it likely comes from the son’s having recorded his father’s words on his phone, which we see him doing.

Whatever their source, the words are plentiful enough for fully written dramatic scenes, most of which tend to be intensely emotional, if not confrontational. There’s also extensive monologic material, especially for the father, whose reactionary tirades on behalf of taking over the Capitol, and his enthusiastic blow-by-blow description of what he was experiencing on January 6, are frightening in their furious, self-righteous rhetoric. 

A great deal of fascinating expository information about the father and son dynamic, not to mention that of the family, emerges, some of which—including a GoFundMe account from which he earned a hefty payoff—doesn’t cast the son in the most pristine light. Regardless of the nuances, however, including Guy Reffitt’s reasons for becoming so deeply radicalized, nothing detracts from the depth of his beliefs or the actions he took before, during, and after the insurrection.

Unfortunately, too much of the performance is played with mad dog ferocity. The father’s raving, macho bombast, punctuated by moments in which he brandishes either his 40-caliber Smith & Wesson or his AR-15, allows Bottitta to demonstrate a powerful pair of lungs and the tour-de-force ability to maintain an attitude of high dudgeon over a significant stretch. While it’s an impressive demonstration of histrionic commitment, I felt like I needed a dose of ibuprofen to recover from the barrage of shouting, which felt like an audition for King Lear’s storm speech.

Khaja and Poindexter as the polished attorneys are much like those seen in countless courtroom dramas, determined, focused, crafty, and smooth. Keleher’s Son is both fragile and tough, although one wonders how even a devoted son could love so overtly fanatical a father. The son admits that he and his once well-liked dad used to have “a pretty great father/son relationship,” but we not only learn that Reffitt once held a gun to his wife’s head, we also watch as he threatens to kill his own son. 

All in all, the show’s dependence on reenacted situations, with their sometimes excessive emoting, more than on courtroom process, creates something of a dramatic imbalance. On October 3, another Trump-related courtroom docudrama, this one on film, will be released, its subject the E. Jean Carrol sexual assault suit against Trump. I hope it sticks to the trial and, unlike Fatherland, leaves the reenactments to our imagination.

Fatherland ***
City Center Stage II
131 W. 55th Street, NYC
Through November 23, 2024

By: David Sheward

September 29, 2024: Estranged siblings gather at the bedside of a dying parent. Crushed dreams have an inextricable hold on the family. A dying town symbolizes those dashed hopes. The most charismatic character delivers an amazingly self-aware monologue summing up everyone’s problems including her own. Jez Butterwoth’s The Hills of California, now at the Broadhurst after a hit run in London, has all these familiar tropes and yet it’s a stunningly satisfying piece of theater, thanks to Butterworth’s incisive portrayal of a shattered family (despite the recognizable storyline), Sam Mendes’ insightful direction, a powerhouse, versatile cast (many play dual contrasting roles), and dazzling set and costume design by Rob Howell.

As noted, a plot summary will sound remarkably like such Broadway favorites as Beth Henley’s Crimes of the Heart, Tracey Letts’ August: Osage County, Brian Friel’s Dancing at Lughnasa, and even Sondheim, Styne and Laurents’ Gypsy. In rundown 1976 Blackpool, the Webb sisters reunite at the shabby family-run hotel the Seaview (where there is no view of the sea). The off-stage mother Veronica is dying in an upstairs bedroom, all of which are named for states in the far-off dream world of the US. 

Youngest daughter Jill (Helena Wilson, brilliant at desperation) has never left Veronica’s side and remains a virgin. Frustrated Ruby (endearing Ophelia Lovibond) and perpetually enraged Gloria (spectacularly shrewish Leanne Best) are trapped in unhappy marriages to alcoholic Dennis (Bryan Dick) and milquetoast Bill (Richard Short) respectively. Missing is the eldest sibling Joan (a remarkable Laura Donnelly), absent from the family for 20 years with no communication, now living in their idealized land of California. In another dramatic echo, the Webbs are like Chekhov’s Three Sisters, longing for the Golden State in America rather than Moscow.

The family’s tragic past is revealed in flashbacks to the mid-50s when Veronica (also Donnelly in a totally different characterization) maniacally drilled her girls into a close-harmony quartet, modeled on the out-of-fashion Andrews Sisters. Mendes, Howell and lighting designer Natasha Chivers accomplish the time shift through a breathtaking piece of staging involving a revolving set and teenaged actresses to play the sisters. Nancy Allsop, Nicola Turner, Sophia Ally and especially Lara McDonnell as the younger Joan deliver accomplished performances as the girls. They sharply convey the beginnings of the traits which mark their elder counterparts—Joan’s rebelliousness, Gloria’s envy, Jill’s and Ruby’s hunger for affection.

Veronica is at the latest in a long line of monster mothers, much like Mama Rose in Gypsy, Amanda Wingfield in The Glass Menagerie, and Phyllis in Paula Vogel’s Mother Play from last season. Like her dramatic predecessors, Veronica is a driven woman, determined to escape her ramshackle circumstances and the betrayal of a long-absent husband. Also like the aforementioned anti-heroines, she indulges in comfortable illusions, inventing a past (the exact details of the alleged death of her man in World War II keep changing) and banking on an unlikely future.

In an exemplary ensemble, Donnelly stands out in a remarkable dual performance. Her Veronica is a bulldozer, running down anyone who gets in the way of her dream of stardom for her daughters and willing to sacrifice anyone or anything, even one of the girls, to get the remaining three on stage. Then she makes a third-act entrance as the drugged-out adult Joan, finally arriving from America for her mother’s last moments, and she’s a completely different person, though you can see traces of the sparkling young potential star played by McDonell. Like her mother, this Joan has been through the mill, though a totally different one from Veronica. Her tired, California-inflected voice speaks of a thousand unsuccessful auditions, miles of touring with third-rate bands, and decades of disappointment.  

Director Sam Mendes juggles multiple storylines and characters so expertly that it’s always clear what’s going on, despite the thick regional British accents. The musical staging for the girls’ earnest but hopelessly amateur act is perfectly provided by choreographer Ellen Kane. Nick Powell’s sound design and original music create the appropriate nostalgic mood. In addition to those already mentioned in the cast, there is memorable work from Ta’Rea Campbell as a compassionate caregiver, Richard Lumsden as a crude piano tuner and the sisters’ long-suffering accompanist, and David Wilson Barnes as a slick agent.

Though Hills of California has echoes of many previous dysfunctional family dramas, it sings with a voice of its own and is a highlight of the new fall Broadway season.

The Hills of California *****

235 W. 44th St., NYC.

By: David Sheward

September 24, 2024: Musical theater conventions past, present and future come in for a riotous ribbing in the latest edition of Gerard Alessandrini’s perennial parody revue Forbidden Broadway. This one’s subtitled Merrily We Stole a Song and it ties in with the recent revival of Merrily We Roll Along which originally opened the same year as the first Forbidden show, 1982. This latest edition was initially announced to open on Broadway (a first for the series) at the Hayes Theatre. But those plans fell through and this compact, delightfully intimate show is snugly at home at Theater 555, way Off-Broadway, practically on the West Side Highway. Alessandrini’s satiric lyrics and smooth direction are as sharp as ever, offering a comically distorted snapshot of the current Broadway scene as well as a tribute to its past.

The program opens with a spot-on jab at tardy theatergoers set to a familiar tune. Instead “Sit Down You’re Rocking the Boat” from Guys and Dolls, an angry usher warbles “Sit Down You’re Blocking the Aisle.” Right away, Alessandrini’s piercing wit is front and center—he miraculously rhymes “shih tzu” with “jiu jitsu”—and we are off to the races.

There are lampoons of almost every show now or recently running on the Main Stem and even a few in the near future. The new Sondheim revue from London, Old Friends, offers an opportunity to poke fun at its star Bernadette Peters, magnificently mimicked by Jenny Lee Sterns, a FB veteran. She also displays impressive impressionist abilities with her hilarious turn as Patti LuPone, alternating between over-articulating and blurring her lyrics, a smug Hillary Clinton revealing in her role as a Broadway producer, and Shaina Taub, author and star of Suffs. 

Equally adept at shifting personae is Danny Hayward who transforms to all the Emcees in Cabaret—Joel Grey, Alan Cumming and Eddie Redmayne—in a wicked takedown of the current overblown revival. He also does a mean Jeremy Jourdan in a nasty take-off of The Great Gatsby which incorporates a tap number from Singin’ in the Rain. Nicole Vanessa Ortiz displays impressive pipes and range as she demolishes Audra McDonald’s upcoming Mama Rose in Gypsy, Elphaba in Wicked, and the leads in Hell’s Kitchen and & Juliet. Chris Collins-Pisano has a jolly time impersonating everyone from Cole Escola in Oh, Mary! to  Ben Platt in his Palace Theater concert to the silly, soulful lead in The Outsiders, which Alessandrini cleverly morphs into “Gee, Officer Krupke” from West Side Story.

My only caveat is the framing device of Marty McFly and Doc Emmett Brown from Back to the Future visiting Broadway’s past and future in their time-tripping DeLorean gets a bit repetitive. The reliable and versatile Fred Barton returns to tickle the ivories and act as music director in this latest fun frolicking Forbidden Broadway.

While Forbidden Broadway has been merrily chugging along for over 40 years, the musical satire genre has not had many other successful offerings, particularly of the political variety. Perhaps it’s because our current political landscape is so ridiculous (the eating of cats and dogs is now a big issue) that parody would seem redundant. The 1960s and ’70s were rife with political comedies like Barbara Garson’s MacBird, Gore Vidal’s An Evening with Richard Nixon and Peter Ustinov’s Who’s Who in Hell. The last revue tackling real-life national issues I can recall was written by Alessandrini in 2001 when he “politically corrected” and adapted Irving Berlin’s 1962 musical Mr. President to reflect the Bush-Gore election. The results were mixed. The same can be said for a new attempt at current-event comedy: Ghost of John McCain at SoHo Playhouse.

The basic idea by Grant Woods and Jason Rose, who receive a “Conceived by” credit, is intriguing. (Scott Elmegreen wrote the book and Drew Fornarola the songs.) After his death in 2018, John McCain (Jason Tam doing his best in a relatively straight role surrounding by caricatures) finds himself inside Donald Trump’s brain. The Orange One evidently can’t get the Arizona Senator and former Presidential candidate out of his mind. After encounters with Hillary Clinton, Lindsay Graham, Roy Cohn, a stand-in for Trump voters named Karen, and myriad others, McCain resolves to convince Trump to give up his authoritarian, scatter-shot ways and become a truly responsible conservative leader. Good luck with that!

The trouble is Elmegreen’s book and Fornarola’s songs push too hard and come too fast. One outlandish idea follows another in such rapid succession (Catie Davis is the speed-demon director), we scarcely have time to get the joke, let alone laugh at it. The gags and concepts are too often scattered and confusing. For example, Trump is represented by both his teenage image of himself (the energetic Lukas Kolbe Mannikus who is an able singer and dancer) and Trump’s actual brain (Aaron Michael Ray, reasonably funny). 

There are some insightful moments amid the chaos. Zoya Love does a marvelous job of delineating the alienated Trump voter Karen in Fornarola’s surprisingly moving song, “Invisible” in which the motivations behind the MAGA movement are movingly explained. Lindsay Nicole Chambers provides several incisive portraits including a justifiably enraged Hillary Clinton (her song “I Told You So” is a highlight), Trump’s bubbled-headed daughter-wife (a combination of Ivanka and Melania), and a Sexy Lady Fox News Anchor. When the latter is asked her name, she replies “It doesn’t matter.” Ben Fankhauser completes the cast with an over-the-top Lindsay Graham in black-mesh and as Joe Biden as a doddering janitor. 

Mieka Van Der Ploeg does have fun with the costumes including garments representing the COVID-19 virus, an actual brain for Trump and, for some reason, a giant dancing cheeseburger. Set designer Lawrence E. Moten III efficiently uses the small Soho Playhouse space to create the illusion of a second-rate hotel lobby. 

The point of Ghost of John McCain is that Trump’s mind is a jumbled mess, but unfortunately, so is the show, but there are some laughs to be had. Ironically and sadly, our current election season is much more absurd than the events depicted onstage.

Forbidden Broadway: Merrily We Stole a Song ****

By: Samuel L. Leiter

September 22, 2024: Nearly 20 years ago I was reading whatever I could find about theater in Sri Lanka (formerly Ceylon) as background for the two-volume Encyclopedia of Asian TheatreI was editing. Not I, though, but Sri Lankan native Neluka Siva wrote the excellent entry on that oft-suffering island nation, which resembles a large teardrop dripping from India’s southeast coast. Following occupations by Portugal in the 16th century, the Dutch in 1658, and the British in 1814, Ceylon became an independent part of the British Commonwealth in 1948, and gained complete independence, as Sri Lanka, in 1973. 

At that time, Sri Lankans spoke some combination of either English, Tamil, or Sinhala, if not all three. Language became a major political issue; it even contributed to the separatist goals of the Tamil minority, headed by the Tamil United Liberation Front. Violent conflict between the Tamil Tigers and the Sinhalese majority erupted in 1983, thousands died, and, as tensions continued over the years; as many as 200,000 Tamils fled. 

Political crises have continued to roil the nation. In fact, Sri Lanka was back in the international news this week when Marxist lawmaker Anura Kumara Dissanayake was elected president in what is considered a striking rejection of the old political guard accused of having caused the nation’s economic decline in recent years. 

I offer this bite-size background as prelude to discussing Counting and Cracking, by S. Shakthidharan, a playwright of Sri Lankan heritage born in Australia to a refugee mother. His play, while not precisely autobiographical, hints at his own experiences—much of it in terms of a chief character’s relationship with his mother—as he portrays the political and cultural world of a nation of which he was largely ignorant until, in his maturity, he sought to learn as much about it as he could. 

I wasn’t able to see Counting and Cracking until too late in its limited run to recommend a visit; had it remained longer (it closed Sunday, September 22), I’d have been advising you to get down to Greenwich Village to catch it while you can. It was at the Skirball Center for the Performing Arts, which the presenter, the Public Theater, appropriated because its expansive space is best suited for the three and a half-hour play’s epic nature, with its 16 actors and 3 onstage musicians. 

This ambitious, generation-spanning work, accompanied throughout by marvelously appealing South Asian-style music, composed by Stefan Gregory, is set mainly in Sydney, Australia, and Colombo, Sri Lanka. It tells the story—too complex to synopsize here—of a well-off Tamil family torn apart by the civil war that broke out in 1983.  The Sinhalese husband, Thirru, is detained in prison at the conflict’s onset, while his pregnant Tamil wife, Radha, who—thinking him dead—won’t know his fate for years, flees at the last minute to Australia. There, her son, Siddhartha (Shiv Palekar), is born, grows up, and becomes a college student of media studies. He falls in love with another outsider, of sorts, the indigenous Australian, Lily (Abbie Lee Lewis), while also becoming fascinated by his ethnic heritage. 

Because the play is set in 1957 (when Radha is born), 1977, 1983, and 2004, although not in that chronological order, a few characters are played by two actors, one young, the other older. Nadie Kammallaweera thus plays the mature Radha, and Radhika Mudallyar performs Young Radha, while Young Thirru is acted by Kalvalya Suvarna, and his older version by Antonythasan Jesuthasan. Occasionally, both younger and older versions of the same character are present on stage. 

As the play moves back and forth across the years, it contrasts the relatively idyllic world of pre-conflicted Sri Lanka with that of the ever more politically riven nation, where personal friends from opposite sides of the Tamil-Sinhalese divide become political enemies. Such tragic divisions become a significant thematic strain; one can’t escape feeling the relationship between such situations and what’s been happening in this country in recent years. Similarly, the play’s reflection of immigration issues pertaining to those leaving their homelands because of political persecution could not be more pertinent.

Radha’s wise grandfather, Apah (Prakash Belawadi), a mathematician who moralizes with numbers, is an important government figure, aghast to learn that English is to be replaced as the official language by Sinhala; he realizes that this will cause major social disruptions. Apah’s centrality to the outside events allows for a direct connection to and explanation of them to life inside the bustling family compound. (N.B. Online sources say that Sinhala was made the official language in 1957, which I’m unable to reconcile with what the play says.)

Director Eamon Flack, who staged the original for Sydney’s Belvoir St. Theatre, handles the sprawling action masterfully, blending numerous theatrical effects (including traditional South Asian dance) into the flow. One of the most striking images comes when Siddhartha and Lily slide rapidly toward the audience on sheets of wet blue plastic as if they’re body surfing in the ocean. Dale Ferguson, who designed the neutral space, with its green walls and gated upstage area, where street signs locate us in time and place, also did the colorfully authentic costumes. These, especially the women’s saris, add immeasurably to the visual experience, as does Damien Cooper’s lighting.  

I admit to now and then having been confused by the linguistic flux, which requires steady concentration, since the dialogue keeps shifting not only among English (mostly), Tamil, and Sinhala, but Turkish and Yolngu Matha, an indigenous tongue. Usually, someone—either another character or an actor not in the scene itself—is designated to translate, but there are moments where the give and take of the dialogue is hard to follow.

There’s no denying, however, that this is one of the best acted shows in town. Early on I was floored byKammallaweerer’s forceful maternal presence as the no-nonsense Radha, but it wasn’t long before each member of the ensemble demonstrated the kind of vocal and physical talent that makes this such a memorable production. If another actor had to be named as being hard to forget it would be Prakash Belawadi, as the indomitable patriarch Apah.

Counting and Cracking brings to mind Our Class,another fine epic show of nearly the same length, which I saw for the second time the night before, and to which a few parallels regarding clashes between different ethnicities living under the same flag might be drawn. That one is still running and you can find out more about it here.

Counting and Cracking ****1/2
Skirball Center for the Performing Arts
566 LaGuardia Place, NYC
Through September 22, 2024

By: Samuel L. Leiter

September 22, 2024: The Witness Room is a fierce, flawed, and familiar cop drama at Off Broadway’s intimate, smartly refurbished AMT Theatre, set around a table in a small, scruffy room somewhere in a New York City courthouse. Four hardnosed plainclothes officers are waiting to be individually questioned about a questionable bust they recently executed. 

Playwright Pedro Antonio Garcia, an experienced defense attorney, has crafted a work reminiscent of TV shows like “The Wire” and “Law and Order” that capture the gritty reality of how police talk and behave when under pressure by the legal system they’re sworn to uphold. Racism, misogyny, police corruption, law, religion, truth, ethics, and morality all play some part in the proceedings of this work, originally seen at L.A.’s Whitefire Theatre.

Dominated by a theme recalling the so-called blue wall of silence (a.k.a. blue code and blue shield), which demands that cops keep quiet in the face of their colleagues’ misdeeds, it wears its polemics too openly on its sleeve. It also suffers from a directorial thumb that weighs heavily on the melodramatic scale. Still, it holds your interest and, at an hour and 15 minutes (a bit longer than a TV episode), gives you something to talk about on the way to the subway.

The four, ethnically diverse, officers are the slickly dressed Italian American T.J. Moretti (Dave Baez); the African American Terrence Sampson (Moe Irvin), his shoulder holster and firearm prominent; the Irish American Kevin Brennan (Jason SweetTooth Williams), whose silhouette instantly clarifies the connection between donuts and cops; and the clean-cut Latino Eli Torres (J.D. Mollison), morally conflicted. Only Terrence is armed, the others having had their weapons checked on entering the building. The rationale for Terrence’s exception is a stretch, surely done to justify the presence of a gun where one wouldn’t normally be allowed. And, of course, as per Chekhov’s famous dictum about guns, it does its best to play its expected part. 

The sole other character is the tough-as-nails Asst. D.A. Andrea Volpi, an ambitious Italian American powerhouse serving as Bureau Chief of Narcotics, her eyes fixed on becoming District Attorney. Hearing a hint she may be gay, she slings back, “I like dick just as much as you do.”

The cops, each with blots on their escutcheons, are preparing for questioning by both Volpi and an unbending defense attorney in a hearing (not a trial) before a retired judge. They’re present to defend  their disputed actions in arresting a drug bust suspect for being armed when, in fact, he was not. Moretti, Sampson, and Brennan, typically profane bros, who casually use words like nigger and spic, are cockily assured they’ll slide through a slam-dunk hearing and soon be on their way. 

As they prepare to be interrogated under the coaching of the super-confident Volpi, they need to ensure that their stories match. The most complicated character is Eli, who’s found God, and is involved in a custody battle. He also admits to once having exceeded the proper use of force, and is teeming with guilt, making him reluctant to go along with the account of the bust being propagated by the others. This, of course, leads to vociferous personal, legalistic, and moralistic confrontations with both his fellows and Volpi, who wants to succeed no matter how the truth is twisted.

Playwright Garcia obviously knows the legal language and procedures, as well as the NYPD lingo, including the macho ways cops needle each other; there are so many specialized terms that a “legal glossary” accompanies the online program for words like “cap: person of interest,” “D-V Court: Domestic Violence Court”; “touched up: beat up someone badly,” and many more I didn’t know and don’t have room to repeat. 

Some passages seem straight out of a lawbook, as when Volpi follows a Moretti answer with: “Good. That covers the predicate for the pursuit of the defendant as you will have testified that you had reasonable and articulable suspicion to believe that a crime was occurring. . . .” Garcia can’t resist allowing his trash-talkers to soar into loftier atmospheres, especially during arguments over God’s existence, ethics, or morality, when, even with the inclusion of expletives, they sound more educated and eloquent than their circumstances or characters would indicate. 

Aside from a few off-notes, the actors sound (and look) sufficiently like NY undercover cops (as seen and heard in countless TV shows and clips). Most effective is Mollison, who invests Eli’s tortuous struggle with honesty and depth. He manages to escape the trap set for the others by Will Blum’s heavy-handed direction, which allows the actors to shout too many scenes when a more nuanced approach might have deepened the play’s naturalism. Worse, his sometimes inelegant staging has the actors frequently speaking their dialogue not to each other but directly to the audience; I sometimes wondered what it was on the invisible fourth wall that so often demanded their attention.  

Daniel Allen’s set, one corner of which is piled to the ceiling with file boxes, efficiently captures, with the help of Aiden Bezark’s lighting, the little room’s grungy atmosphere. The costumes, by Gina Ruiz, look right, from Volpi’s pantsuit to Officer Brennan’s baseball cap and t-shirt. 

I should record that at the preview I attended the show was stopped midway through because of some unexplained technical glitch. The actors were asked to leave the stage until it was fixed, several minutes later. It was the second time this week this happened at a show I was watching, the first being at Table 17, as reported in my review, where the actors remained in place, giggling throughout.

There are a few giggles in The Witness Room but, for the most part, it’s a dark look at the way our legal system works, with truth being secondary to concerns that have little to do with justice. Imperfect as Pedro Antonion Garcia’s play is, though, it’s probably more truthful than one would like to admit.

The Witness Room ***1/2
AMT Theatre
354 W. 45th Street, NYC
Through October 6, 2024

September 19, 2024: [Note: In January of this year Theater Life posted my ***** review of Our Class, a Polish play by Tadeusz Slobodzniak directed by Igor Golyak at BAM’s Fisher/Fisher Space. The same basic production is now at the Classic Stage Company’s Lynn F. Angelson Theater. At the Fisher/Fishman, the audience sat on a sizable bleacher structure facing the production head on in traditional end-stage fashion. At the far smaller CSC, the acting area is standard three-quarters round, bringing the action much closer to the audience. Golyak’s staging has therefore made various changes, even using a high corner of the audience area opposite the stage for some business. 

However, seeing the play in this intimate format (I sat on one of the sides) only served to make Golyak’s incessantly inventive direction more prominent. Even more than in January, it privileges the show’s artistic ingenuity over its emotional impact. Also, the intense efforts of the talented actors—who wear the same adult costumes throughout, even when playing children—to seem natural within this highly theatricalized aesthetic, can appear artificial under such close-up scrutiny. Finally, despite the energetic pacing, the show’s three hours now feel overlong, the play’s dramatic heart dissipated by its epic, years-spanning, multi-focus structure. Accordingly, I’m giving this revival of Our Class an appreciative **** instead of a shining *****. 

Since so much else remains the same, I’m reposting a slightly edited version of my original review below. A few new comments have been added in parentheses.]

January 22, 2024: Just a little more than a week ago I reviewed the Broadway production of Josh Harmon’s Prayer for the French Republic, a searing drama about contemporary anti-Semitism in France, with a subplot set during the German occupation of Paris. My very next theatre visit was to see Polish playwright Tadeusz Słobodzniak’s Our Class, a similarly devastating work about anti-Semitism in pre-war, wartime, and postwar Poland. With the striking rise in attacks on Jews here and abroad, not to mention the war between Israel and Hamas, in which millions of people are supporting the instigators, plays like these couldn’t be timelier, even if they’re equally depressing. 

First performed in 2009, Our Class has had several international and American productions, all staged in creatively theatrical ways. The present one, adapted by Norman Allyn from a literal translation by Catherine Grovesnor, is in the deftly capable hands of Ukrainian-born director Igor Golyak, founder of the Boston area’s Arlekin Players Theatre, under whose banner the play is produced.

As an online note suggests, “Our Class is an exploration of humanity, an effort to comprehend who we are, who we can become, and how we might heal or and live together with some meaning.” Such optimistic statements often accompany plays of this nature; in reality, though, few pay any attention and, by and large, hatred continues too frequently to trump community.

Słobodzniak’s play is centered on an actual historical tragedy, the 1941 mass murder by arson of hundreds of Jews (perhaps 1,600) in the village of Jedwabne. What happened has been debated, since it was claimed that responsibility lay with the Nazis, while research in a 2001 book which became the play’s inspiration declared that Polish Catholics, the very neighbors of the victims, were the evil perpetrators. Despite formal apologies to Poland’s Jews (most of them liquidated) by Polish leaders, the Polish government again prefers to blame the Nazis. 

Regardless, the play demonstrates what happened to the survivors, including the aftermath of marriage between a converted Jew and a Catholic, attempted retribution against former classmate by a Jew-turned-Israeli, aging, illness, and death, not to mention the bitter irony of Poles with blood on their hands being recognized for their righteousness in saving Jews.

Our Class is told through the interactions of 10 classmates of the 1930s, five Jews and five Catholic Poles, seven men and three women. We see, through their relationships over the years, how what begins as childish teasing becomes mortally lethal when social and political pressures—the Soviet invasion followed by the Germans—incite more violent forms of expression, among them the vicious murder of a classmate (Stephen Ochsner) and the gang rape of another (Gus Birney). This, while the group ironically continues to consider its bond as “classmates” as strong as, if not stronger than, family.

Issues of guilt, remorse, responsibility, revenge, and the like pursue the living through the years, much of it revealed through the letters (seen here as video segments) between the sole Jew, Abram (Richard Topol, in a heartfelt performance), to have left Poland for America, where he became a rabbi, to his classmates. (Topol, reportedly, will be playing Shylock in a forthcoming production with this company of The Merchant of Venice, directed by Golyak at the CSC.)

The excellent actors, ranging in age from their twenties to their early sixties, establish their characters’ aging—those who live long enough—through movement and gesture. Sasha Ageeva’s simple yet characteristic costumes also contribute greatly. Several actors hail from Eastern Europe, as noted by their accents. The actors are Gus Birney, Andrey Burkovskiy, José Espinosa, Tess Goldwyn (whose movie star dad, Tony, was in the house at the CSC production), Will Manning, Stephen Ochsner, Alexandra Silber, Richard Topol, Ilia Volok, and Elan Zafir.

In a manner that flows easily back and forth between dialogue and direct address (sometimes in the same speech), and with occasional infusions of song and dance, they present the story, covering 1925 to 2003, in a manner that ignores the fourth wall, suggesting both docudrama and story theatre. Sometimes they briefly interact with people in the audience. 

The atmosphere is that of a classroom, augmented by each of the 15 scenes being called a “lesson,” its number both being announced when the scene begins and written in chalk (with the year or years it represents) on the towering, multifunctional blackboard (set by Jan Pappelbaum) that backs the stage. A tall, shiny, much-used, aluminum ladder leans against it. “Offstage” actors remain visible while waiting for their cues. 

With its frequent recourse to videography, both prerecorded and live, including actors shown recording what we see on either a standard TV screen or on the blackboard, the style is distinctly reminiscent of Dutch director Ivo van Hove’s. (It also struck me as both anachronistic and intrusive.) Our Class’s emphasis on instructing the audience via artistic jeux rather than realistically recreating the story—enhanced by the deliberately self-conscious, ominously shadow-casting, white lighting of Adam Silverman—evokes a decidedly Brechtian affect. 

For example, the hundreds of Jews callously burned to death by their neighbors are depicted by helium-filled balloons with weighted strings on which cartoon faces have been drawn by the cast. As a result, its innately powerful narrative of the horrific events that occurred before, during, and after the conflagration becomes more cerebrally engrossing than emotionally overwhelming. You recognize and shrink from the experience while aesthetically distanced from its impact on your emotional core; at least, that was my response. 

Our Class is a work to see, and, if not to savor, then definitely to remember. 

Our Class ****
Classic Stage Company (CSC)
136 E. 13th Street, NYC
Through November 3, 2024

September 18, 2024: Table 17, a slight, charming, if mostly familiar rom-com by Douglas Lyons (Chicken and Biscuits) at MCC Theater is proof positive that even the frothiest of plays can be spun into theatrical pleasure (if not gold) with the right combination of acting, directing, and design. 

With part of the audience seated at illuminated cabaret tables in the forestage area, and a clever unit set provided with a platform that thrusts into this space, Table 17 allows for considerable fourth wall breaking. That includes when each partner in the romantic duo at its heart turns to the audience for feedback and moral support. Direct address monologues are frequent, both from the leads and the supporting characters, providing amusing exposition and allowing the characters to explain their feelings, the sentences cast in colorful African American rhythms and expressions. 

The basic situation concerns the on-again, off-again love affair of stylishly sexy air hostess Jada, played with broad comic panache by Kara Young, and tall, handsome songwriter Dallas, her earnest but work-distracted ex-fiancé, who thinks he’s ultra-cool. Biko Eisen-Martin (Soft) portrays him with leading man appeal. Young, who won a Tony last season for Purlie Victorious, continues to demonstrate her enormous well of comic and emotional vivacity, her face, voice, and movements capturing every nuance of Jada, a woman in love with her own hotness yet uncertain of her hold on the man she loves. 

After several years together, culminating in Dallas’s proposal, the couple broke up two years ago. The flashbacks and monologues show us what happened; little of it, I must report, is especially novel. But Dallas, unable to get Jada out of his dreams, although he has reason enough to ignore them, invites her out to see if the fires can be rekindled. They meet for dinner and drinks at Bianca’s restaurant, where they always sat at Table 17 on what Jada calls their “date-a-versary.” 

As the promise of rapprochement hovers, flashbacks inform us of how they met, fell in love, broke up, and, despite still being in love with each other, hooked up with different people. Table 17 asks the eternal question: will they or won’t they try again? Given what we’ve learned, the lesson is that love can be both unpredictable and messy.

As I assume is true of Lyons’s influences, which he acknowledges in his script to be the “classic Black films” Love & Basketball, Love Jones, and Poetic Justice, this roller coaster relationship requires the support of colorful minor characters. In Table 17 there are three, all played by the awesomely versatile Michael Rishawn (Ain’t No Mo), his head shaved apart from a thatch of braided locks on top. Rishawn projects chameleon-like alchemy as he enacts the snippily waspish, loose-wristed, gay head waiter, River; the nameless, lithe, supremely self-confident, lady-killing bartender; and the cockily assertive, flirtatious, basketball-loving flight attendant, Eric, a co-crew member with a jones for Jada.   

Jason Sherwood’s attractive set displays a rear wall adorned with liquor bottles, its three compartments convertible to different backgrounds, the center one able to open for deeper upstage action. Devario D. Simmons offers spot-on costumes, whether it be to highlight River’s stereotypical flamboyance with silver-sequined sneakers, or to give the diminutive Young a panoply of sexy looks, even when all she’s wearing is denim short shorts, high heels, and a buttoned silk blouse allowed to casually hang loose on one side. Nikiya Mathis provides Young with a striking, blond-streaked wig she tosses about with perfect flair. 

Ben Stanton lights the play with taste, although the night I went something blew, forcing the action to stop, and the stage manager to ask for our patience. Meanwhile, the actors, especially Young, struggled to keep straight faces as they froze in place; fortunately, the direct address-style of the play enhanced rather than destroyed the moment. And when the tech issue was fixed, the stage manager’s miked voice got a huge laugh when she drily instructed the actors to resume from “If you say that shit one more time.”

Director Zhailon Levingston (Tina: The Tina Turner Musical) keeps the play moving with spirit and élan, and is particularly good at inducing memorably crafted comedic performances. By: David Sheward

September 17, 2024: In recent years, the romantic comedy genre has had several hits on screen, but few on stage. The musical version of Pretty Woman and the original First Date had short runs. Defying this trend, Douglas Lyons’ non-musical Table 17 at MCC Theater’s Off-Broadway space is currently packing in audiences and might make the leap to a commercial run. Lyons’ only previous Broadway playwriting credit is the sitcom-ish Chicken and Biscuits, but Table 17 is a deeper and more satisfying dish.

The premise sounds a bit too close to numerous TV tropes. Exes Jada and Dallas are getting together two years after their painful breakup. Is their dinner rendezvous a date? A civil reunion? A settling of old scores? Thanks to Lyons’ sensitive insight and the layered acting of Tony winner Kara Young and Biko Eisen-Martin as Jada and Dallas and Michael Rishawn as all the other male characters, this three-hander goes far beyond the expected easy yucks and delivers a moving and truly funny, not just silly, map of the rocky road to love.

Before the play starts, the audience gets the idea they are in for something different. A portion of the attendees are seated at tables in Jason Sherwood’s clever set, creating both a swank eatery and a theater setting. The program includes a menu with features a note from the author to feel free to speak up and offer advice to the characters when it is solicited. After the lights dim, Young as Jada is discovered modeling an outlandish outfit for her encounter with Dallas (Devario D. Simmons created the stylish and fun costumes.) She asks the audience for their thoughts on her attire and if it’s the right look for meeting an ex-lover. This ploy could come across as a gimmick, but Lyons wisely uses it sparingly so that it draws the theatergoers into the story without overwhelming it. He mixes direct address to the audience with dialogue scenes skillfully, sometimes switching from one to there in seconds to comic effect. Zhailon Levingston’s rapid-fire direction and Ben Stanton’s quick-change lighting combine for dazzling hilarity.

Lyons takes his basic set-up—the preparations for the meeting, then the “date” itself at a popular restaurant and a final resolution to the relationship—and manages to stretch this potentially thin outing to 90 minutes without appearing to pad his storyline. There are numerous flashbacks to Jada and Dallas’ first meeting, moving in together and bumps in their relationship as Dallas pursues a music producing career while working as an auto mechanic and Jada feels neglected. She eventually turns to her attractive co-worker Eric for solace which precipitates the break-up. By the play’s ambiguous conclusion (no spoilers here), we feel we know these two. There are plenty of sharp laughs along the way, but they never dominate the proceedings. 

All three performers are exemplary in juggling the lighter and darker moments. Young again demonstrates her prodigious comic flair which she exhibited with such élan in last season’s revival of Purlie Victorious. Her Jada does not take any nonsense, but she has a hard time when called on her own. Young captures her brittle wit as well as her vulnerability. Eisen-Martin holds his own, conveying the conflicted emotions of Dallas, simultaneously pulling back from and being drawn to Jada. Rishawn completes the ensemble perfectly, displaying versatility as attitude-dripping host-server River, Jada’s amorous colleague Eric, and a macho bartender. It’s important to note that Rishawn could have made the gay River into a swishy stereotype, but Lyons didn’t write him that way and Rishawn avoids playing him like that. He has as many romantic needs as the principals. In this and his savvy depiction of Jada and Dallas’s tumultuous relationship, Lyons and company go beyond rom-com to a believable portrait of modern dating and connections. The playwright, director, and cast have cooked up a filling and tasty meal.

By: Paulanne Simmons

September 15, 2024: Becoming a parent can certainly change your life. Children can make life rewarding or, let’s say, challenging. Written by real-life Mom and Dad team, Graham and Kristina Fuller, and directed by Jen Wineman, That Parenting Musical chronicles the ups and downs of parenthood in twenty-four songs and one reprise.

The songs are held together and introduced by the Narrator (Brian Owen) and performed by Mom (McKenna OGrudnik), Dad (Dwayne Washington), Single Friend (Natalie Bourgeois), Child 1 (Max Crumm) and Child 2 (Vidushi Goyal ). They have titles any parent can relate to: “Babysitter Shuffle,” “Date Night,” “A Little Bit of Space.” They all have singable melodies in a variety of genres, from rock to Gilbert and Sullivan’s operettas.

As evidenced by the generic nature of the characters, the musical doesn’t get into many specifics. This is probably intentional. But somewhere in the middle of the first act many in the audience may be searching for something more. We all know about the trials and tribulations of parenthood. What we want to learn is what makes these people special, aside from their having nice voices.

There is a plot, of sorts. Mom and Dad have two children, one quickly following the other. They also have a single friend. The kids grow up. The parents grow tired. The friend gets a boyfriend. The humor is broad. How do you pee in an airport bathroom while holding an infant?

There’s something clownish about the entire production, from the acting to the costumes (by Tina McCartney). Wineman keeps the scenes moving along at a frenetic pace, which might not be a bad thing, considering how little they are trying to convey.

The Parenting Musical should really be called That Parenting Musical Revue. Even so, it should have far fewer songs and fewer singers. At 30 minutes it might be fun. As a full-fledged two-act, it becomes pretty boring.

By: Paulanne Simmons

September 15, 2024: Vocalist Susan Gregory is no stranger to one-woman shows. But while her previous shows have been largely autobiographical, her newest one proudly announces “It’s Not About Me.” In fact, this show has a song list that ranges from Stephen Sondheim to Bob Dylan and Jerry Herman to Phil Everly. There’s even a song by longtime friend, Jeffrey Stock: “Somewhere Between Your Place and Mine,” about a failed New York City uptown/downtown relationship.

Other songs such as Bob Dylan’s “Make You Feel My Love,” Harold Arlen and Ira Gershwin’s “The Man that Got Away” and Phil Everly’s “When Will I Be Loved” are also about finding that special someone. And with Kander and Ebb’s “Ring Them Bells” (accompanied by the band jingling those little instruments at appropriate moments) Gregrory addressed the subject with a lighter touch.

But Gregory’s repertoire included Joni Mitchell’s “Both Sides Now,” George Jackson and Thomas Earl Jones III’s “Old Time Rock and Roll” and Stephen Sondheim’s “Not While I’m Around,” as well. From the playful to the poignant, Gregory knows how to fully capture the moment, emotionally and vocally.

It’s Not About Me may not have been autobiographical, but it did include some very personal stories, such as one about a fellow Yale graduate who ended up living in a tent in California, until he was rescued by another Yale graduate; and another about a friend’s long search for a partner.

Gregory has a masterful control of her voice and her material. With Michael Schiralli as her director and Daryl Kojak as her musical director and backed by a substantial band on the Triad’s small stage, Gregory made ample display of all those skills.

“It’s Not About Me” has something for everyone, whether you’re into Broadway or rock ‘n’ roll, uplifting stories or funny anecdotes. Gregory captures the mood and your heart.

It’s Not About Me *****

By: David Sheward

September 12, 2024: The Roommate, Jen Silverman’s slight two-character comedy at the Booth, begins in an unusual way. After the house lights have dimmed, the play’s stars Mia Farrow and Patti LuPone enter. Their names and a photo of them are projected on Bob Crowley’s sprawling farmhouse set. They acknowledge the audience’s applause, exit, and then re-enter in character to start the show. This tactic may just be a decision on director Jack O’Brien’s part to get the star factor out of the way and allow us to concentrate on the play at hand, but this blatant celebrity intro is an inadvertent acknowledge of the production’s raison d’être. We’re here to see two big names in rare circumstances—this is one of Farrow’s few stage appearances and an infrequent non-musical outing for LuPone, particularly after she very publicly renounced her Equity membership. Silverman’s play is a secondary consideration.

The Roommate itself is a flimsy effort derived from a familiar template. Two mismatched mature women, each seeking a new start after a crisis, are thrown together in a confined setting—in this case Crowley’s rambling, void-of-personal-details Iowa abode. One is retiring and shy (Farrow’s Sharon), the other eccentric, risk-taking, somewhat mysterious (LuPone’s Robyn). LuPone unbelievably has driven all the way from NYC, the Bronx to be specific, to share Farrow’s Midwestern home. Presumably they met through an Internet ad. Sharon has “retired” from her marriage. The cryptic Robyn appears to be on the run from an unspecified shady past. There is the inevitable pot-smoking scene, wherein weed virgin Sharon lets her hair down. 

The formula is tried but not so true with the ladies, after some forced comedy about eating habits and estrangement from their respective grown children, bonding to become fast friends. John Ford Noonan’s A Coupla White Chicks Sitting Around Talking applied this trope with more skill as did David Auburn in his much stronger Summer, 1976 two seasons ago. 

Predictably, the mousy Sharon breaks out of her conventional shell and finds Robyn’s unconventional habits attractive. Robyn is gay, vegan, grows marijuana, and refuses to conform to sexual or social labels. Without revealing any spoilers, we eventually learn the true nature of Robyn’s shadowy background and it further entices the curious, thrill-hungry Sharon. As expected, the conflict arises when Sharon goes too far into Robyn’s sketchy domain and Robyn backs off. 

One particular scene exemplifies the play’s unrealized potential for insight and commentary. The formerly staid Sharon, now deeply into Robyn’s sphere of borderline nefarious activities, proudly displays a new AR-15 rifle she picked up with no hassles at the local Walmart. Robyn is freaked out and demands she take it back. Not only does Silverman break Chekhov’s Gun Rule—never display a firearm unless someone on stage is going to use it—but she fails to develop the issues raised by Sharon’s purchase. Sharon speaks of the seductiveness of owning a powerful weapon while Robyn, used to dealing with danger, sees only tragedy. The magnetic pull of firearms and the horrific rift they cause in our current political scene are barely touched on. Sharon puts the gun away and promises to return it. The two late-in-life characters, their roles in the larger society and how it treats them, are similarly shortchanged. Crowley’s skeletal set also has little evidence of either woman’s life or interests. But his character-suggesting costumes offer clues as to their backstory as does Natasha Katz’s evocative lighting and David Yazbek’s warm, rich original music.

Despite the slimness of Silverman’s script, her stars, directed with economy and precision by O’Brien, do their best to beef up their scrawny roles. Farrow delightfully conveys Sharon’s slow blossoming as she invents fanciful scenarios to flesh out her fantasies. Her relish at creating a life beyond the vast midwestern spaces is infectious. LuPone has less to work with since Robyn reveals less of her inner life and motivations for her not-quite-legal background. But she endows her character with a rich subtext, hinting at her past through sly smiles and a far-away mistiness in her eyes. Her look of regret and fear when Farrow hovers around the edges of peril suggests an untold narrative informing her reserve. There are hints of depth in LuPone’s Robyn. Too bad Silverman fails to deliver them.

The Roommate **1/2

By: David Sheward

August 19, 2024: A truly unique theatrical experience is hard to come by these days, even if the Drama Desk Awards do have a category for it. If you searching for an event that you wouldn’t get anywhere else, the best place is the Sheen Center for Thought and Culture in the East Village where Odd Man Out, a total immersive production in pitch darkness, is playing. Originally presented in Buenos Aires, Argentina, this 90-minute drama employs all the senses but sight and totally engages the audience.

The script by Martin Bandone is entertaining enough, recounting the tumultuous life of Alberto, a blind jazz musician. But the main attraction here is the direction by Bandone, Facundo Bogarin, and Carlos Armesto and the bombardment of the senses.

We begin in the lobby of the Sheen Center which laid out to resemble an airport lounge (Tyler Herald is credited with “Environmental Design,” which I assume includes the detailed setting to make us think we are at JFK ready for take-off.) After phones and watches are silenced and stowed, attendees are lead into the playing pitch-black playing space. Drinks and snacks are handed out and our fellow passengers are Alberto and his rowmates the boisterous Christian, ready for camaraderie, and Julieta, fresh off a divorce and equally ready for a kind word and a story.

With a little prodding, Alberto spins his tale. Flashbacks take us from the passenger cabin to village of Alberto’s youth. Mainly through sounds and smells, we experiences his run-ins with the authoritarian Argentine government, his romance with Clara, a valorous social worker and his pursuit of a career in the US. The resolution is a mite melodramatic and Christian’s run-ins with a bossy stewardess are forced comedy relief, but the sensations provided are memorable and sometimes stunning. When Alberto is arrested while attending a protest, his torturous treatment is brought shockingly alive with the sounds of waterboarding. His childhood home is summoned up through the smells of tangerines. We are splashed lightly with water as he frocks with Clara in a neighborhood stream. 

The vocal performances of Pablo Drutman, Carmen Borla, Agustina Cedraschi, Bree Klauser, Andrés Montejo, Lorenza Bernasconi, and Mauricio Marte add depth to this unforgettable experience.

Odd Man Out ****
July 8—Aug. 24. Pitch Black Immersive Experiences in association with Radio Drama Network at Sheen Center for Thought and Culture, 18 Bleecker St., NYC. Running time: 90 minutes with no intermission.

By: Samuel L. Leiter

August 16, 2024: It’s been only eight and a half years since New York’s last revival of Once Upon a Mattress,the goofy 1959 musical comedy retelling of Hans Christian Andersen’s children’s story, “The Princess and the Pea,” which opened at Off Broadway’s Phoenix Theatre, moved to Broadway soon after for 244 performances, and made a star of Carol Burnett as the ugly duckling, wannabe bride, Princess Winnifred (who goes by “Fred”). The show, seen in an Encores! revival, starring Sutton Foster, this past January was apparently so well received it’s now running at Broadway’s Hudson Theatre. Chacun son goût. 

Comedienne Jackie Hoffman, of the bespectacled sad sack punim, was (even at 55) a funny Winifred in the 2015 revival at the Abrams Arts Center; she also delivered the musical goods. With Sutton Foster (The Music Man), the new production stars one of Broadway’s most celebrated, multitalented musical stars, who not only has first-class comic and vocal chops, but dancing ones to match. Her performance aside (mostly), though, the production—directed by Lear deBessonet (Into the Woods)—pushes too hard to rake in the laughs. 

Once Upon a Mattress has music by Mary Rodgers, a book by Jay Thompson, Marshal Barer, and Dean Fuller, and lyrics by Marshal Barer; the script has been newly adapted by Amy Sherman-Palladino (TV’s “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel), although not to notably great effect. It belongs to the category of fairy tale-like musicals set in medieval worlds (like Camelot, A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court, Into the Woods, Cinderella, Pippin, Spamalot, Shrek, and so on). 

In a pea shell, it introduces the ultra-controlling Queen Aggravain (Anna Gasteyer, Wicked), whose husband, King Sextimus the Silent (David Patrick Kelly), has been turned mute by a curse, and can communicate only with gestures. Anxious to retain her power, Aggravain does all she can to prevent her naïve, intimidated son, Prince Dauntless (Michael Urie, Spamalot), from getting married, which means no one else in the kingdom can marry either. The situation is especially dire for the beautiful Lady Larken (Nikki Renée Daniels) and her vain swain, the handsome Sir Harry (Will Chase), because she’s pregnant. 

The queen’s impossible tests have caused 13 eligible princesses to fail in their quest to marry the prince. About a half hour into the show, the surprise appearance of a new contender, the gawky, funny-looking, brash, and openhearted Princess Winifred—soaking wet and covered with leaches after swimming the castle moat—unsettles the domineering queen. She now must find a trial to foil this unexpected claimant, who wins Dauntless’s love when she sings of “The Swamps of Home.” Ultimately, 20 mattresses are piled high and a pea is stashed at its bottom to test Fred’s royal sensitivity. If the pea fails to keep Fred awake, the marriage is off. Need I say more?

Like Spamalot, Once Upon a Mattress has a single, overarching purpose—to rock the theater with laughter. But even the talented company assembled here can do little more than to garner the kind of politely amused reaction one gives when one knows how hard the performers are trying to be funny. The fact is that Once Upon a Mattress, whatever it once may have been, is not as amusing as it wants to be. Much of it, indeed, is childish and silly, dependent more on the actors’ ability to turn broad, farcical shtick from comic dross to gold. Lacking the necessary alchemy, the humor rarely surpasses superficiality.

deBessonet’s direction keeps things lively, and her company of 20 and onstage orchestra of 17 work hard at having fun, but the stakes remain too juvenile—especially for anyone familiar with the show—to overcome. For me, Foster is the big takeaway, even when I was appreciating her capers more for their technical expertise than for their ability to stir my laugh muscles. A highlight, for instance, is the acrobatic sequence of contortions she does when trying to find a comfortable position atop the piled-up mattresses. Admirable? Yes. Hilarious? Not really. 

And, like Hoffman before her, when, after swimming the filthy moat, she belts out the show’s most memorable number, “Shy,” her ear-splitting zest contradicting her outrageous exuberance on the title word, you’ll wish you’d brought along your ear plugs. Michael Urie, whose comic genius has been displayed unforgettably in such works as The Government Inspector and Spamalot, has a few laugh-worthy moments, like when he plays up Dauntless’s fear even of bounding up steps (he crawls, step by step), but otherwise is forced to exaggerate with vocal and facial mugging.

The biggest show stealer in 2015 was the renowned drag artist John Epperson a.k.a. Lypsinka as the queen, but Anna Gasteyer, who practically shouts the role, falls short. Neither Brooks Ashmanskas as the fey, bumbling Wizard, nor Daniel Breaker as the supercilious Jester (whose soft-shoe routine, “Very Soft Shoes,” remains as extraneous as ever), break much comic ice, but the elfin, white-bearded Daniel Patrick Kelly is a pleasantly enjoyable presence as the silent king.

Despite the lack of any songs that have become standards, the score—with its 1950s Broadway sound—is generally entertaining, more so than many highly touted recent shows. It retains much of the comical brio that’s made the show a perennial favorite among school and amateur groups. That may partly be because, while sex plays a role, the dialogue and lyrics avoid smuttiness, even in the ingenious “Man to Man Talk” number, in which the mute king, communicating with gestures, teaches his dufus son the facts of life. The book, however, has too many minor diversions, and—the lyrics apart—there’s not enough wit to sustain what is, after all, a rather innocuous narrative for a grown-up audience. 

David Zinn’s unit set features a crenelated upstage wall above which the orchestra is seen playing before a cyclorama whose colors often change under the magic touch of lighting genius Justin Townsend. Columns and vertical banners establish the period and downstage units come on and off as needed, without extravagant elements. Andrea Hood’s bright costumes are suitably fairy tale-ish, although the Jester, dressed like a vaudevillian in a shiny red suit and bowler, seems at odds with his castmates.  

The two-hour and 15-minute run time is a bit shorter than that of the 2015 revival, but it still seems long for what’s little more than a blown-up bedtime story. Anyone interested in seeing Carol Burnett’s original performance (and her later ones, including a turn as the queen) can visit YouTube, where other versions reside as well. But even if Sutton Foster could replicate Burnett’s star-making performance, the show would still seem dated on the Broadway stage of 2024. Once Upon a Mattress has proved its value for amateur groups; I suggest that’s where it should remain. 

Once Upon a Mattress ***
Hudson Theatre, 141 W. 44th St., NYC.

By: David Sheward

August 15, 2024: Once Upon a Mattress, the delightful fairy-tale musical, has always been a thin affair. Basically a revue sketch stretched to a full evening, its success has depended on the talents of its leading lady and director. The book by Jay Thompson, Marshall Barer and Dean Fuller takes the story of The Princess and the Pea, gives it a slightly adult spin and adds tangential material for supporting players. The songs by Mary Rodgers and Barer are catchy and sweet, some in the character-building manner of Rodgers’ fabled father Richard. If you have the right cast and director, it can be a pleasant, joyful time. The original 1959 production provided a launching pad for the phenomenal career of Carol Burnett and her persona as an overly enthusiastic, man-hungry, gawky but lovable clown. There were three successful TV adaptations (two with Burnett as the lead and one with her as the nasty Queen), but two major NYC revivals failed to soar because Sarah Jessica Parker (1996) and Jackie Hoffman (2015) were not the right fit.

The new streamlined staging by Lear deBessonet with script revisions by Amy Sherman-Palladino at the Hudson after an Encores! run, benefits from the presence of the sublime Sutton Foster who here proves she can do just about any musical comedy role in the modern canon. Having previously taken on the suppressed librarian Marian in The Music Man and the brassy showgirl-evangelist Reno Sweeney in Anything Goes and made them her own despite memories of Barbara Cooke and Ethel Merman, Sutton does the same for Princess Winnifred the Woebegone. She pays tribute to Burnett’s knock-about style, but adds touches of her own with hilariously inventive business from deBessonet who also found new life in another fairy-tale show Into the Woods.

Take Winnifred’s first entrance. This is an important part of the show as it introduces the star and establishes her character. Foster crawls over the castle wall (behind which the orchestra is seated on a raised platform) and emerges bedraggled and disheveled in Andrea Hood’s cleverly cluttered costume, having just swam the moat. She then proceeds to pull leeches, swamp flora, and various live critters from her bare shoulders, hair and dress, flinging some into the audience. She does all these actions while kidding herself and fawning over the kingdom’s elite, trying to make a good impression. She moves like a wrestler or an acrobat, ready to pounce or embrace in her eagerness to please. She lets us know a ton about Winnifred’s character and objectives while wringing belly laughs out of deBessonet’s staging. That’s not to mention what she does later in the show with a bowl of grapes or the infamous mile-high mountain of mattresses. She also puts across Winifred’s torch number, “Happily Ever After” and her novelty spot “The Swamps of Home” like an expert batter scoring two home runs. Sutton is sublime.

Her so-star Michael Urie is almost as inventive and expressive as the arrested-development adolescent Prince Dauntless, the object of Winnifred’s martial quest. He makes the Prince’s cluelessness about the birds and the bees into a driving force for the character’s objective: discovering the truth about sex. This makes the riotously funny “Man to Man Talk” duet with his mute father, the king (marvelous mime David Patrick Kelly) into a breakthrough moment. He also has a physical bit defining Dauntless’ struggles. He make mounting a series of steep stairs into a battle to prove his burgeoning manhood. When he finally ascends without a misstep, the audience bursts into applause.

Danutless’s domineering mother, the overbearing Queen Aggravain is made into a comic bulldozer of maternal suffocation by the hilariously bullying Ana Gasteyer. deBessonet gives further subtext and detail to the Queen by transforming the “Sensitivity” comedy number into a beauty spa treatment for the obsequious wizard (magnificent Brooks Ashmanskas) to apply to her demanding Majesty. Ashmanskas gives Gasteyer a massage, a foot run, offers a pep pill, and paints her nails all while important information is dispensed.

In Sherman-Palladino’s tightened new book, the role of the narrating Minstrel is folded into the Jester, played with a deft touch by Daniel Breaker who gets to lead the talented chorus in “Very Soft Shoes,” choreographer Lorin Latarro’s sparkling tribute to Bob Fosse’s “I Wanna Be a Dancing Man.” Latarro also supplies appropriately goofy, off-kilter steps for the frantic “Spanish Panic” and additional zany numbers. Will Chase and Nikki Renee Daniels give the secondary pair of lovers, Sir Harry and Lady Larkin the right sharp satiric edges to prevent them from becoming gooey stereotypes. Their two duets “In a Little While” and “Yesterday I Loved You” are impressively and sweetly sung.

In additional to all these splendid elements, David Zinn’s cartoonish sets, Hood’s wacky costumes, Bruce Coughlin’s rich orchestrations, and Mary-Mitchell Campbell’s expert music supervision make this the downiest and comfiest Mattress an audience ever rested their weary, laughing heads on.

If you have the right cast and director, it can be a pleasant, joyful time. The original 1959 production provided a launching pad for the phenomenal career of Carol Burnett and her persona as an overly enthusiastic, man-hungry, gawky but lovable clown. There were three successful TV adaptations (two with Burnett as the lead and one with her as the nasty Queen), but two major NYC revivals failed to soar because Sarah Jessica Parker (1996) and Jackie Hoffman (2015) were not the right fit.
