By: Samuel L. Leiter

August 8, 2024: On the night I saw Catherine Gropper’s political mishmash, The Meeting: The Interpreter, at Off Broadway’s Theatre at St. Clement’s, a single male voice in the sparsely occupied auditorium shouted “Bravo!” during the curtain calls. I know it was intended for the artists, but it could just as well have been for those of us who sat politely throughout its 80 minutes of sheer dramaturgic and directorial malpractice without sneaking out for an early trip home. 

This strangely double-titled play is inspired by a subject with potential dramatic punch: a notorious, if now largely forgotten, 20-minute meeting held at Trump Tower in June 2016, involving a non-English – speaking Russian lawyer, Natalia Veselnitskaya,  Donald Trump, Jr., Paul Manafort, and Jared Kushner, as well as a Russian-American lobbyist, a British publicist, and a Russian-American interpreter. (Gropper was inspired to write the play after a serendipitous meeting with the latter.) Weirdly, the program says “any resemblance to actual people and events is purely coincidental.” If so, why would anyone be even slightly interested in this balderdash?

Later investigations (including by Congress) sought to uncover the purpose of the meeting, which was ostensibly to deal with American adoption of Russian children, but involved ways to dig up dirt on Trump’s presidential rival, Hillary Clinton. It also covered the Magnitsky Act, named for a Russian dissident who died in a Moscow prison, which sanctions foreign governments for human rights abuses. The meeting, discussed in the so-called Mueller Report, has been considered an example of the Trump team colluding with Russia to bolster its campaign. 

If you’re interested in the meeting’s nitty gritty, you can find it here; you’ll certainly not learn about it from Gropper’s play. If you don’t already know the facts, and even if you do, your head will spin from how the playwright and her director, Brian Mertes, have deconstructed the material. Their telling encompasses the event through the eyes of the innocuous Russian-born interpreter (Frank Wood) as he’s interviewed by a journalist—presumably a mask for Gropper herself—played by Kelly Curran. She also plays numerous other roles, male and female; as I gradually lost interest, I couldn’t tell one from the other.

Broken down into a series of scenes often punctuated by the actors snapping their fingers or banging on a table to indicate ellipses in time, the play veers from courtroom-hearing docudrama, with the proceedings read straight from transcripts (including both the dialogue and technical trivia printed on the visibly redacted pages) to intimate conversations. The dialogue ranges from normal speech to passages delivered by Curran (impressively) at Mach speed, so fast it’s impossible to follow.

In a manner recalling the Wooster Group and the productions of Ivo van Hove, a video camera operator (Tatiana Stolpovskaya), sitting on a dolly running on metal rails, is pushed very slowly around the acting area by another crew member; meanwhile, a third crew member spools and unspools cable, as the action is recorded, often in extreme closeups, everything being visible on a large screen occupying the audience right side of the stage. 

Projection designer Yana Biryukova also provides an opening credit sequence that plays like the start of a movie. The play ends with a seemingly endless information crawl about the fates of the people involved in the meeting (including one not even in the play), with a concluding comment on the Magnitsky Act’s international ubiquity. Given the play’s flippantly theatrical, thoroughly confusing treatment of the Trump Tower meeting, this straight-faced, if often banal “Epilogue” makes little sense.

Nor do the frequently bizarre bits of behavior, including an extended dance routine (choreographed by Orlando Pabotoy) to spacey music composed by Daniel Baker & Co., or a scene of the interpreter lying on the floor playing with a pail of sand, or his slowly peeling off the plastic film pasted to a glass booth in which the actors sometimes speak, etc. and so forth. And then there are Julian Crouch’s deliberately crude, papier maché puppets representing certain characters, most represented only by the puppets’ heads talking to one another.

Jim Findlay has designed a neutral, indeterminate space, Barbara Samuels has lit it well enough, and Olivera Gajic has costumed the actors efficiently. Frank Wood, a Tony winner for Side Man, and Kelly Curran, best known as the lady’s maid, Turner, on TV’s “The Gilded Age,” are to be commended for giving their best to this fruitless effort. However, I wouldn’t go quite so far as to shout “bravo!” for anything connected with The Meeting: The Interpreter.

By: Isa Goldberg

August 4, 2024: The conflict at the heart of Max Wolf Friedlich’s two-hander, Job, is not only who gets fired and/or does the firing, but also between real and somatic experience, between what is conscious and conscionable, and what is not. 

A period piece, set in the 2020s, the story delves into the generational clash that is always present and threatens destruction. Just as it was in 429BC when Sophocles wrote Oedipus.

Arriving for her session with the company-appointed psychologist Lloyd (Peter Friedman), Jane’s (Sydney Lemmon) hysterical behavior is overly precocious and very dangerous. Because she’s here to talk about her job – cruising social media for problem issues, threats, and crimes – she provides Lloyd, as well as the audience, with an entire stock of phantasms culled from her workday.

It is not she alone actually. Most of this work is done by bots, computer programs, but what she identifies can only be found by a human. After describing the horrific murder of a child by mutilation, Jane talks about “red rooms – someone being tortured live on webcam. Horses fucking women…mass graves, heroin overdoses, a website for strep throat fetishists.” She goes on, describing the events that are driving her crazy.

Acting out at her job is what got her here. And only a note from the psychologist clearing her crazy behaviors, captured in a video that has now gone viral, will allow her to continue. But since she introduces herself to him with literally murderous intent – including an ultimatum no one could refuse – it’s clear that no matter how he chooses, there cannot possibly be a moral outcome. And, if you’re looking through the eyes of twenty-something Jane, there would be no way this hippy-dippy shrink can arrive at a moral outcome anyway. That is why her strategy is clean.

Having seen the production Off Broadway at The Connelly Theater last season, it’s impressive to see how the actors have grown in their roles.  Speaking somewhat quietly, mostly to himself, Friedman’s earlier work looked like one imagines a Stanislavsky trained actor actually would. His acting was more personal, as though for himself. Watching him now, his character is adamant and determined, not someone easily challenged.

Lemmon, too, has grounded her work, clearly coping with a well of inner panic that wants to control her. In her earlier performance it almost did, but here she engineers her inner fears to shield herself, to seek release. In her mind, she believes her role as a User Care specialist makes her kind of a savior, a hero to those who need help.

Fortunately, in disclosing herself, she proves that the talking cure can work – it’s calming, confidence-building. And it invites honesty.  Finally confiding to her sixty-something therapist, she quips, “Hippies were white kids from the suburbs who came out here to take drugs and fuck with impunity and now they’re pissed something productive is replacing their 50-year-long drum circle.”

There is no doubt that she has it in for him. Conceivably her issues are valid, evidentiary even. But Lloyd maintains, “I do wonder what would happen – crazy idea here – if you stopped attacking me and listened a bit.”

Sensitively directed by Michael Herwitz, the action is perpetrated by sound effects – buzz saw, pornography – and accompanying lighting effects, like a seismic activity running through the conversation. At times, possibly due to such obstreperous interferences, each of the characters leaves reality, as though they are leaving the room and entering their psyche. 

For instance, Lloyd has a reverie in which he remembers his father rebuking him as a teenager, and the rage it caused him. In another, Lloyd dons a horrible mask. While the two are standing there in silence, the audience shares Jane’s perception of him.

Interestingly, the sound effects (Cody Spencer), along with original music by Devonte Hynes, create the social phenomenology of this period piece. Car bombs and orgasms are equally present and public, and confusing to the conversation. And Hynes’ music importantly claims classical roots, before diving into a variety of pop styles.

But unlike the musical gymnast Hynes, neither of the characters on the stage can budge. Given their unyielding positions, there is only impasse, and no exit. Scott Penner’s scenic design provides a large picture framed window for a ceiling, but neither actor ascends.

Jane puts it bluntly, “Any idiot can canvass for Bernie, but if they actually wanted to do something – like to the degree they claimed – they’d kill their parents and redistribute the inheritance.”

In a certain way, it all clicks.

By: Samuel L. Leiter

August 2, 2024: Job, a two-hander by Max Wolf Friedlich, has had a peripatetic history since it premiered last September at Off Broadway’s SoHo Playhouse (where I first saw it). It was resuscitated at the Connolly Theatre, also Off Broadway, and, finally, ended up for a limited run at Broadway’s intimate Helen Hayes Theater, although not under the auspices of that theater’s resident company, Second Stage. Its actors, distinguished veteran Peter Friedman (TV’s “Succession”) and Sidney Lemmon, the late Jack Lemmon’s granddaughter, in her New York debut, have been with it all along, as have most others on the creative team.

Job—a title referencing employment, not the word’s heteronymic Bible story—begins like a thriller, with a young woman, Jane, pointing a pistol across the stage at a much older man. Several unclear moments pass during which things happen and then are reset so they can be viewed otherwise; finally, the frightened man, Loyd, persuades the disturbed woman to put the weapon aside. About 70 minutes later, it reappears shortly before the play ends, indeterminably. 

In between, Loyd, a San Francisco therapist with one ear displaying a diamond stud, engages Jane, who seems embarrassed by her threatening behavior, in a therapy-like session during which he seeks to calm her down and explore her troubled, but sharply intelligent mind. She, in turn, skeptical about therapeutic practice, sometimes turns the tables and gives him the third degree. Her goal, she insists, is to have him sign papers agreeing she’s psychologically capable of returning to the unusual, internet-related job from which she’s been suspended, and which she says she loves, after it led to her having a public breakdown that’s been recorded and gone viral. Given why she’s here, it seems reasonable to assume Loyd already had been informed of what Jane did for a living; that, however, would spoil the scene where she describes the job.

Given Jane’s stressed-out mental state—there are allusions to Xanax, self-harm, and panic attacks—and Loyd’s vulnerability in view of what is really a hostage situation, the garrulous, wide-ranging session (including topics like racism, technology, gentrification, hippiedom, abortion, etc.) seeks to create intellectual and psychological tension. Whatever suspense is generated, though, is more the result of Friedman and Lemmon’s acting chops, his frazzled nerves, as he anxiously takes notes, being set against her dodgy intensity, veering from vulnerable to dangerous. Gradually, we discover her hidden agenda and why the play opens with her pointing a loaded pistol at this presumably benign shrink.

Eventually, we learn that Jane’s eponymous job at a Bay Area office concerns the internet’s most harmful corners. Her job, called either “user care” or “content moderation,” is to monitor and erase images of the worst excesses of human behavior; the horrible things she sees are traumatizing yet clearly in need of a concerned individual to eradicate them. Despite the truly awful videos to which she’s been exposed, which would likely drive anyone nuts, one particular series has gotten so deeply under her skin she’s decided to do something about it. (Question: do freelance companies exist to do such content moderation for businesses unable to do the job themselves?)

Friedlich’s play questions the damage done by our phones and computers to our psychological wellbeing, if not to the social fabric itself. Thus, what passes for a session between a troubled woman and a probing therapist has a valid thematic purpose; however, apart from its topical pertinence, the playwright uses this subject more for its sensationalistic triggers than to seriously explore the limits of censorship and free expression.

Job now seems less plausible than at its first viewing, even before it reaches its the-butler-did-it type conclusion. Of course, just because the dramatic setup is artificial from start to finish doesn’t mean the play might still not be able to provide a gripping 80 minutes in the theater. Numerous thrillers succeed despite the most contrived circumstances. But while Job certainly has its nail-biting moments, the more apparent its improbabilities become, the more it sheds the credibility needed to suspend disbelief.

Scott Penner’s scenic design retains the essence of the Off-Broadway versions, a therapist’s office represented by little more than a pair of facing club chairs set before a black background, supplemented by a few decorative items, with ceiling molding outlining the black, overhead space. Screen-like rectangles, placed here and there on the black background, light up at designated moments (Mextly Couzin did the lights), accompanied by sound created by Cody Spencer and offbeat music by Devonté Hynes. It’s not clear if these sequences are intended to emphasize Jane’s discombobulated state of mind, or to question Loyd’s veracity, but they tend to draw attention to themselves more than they do to heighten the suspense.

Regardless of its melodramatics, Job—reminiscent of the Gabriel Byrne series, “In Treatment” or Steve Carrell’s “The Patient”—provides its fine actors with lots of histrionic opportunities. Michael Herwitz’s taut direction keeps the drama simmering, allowing the actors to perform in a rapid-fire, naturalistic, conversational style underlined, because of Jane’s always shifting volatility, by a sense of peril. 

Both actors—costumed in ordinary street clothes by Michelle J. Li—have notably deepened their earlier performances. Friedman is pitch-perfect as the cautious but professionally inquisitive therapist, struggling to keep his calm, subdue his fear, and resolve the situation without doing anything foolish. The lanky Lemmon, her short hair pinned back, offers a twitchy, intelligent performance as the quirky analysand; speaking with hyped-up rapidity, sometimes almost mumbling, she keeps us wondering just how unbalanced she is, and why. The reasons may be unconvincing, but she’s fully invested in believing them. Each actor also succeeds in sparking laughs with their occasionally ironic lines.

Job doesn’t quite do the job as a play, but enough drama remains in Friedman and Lemmon’s performances to satisfy most theatergoers. And when could be better to see a chiller—even a moderately cool one—than the good old summertime?

Job ***

240 W. 44th Street, NYC
Through October 27, 2024

content.rendered:
By: David Sheward

August 1, 2024: Who says opera and operetta can’t be fun? The Glimmerglass Festival in Cooperstown, NY, opened its 2024 season with two lighthearted productions, Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Pirates of Penzance (1879) and Francesco Cavalli’s La Calisto (1651), both featuring inventive staging, magnificent voices, and lots of frivolity.

Pirates has been a perennial favorite not only of G&S aficionados, but of general audiences as well thanks to a smashing Broadway revival in 1981 starring Linda Ronstadt, Kevin Kline, George Rose, Rex Smith, and Estelle Parsons which ran for 787 performances and was filmed with the original cast (save for Angela Lansbury replacing Parsons.) There will be a production presented by Roundabout Theatre Company in spring 2025, marking the 27th Broadway staging. If the Roundabout version is anywhere nearly as delightful as director-choreographer Sean Curran’s edition (originally presented by Opera Theater of Saint Louis), New York City audiences are in for a rare treat.

Curran takes the right bemused, whimsical approach to the material which, as most G&S works do, satirizes 19th century melodrama and British class distinctions. Conductor Joseph Colaneri and the Glimmerglass orchestra produce a lush and warm interpretation of Sullivan’s classic music and the cast ably delivers Gilbert’s intricate lyrics. I only had to consult the supertitles above the stage a few times in the second act. 

Troy Cook is a rapid-fire wonder, rattling off the tongue-twisting patter song for Major-General Stanley and creating a cunning caricature of English authority. Craig Irvin punctures the Pirate King’s pomposity with a thrilling baritone. Eve Gigliotti is a marvelously conniving Ruth, the pirate maid scheming for, but being thwarted in her search for love. Christian Mark Gibbs and Elizabeth Sutphen are hilariously saccharine as the young lovers Frederic and Mabel, displaying rich vocals and investing the roles with parodistic humor. Too often, these roles are overshadowed by the more comic supporting players, but these two are on a par with the entire company.  

The chorus of pirates is closer to the Lost Boys of Peter Pan than the stereotypical cutthroats associated with seafaring swashbucklers. (One chorister even wears glasses and a top hat, and carries a teddy bear, reminiscent of Wendy’s brothers.) The policemen of the second act, led by a comically quivering Joshua Thomas as the Sergeant, move like mechanized penguins and the young ladies are a wonderfully individualized group of flighty debutantes, all are ably coordinated by chorus director Katharine Kozak. James Schuette’s outlandish sets and costumes are appropriately cartoonish.

In a brilliant stroke, Curran interjects a deadpan Queen Victoria (a comically stone faced Mary-Jo Merk) to deliver the denouement for a rousing finale to this perfect Pirates.

Cavalli’s rarely performed La Calisto is almost as frothy as Glimmerglass’s G&S offering. The silly plot recalls the woodland, supernatural hijinks of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. In disguise as the goddess Diana, the randy god Jove changes genders and seduces the nymph Calisto, a virginal follower of Diana. Jove’s jealous wife Juno descends to earth to wreak her vengeance while the mortal shepherd Endymion pursues the real Diana and nymphs and satyrs indulge in frolicsome carnal play. The story is forgettable so the emphasis in Mo Zhou’s well-paced production is on enjoying the superb music (beautifully conducted by Ron Ainsley) and voices. Eric Sean Fogel’s sensual choreography adds to the sexual spice of the proceedings.

Pirates cast members Craig Irvin and Eve Gigliotti show their versatility with powerful renditions of the lusty Jove and outraged Juno. Emilie Kealani displays a silky soprano range as the innocent Calisto, ascending to celestial heights as she is transformed into a star at the opera’s climax. Schuyler Vargas has the right mischievous, randy glint and dark tones as Jove’s lecherous henchman Mercury. Taylor Raven skillfully embodies both the chaste Diana and the amorous Jove in disguise. Costume designer Carlos Soto cleverly differentiates between the two in the garments for the dual characterization, adding war-like touches to Diana’s diaphanous drapery.  

Counter tenor Kyle Sanchez Tingzon sustained Endymon’s difficult notes while Winona Martin gave a sharp comic spin to the young nymph Linfea (Soto went with a contemporary style for her costume, giving her Auntie Mame-ish lounging pajamas. She was also equipped with a modern long cigarette holder, wielded to humors effect.) Amanda Sheriff was an impish satyr, vying for Linfea’s affections.

Calisto’s sexual politics reflect both a 17th century and 21st view of gender roles. Callisto can enjoy physical pleasure when Jove is transformed into a woman, yet she is also a victim of the male god’s lust and his wife Juno’s wraith. Juno casts a spell on the poor girl, turing her into a bear. But Jove redeems her by making her a starry being once the bear transformation wears off. As noted, the ridiculous story is not the main point of this production which is to display the magnificent voices and Cavalli’s sublime music.  

Alice Busch Opera Theater, Glimmerglass Festival, 7300 NY-80, Cooperstown, NY. www.glimmerglass.org.

By: David Sheward

July 30, 2024: The play starts with a bang—well, not literally. After being bombarded with high-decibel rock music before the lights dim, the audience is confronted with two characters, one wielding a gun pointed at the cringing other. There follows a series of short false beginnings with the target responding in a number of different ways to the threat, separated by quick blackouts. When the action finally settles down, Max Wolf Friedlich’s psychological thriller Job, now at Broadway’s Hayes Theater after successful Off-Brodway runs at the SoHo Playhouse and the Connelly Theater last season, is gripping and thoughtful examination of our data-driven, over-informed world.

The central action at first appears to be a confrontation between Jane, a Gen Z techie (the gun-wielder, an intense Sydney Lemmon) and Loyd, a crisis counselor (a thoughtful and nuanced Peter Friedman). Jane is desperate to be reinstated in her position at an unnamed web giant after a workplace meltdown that has gone viral and made her an unwilling Internet sensation. Loyd has been assigned to give her a psychological evaluation and deliver a thumbs up or down to her return. Gradually, once the gun is put away in Jane’s bag, we learn the details of her breakdown and the surprising nature of her occupation. Without revealing any spoilers, the script is eventually flipped, all our expectations are reversed and Friedlich delivers a shocking twist ending to 80 minutes of taut suspense.

There are a few flaws in Friedlich’s construction. It’s hard to believe Loyd would be able to conduct a constructive therapy session with the threat of a loaded firearm and the conclusion (which I will not reveal) is bit too tidy. But, the dialogue is sharp, funny and insightful, full of piercing observations on our screen obsessed society. Jane makes several smart points on the pearl-clutching of anti-tech elders (“People do bad things, not phones.”) She even challenges the whole premise of therapy and rejects the need for it. Loyd hits right back with a spirited defense of his profession, his hippie generation’s idealism and its own brand of anti-establishment rebellion. 

Director Michel Herwitz skillfully builds the tension between the antagonists, employing Mextly Couzin’s computer-inspired lighting and Cody Spencer’s jarring sound design to simulate the broken connections in Jane’s frazzled psyche. (Scott Penner designed the set which at once conveys Loyd’s 1960s sensibilities and Jane’s warped perceptions.) Lemmon and Friedman are the perfect pair for this scary round of mind games. Lemmon endows Jane with a fierce intellect and determination, but also displays her fractured self-image and insecurities. Friedman starts as a compassionate healer under the gun (literally) but he subtly exposes the cracks in the character’s gentle facade till both doctor and patient are fully exposed.

Beyond its thriller template, Job is a fascinating portrait of the powerful impact the omnipresent internet has on our delicate global community and what can happen when the worst of human impulses become nothing more than click-bait. See it and be shocked by the ending.

240 W. 44th St., NYC.

Jeff Harnar sings Sammy Cahn The Second Time Around

By: Alix Cohen

July 29, 2024: Had Jeff Harnar come up in the forties and fifties, he would’ve been a boy singer with Goodman or Dorsey, appeared at The Paramount, made radio appearances, played sophisticated nightclubs and recorded on vinyl. Fan clubs would’ve formed. The vocalist personifies our golden age of American Songbook with respect for and appreciation of lyrics, keeping even creative arrangements true to songwriter intention. Long may he thrive.

Twenty-five years ago, Harnar and Alex Rybeck’s Sammy Cahn salute was recorded for Jerome Records which prematurely shut its doors. This iteration has been rearranged (for a new CD) with new tracks, several duets, and some pronoun changes

Sammy Cahn (1913-1993) neé Samuel Cohen (no relation) put more words into the mouth of Frank Sinatra than any other lyricist. In addition to hit parade songs, he wrote for films and musicals garnering 26 Academy Award nominations, four Oscars, and an Emmy. 

Harnar begins off stage with “All the Way” (music James Van Heusen). It’s a Rainbow Room foxtrot. Marc Phaneuf ‘s sax adds sheen. These are not just words. The vocalist is earnest. “Teach Me Tonight”- do-do-ten-do-do-do, he sings flirting. Eyebrows rise and fall. Every “teach me” lands differently as befits hope, request, suggestion. Resonant bass (Steve Doyle) winks. Rybeck offers harmony.

The title song is performed reflecting, remembering; eliciting complicity. “It makes you think, perhaps…” He nods.  “That love like youth…” A wistful smile hovers. “Is wasted on the young.” (music James Van Heusen) “I fall in Love Too Easily” emerges slowly, like an admission. The hushed tune builds-sax, then bass (Steve Doyle)  then piano. Brushed cymbals (Ray Manchica who later excels on bongos) evoke rustling leaves. Brow furrowed, Harnar sighs. The 1944 song hasn’t aged. (music & lyrics-Jule Styne/Sammy Cahn)

Guest Eric Comstock, co-creator and star of the long running My Sinatra, duets on a tandem “Come Dance With Me”/“I Like to Lead When I Dance.” (music James Van Heusen) Animated, Comstock dances around his friend (since college) conducting air. Voices blend. The jaunty number arrives by way of dapper, first rate vocalists having an infectiously good time. 

“I’ll Only Miss Him When I Think of Him” (in 2017, the vocalist sang “her”) and “Call Me Irresponsible” are interpreted as cha-chas. Rhythm causes chair dancing. Harnar’s heart is in his throat. (music James Van Heusen) An appealing World War II medley (music by Jule Styne) is bathed in nostalgia for an era before that of the artist. We all sing the last verse of “It’s Been a Long, Long Time.”

Guest Sally Mayes duets “Come Fly With Me” (music James Van Heusen). Also, old friends, the performers symbiotically swing. Mayes urbanely scats up a storm. Lyrics skibble, skip and twirl. Harnar looks at her not just appreciatively, but proud. Even the band is grinning. Musically: accomplished. Outlook: carefree. Experience: fun. 

Sill wrapped in high spirits, we’re treated- like a cherry on top- to an inspired arrangement of “Bei Mir Bist Do Schon” (Means That You’re Grand) in English, Yiddish and, wait for it-Swahili, native language of Moipei. The triplets have personality, polish, and virtuoso skill with harmony. Collaboration is euphoric. More please. (music Shalom Secunda)

“As much as I loved this song at 40, tomorrow I’ll be 65, and it means so much more” introduces “Time After Time” (music Jule Styne) Piano ripples like a quiet brook. Flute touches melody like light. The artist’s tender phrasing is very much his own.

Musicianship is superb. As always, multifaceted contributions by Alex Rybeck are priceless. The show is a substantial taste of the wonderful Cahn replete with selective anecdotes, joy of presentation, and Jeff Harnar’s unequivocal talent.

Caveats: Two songs from the musical Skyscraper don’t weigh in with the quality of other selections and, aside from a song updated to the 1950s, Harnar’s falsetto sounds out of place.
